By causing beings born in various world-systems to hear the name of the Buddha, one inspires faith in them and causes them to be reborn in world-systems where they are never separated from him.
Regarding the meaning of "yoga," there is this verse:
"And he indeed becomes capable of maturing sentient beings, just like a bird whose wings have fully grown."
He receives excessive praise from the Buddha and his speech becomes authoritative for all beings.
He demonstrates a threefold yoga:
the yoga of the power to mature sentient beings, the yoga of praise, and the yoga of having speech that is accepted.
This verse is undertaken for the purpose of explaining the commentary.
The sixfold supernormal knowledges, the threefold sciences, the eight liberations, as well as the eight bases of mastery,
the ten totalities, and the immeasurable concentrations— such is the power belonging to the steadfast.
The power of a bodhisattva operates through six distinctions:

the distinctions of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the sciences (*vidyā*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and the immeasurable meditative concentrations (*apramāṇasamādhi*).
Having thus shown power by means of these six points characterized by their classification, there is a verse intended to manifest its greatness.
For he, having attained a mind of supreme mastery, constantly brings the world—which is otherwise powerless—under his own control;
delighting solely in accomplishing the welfare of others, the wise one indeed moves through the realms of existence with the great fortitude of a lion.
It demonstrates a threefold greatness:

the greatness of mastery, because by attaining mastery over supreme knowledge oneself, one establishes the world—which is otherwise not under its own control due to the afflictions—under one's own control;
and the greatness of delight, because one always finds sole joy in performing what benefits others.
And the majesty of fearlessness regarding existence.
This is the seventh chapter on Power in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
The eighth chapter [begins].
A verse on the gathering [of beings] for the maturation of Bodhisattvas:

Delight, serene faith, tranquility, compassion, patience, as well as intelligence, strength, and being fully endowed with the limbs that are unshakable—these are the characteristics of the maturation of a Son of the Conqueror. (MSA 8.1)
Delight in the Dharma taught in the Mahāyāna, serene faith in its teacher, tranquility regarding the afflictions, compassion for sentient beings,
patience in the performance of difficult practices, intelligence in grasping, retaining, and penetrating [the teachings], strength in realization, and being unshakable.
Being endowed with the factors of striving against Māra and the proponents of other doctrines;
"intensely" indicates the excellence of zeal and the other qualities.
In brief, this ninefold maturation of oneself by Bodhisattvas should be understood.
Regarding the maturation of zeal, there is this verse:

"The triad beginning with good friendship, fierce vigor, the ultimate excellence for the sake of others, and the gathering of the supreme Dharma—this is considered the characteristic of correct maturation for a compassionate one in the great undertaking of the True Dharma. (MSA 8.2)
The triad beginning with friendliness consists of attending upon virtuous persons, hearing the true Dharma, and proper mental attention.
Intense vigor is the undertaking of supreme effort.
Reaching the ultimate limit for the sake of others is the state of being free from doubt regarding all inconceivable points.
The "gathering of the supreme Dharma" is the protection of the Mahāyāna Dharma, because it protects those who have entered upon it from calamities.
With reference to the Bodhisattva’s appropriation of the Mahāyāna Dharma, this should be understood as the characteristic of the maturation of inclination;
that by which one matures is through the triad beginning with having good friends.
Its maturation is a nature endowed with fierce vigor and reaching the ultimate limit;
its activity consists in effecting the gathering of the supreme Dharma—this is what has been elucidated by this [verse].
Now follows a verse concerning the maturation of serene faith (*prasāda*).

Knowledge of virtues, the swift attainment of meditative concentration, the experience of the fruit, and the non-differentiation of the mind—these are considered the characteristics of perfect maturation for the sake of full realization toward the Son of the Conqueror and the Teacher. (AMsa 8.3)
That maturation is also elucidated in terms of its cause (*kāraṇa*), its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and its function (*karman*).
"Knowledge of qualities" (*guṇajñatā*) refers to the cause, explained in detail as "the Blessed One is a Tathāgata," and so forth.
Its intrinsic nature is the state of an unshakable mind resulting from the attainment of power after having understood [the truth].
The function [of this stage] is the swift attainment of meditative concentration and the personal experience of its fruits, such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Regarding the maturation of tranquility (*praśama*), there is this verse:
"There is excellent restraint, the avoidance of afflicted discursive thoughts (*kliṣṭa-vitarka*), the absence of obstacles, and a delight in what is wholesome."
For that intention, directed toward the Son of the Conqueror for the sake of dispelling afflictions, indeed possesses the characteristic of complete maturation.
The pacification of a bodhisattva is the removal of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Its maturation is also elucidated by way of its cause, its intrinsic nature, and its function.
The cause is the thorough restraint of the sense faculties through mindfulness and clear comprehension.
The nature [of this state] is the avoidance of afflicted discursive thoughts;
its function consists in being free from interruption during the cultivation of the antidotes and in delighting in what is wholesome.
Regarding the characteristic of the maturation of compassion, there is this verse:

Compassion by nature, the perception of the suffering of others, the complete abandonment of a base mind, the attainment of distinction, and being born as the foremost in the world— these are the characteristics of the maturation of supreme empathy for others.
The cause is that [the mind] matures by means of its own nature, its lineage, the perception of the suffering of others, and the avoidance of the inferior vehicle.
Its essential nature (*svabhāva*) is the tendency toward excellence, because it proceeds toward the increase of maturation.
Its activity (*karman*) is the possession of a physical existence (*ātmabhāva*) superior to all the world on the stage of non-retrogression (*avinivartanīya-bhūmi*).
Regarding the characteristics of the maturation of patience, there is this verse:

Fortitude by nature, cultivation through analytical reflection, the constant endurance of extreme suffering such as cold and so forth, the state of progressing toward excellence, and delighting in the wholesome—these are considered the characteristics of the maturation of patience. (AMsa 8.6)

Fortitude (*dhṛti*), endurance (*sahana*), and patience (*kṣānti*) are synonyms. Their maturation has as its causes the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*), and meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the patient acceptance of intense sufferings such as cold and the like.
Its function (*karma*) is the progression toward excellence for one who is patient and a delight in what is wholesome (*kuśala*).
Regarding the maturation of intelligence (*medhā*), there is this verse:

The purity of ripening, the non-forgetfulness of what has been heard and so forth, as well as penetration into the well-spoken and the ill-spoken; and the fitness for the arising of great wisdom and for mindfulness—these are the characteristics of the maturation of excellent intelligence. (MSA 8.7)
In this context, the cause is the purity of maturation that is conducive to intelligence (*medhā*).

The nature of the maturation of intelligence consists in the non-forgetfulness of what has been heard, reflected upon, cultivated, long ago performed, or long ago spoken, as well as the thorough penetration of the meaning of both well-spoken and ill-spoken words.
Its function is the capacity for the arising of supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-prajñā*).
Regarding the maturation that consists in the attainment of power, there is this verse:
Through the two kinds of merit, there is the nourishment of the two elements; at the arising of the fruit, there is supreme fitness of the basis.
The fulfillment of one's aspirations and the state of being the foremost in the world—these are the characteristics of maturation in the attainment of power. (AMsa 8.8)
In this context, the nourishment of the seeds of that twofold merit and wisdom by means of the twofold merit and wisdom is the cause for their maturation.
The nature of that maturation is the fitness of the basis (*āśraya*) with respect to realization.
Its function is the fulfillment of one's aspirations and the state of being the foremost in the world.
Regarding the maturation of being unshakable, there is this verse:

The intention to investigate the correct nature through reasoning, the attainment of excellence, the refutation of opposing positions, and furthermore, the constant absence of obstacles from Māra—this is the characteristic of the maturation of being unshakable. (MSA 8.9)
The cause for that maturation is the intention formed by investigating the true Dharma through reasoning;
its essential nature is the absence of Māra’s interference, which occurs when Māra is no longer able to create an obstacle.
The attainment of distinction and the refutation of opposing positions constitute its function.
Regarding the maturation of the endowment with the factors of exertion, there is this verse:
"The accumulation of merit, the fitness of the basis for effort, seclusion, and delighting in the sublime virtues."
For it is held that the characteristic of perfect maturation consists in the son of the Conqueror being endowed with the [spiritual] factors.
The cause for its maturation is the accumulation of roots of virtue;
its intrinsic nature is the fitness of the basis to initiate vigor;
and its function is the excellence of seclusion and delight in the wholesome.
A verse concerning the majesty of the ninefold maturation of the self:
Thus, when the self has been matured in these nine ways, it attains the fitness for maturing others;
with its nature constantly increased by virtuous qualities, it becomes forever the foremost kinsman of the world. (AMsa 8.11)
That greatness is twofold:
being a refuge for the ripening of others,
and the constant increase of the Dharma-body.
Therefore, regarding the supreme kinsman of the world,
there are eleven verses on the classification of the ripening of sentient beings:
Just as ripening is recognized in both a wound and in food, according to their respective fitness for draining and for consumption;
Likewise, in this basis, there is the tranquility of the two sides; and likewise, there is the state of being well-peaceful through the aspect of enjoyment.
By this, he demonstrates the nature of maturation:
just as the ripening of a wound is its fitness for draining,
and the ripening of food is its fitness for consumption.

Thus, in the case of sentient beings, upon the basis— which is comparable to a wound and its food— the pacification of opposing factors is comparable to the draining [of pus], and the enjoyment of the remedies is comparable to the enjoyment of [nutritious] provisions;
the maturation of the basis consists in its becoming fit for these.
In this context, the two sides should be understood as the adverse factors (*vipakṣa*) and their remedies (*pratipakṣa*).
The second verse states:
"There is ripening (*vipācana*), likewise full ripening (*paripācanā*), further ripening (*prapācanā*), and another, continuous ripening (*anupācanā*)."
Among embodied beings, it is considered to be well-maturing, further maturing, bringing to maturity, and producing maturity.
By this, he shows the classification of maturation:
maturing through the removal of afflictions is *vipācanā*;
maturing by means of all three vehicles in every respect is *paripācanā*.
Because it is distinguished by the ripening of others, it is "superior ripening" (*prapācanā*).
Because it teaches the Dharma according to those to be trained, it is "conformable ripening" (*anupācanā*). Because it ripens with respect, it is "thorough ripening" (*supācanā*).
Maturation through realization is *adhipācanā*, in the sense of being non-erroneous;
constant maturation is *nipācanā*, in the sense of being irreversible;
and gradual maturation, proceeding higher and higher, is *utpācanā*.
Thus, this is the eightfold classification of the ripening of others.
The third and fourth verses [state]:
"Just as the Son of the Victor is established here with an intention for the welfare of the entire world, ripening it..."
Likewise, neither mother, nor father, nor kinsmen are firmly established even toward their own children or relatives.

Likewise, ordinary people are not considered as affectionate toward themselves as a compassionate being is toward other sentient beings who are dear to them; for the latter seeks to establish those others in welfare and happiness as if they were his own self.
What does he show by these two?
He shows the kind of intention with which a bodhisattva brings sentient beings to maturity—
an intention superior to that of parents and relatives, and superior to the worldly self-cherishing, because it joins them with benefit and happiness.
The world, however, being fond of itself, applies itself to its own welfare and happiness.
With the remaining verses, he demonstrates by means of the practice of the perfections (*pāramitā*) the method through which one brings sentient beings to maturity.
The following verse concerns the kind of giving by which one brings sentient beings to maturity.

There is nothing whatsoever that a bodhisattva cannot give away to others, whether it be his own body or his possessions. Maturing others through these two kinds of assistance, he is never satiated by the equal virtues of giving.
He brings others to maturity through three kinds of giving:
by the giving of all one's possessions, body, and enjoyments; by impartial giving; and by insatiable giving.
How does he bring them to maturity? By providing assistance in both the present life and future lives.
Because he fulfills their wishes by not causing them harm,
and because he gathers them through future [benefits] by establishing them in the wholesome;
regarding the kind of ethical discipline with which he ripens sentient beings and how he does so, there is this verse:
Always by nature supremely non-violent, himself delighting in this and being vigilant, he establishes others in it;
performing benefit for others in two ways, he matures them through the qualities of both maturation and natural outflow.
By means of fivefold morality:
constant morality, natural morality, and perfect morality, because of being exceedingly non-violent;
for one who is perfectly non-violent is "exceedingly non-violent" (*adhyavihiṃsaka*).
He has fulfilled the ten paths of wholesome action,
as described in the second bhūmi;
he possesses the morality of realization through his own delight [in it], and through his vigilance, he possesses a morality that is uninterrupted and unerring.
And how does one bring them to maturity? By establishing them in ethical discipline through two kinds of beneficial action.
In both the present life and the future life,
it brings about benefit for others in the future through the qualities of its maturation (*vipāka*) and outflow (*niṣyanda*) in a continuous succession;
this is because there is no interruption between those two, as their maturation and outflow are mutually compatible.
Regarding the kind of patience with which he brings sentient beings to maturity, there is this verse:
Possessing the perception of benefit toward others who act harmfully, he endures even severe transgression;
through skillful means and thoughts that endure such injury, he leads those who cause harm to engage in virtue. (AMsa 8.18)
One ripens others through the patience that endures severe harm by perceiving the harmer as a benefactor.
Furthermore, this state of perceiving them as benefactors should be understood as a mode of conduct conducive to the fulfillment of the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).
How does one ripen them?
Because he endures harm through favoring them in this present life,
and because he favors them in future lives, the one who knows the means wins over those who cause him harm by establishing them in virtue through those very acts of enduring harm.
Regarding the kind of vigor with which he brings sentient beings to maturity, there is this verse:

Furthermore, relying upon supreme effort, the Son of the Conqueror does not grow weary even over billions of eons as he brings the multitude of sentient beings to maturity for the sake of a single virtuous thought of others.
Through vigor characterized by tirelessness over an extremely long period, there is tirelessness over a long time because of maturing infinite sentient beings;
for the sake of even a single virtuous thought in another, one does not grow weary for billions of trillions of eons.
Thus, it is explained how one brings others to maturity.

Because he establishes them in wholesome states, he benefits them both in this life and in future lives. Regarding the manner in which he ripens sentient beings through such meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), there is this verse:
Having attained unsurpassed mastery over the mind, he draws others toward this supreme teaching;
having destroyed all desire for contempt, he causes them to flourish once more through virtue. (AMsa 8.20)
He brings them to maturity through meditation that has attained unsurpassed mastery and is free from worldly desire, having destroyed all longing for contempt.
He brings them to maturity by attracting others to the Buddha’s teaching and, once attracted, by increasing their wholesome qualities.
Regarding the kind of wisdom with which he brings sentient beings to maturity and the manner in which he does so, there is this verse:
Being well-ascertained in the system of the meaning of the true nature of reality, he makes sentient beings free from doubt;
and consequently, through that teaching of the Victor, they cause themselves and others to flourish with auspicious virtues.
That bodhisattva brings them to maturity through wisdom that is well-ascertained regarding both the method of ultimate reality and the method of intentional meaning.
How does he bring them to maturity? By removing the doubts of sentient beings;
and because of their resulting great respect for the teaching, by acting as one who increases the virtues of both themselves and others.
The verse on discipline:

Thus, out of compassion, that Bodhisattva disciplines the entire world—whether it has reached a happy rebirth or possesses the three types of virtue—by means of mild, supreme, and intermediate methods, through a course of conduct identical to that of the world. *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* 8.22.
By this [compassion], he guides the entire world toward the attainment of happy rebirths or the three vehicles;
he guides it by means of compassion.
And by explaining who the bodhisattva is that disciplines others, by what kinds of methods of ripening— whether mild, supreme, or middling—
and for how long a time, he demonstrates, in brief, the majesty of ripening.

In this regard, the "slight" degree [of ripening] for a bodhisattva on the stage of practice through aspiration (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*) should be understood as the highest; the "middling" degree on the eighth stage and those following is the middle; and the [degree] lasting as long as the existence of the world proceeds in a manner equal to that [existence] is the ultimate—this is the meaning. This concludes the eighth chapter, on Ripening, in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
The ninth chapter on the knowledge of all aspects consists of two verses;
the third [verse] serves as their detailed exposition.
Through hundreds of immeasurable difficult feats, through immeasurable accumulations of merit,
over an immeasurable period of time, and by means of the destruction of immeasurable obscurations.
The attainment of omniscience, purified of all obscurations,
is declared to be Buddhahood, like an opened casket of jewels.

Having performed what is difficult and marvelous through hundreds of labors, having accumulated all that is auspicious over a vast period of time—the supreme vehicle of the eon—through the exhaustion of all obscurations;
and by uprooting even the subtle obscuration residing in the stages, Buddhahood has been opened like a casket containing jewels of great power.
Buddhahood is elucidated by way of its realization, its intrinsic nature, and its analogies.

Its "realization" (samudāgama) consists in its arising through as many hundreds of difficult feats, as many accumulations of merit and knowledge, over as much time, and by means of the abandonment of as much of the obscuration of afflictions and the obscuration to the knowable.
Its "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) is the attainment of the knowledge of all aspects, purified of all obscurations.
The opened jewel casket is the simile for that very Buddhahood. There are two verses concerning its non-dual characteristic and its majestic power:
"All phenomena are Buddhahood, yet there is no phenomenon whatsoever."
And that consists of pure dharmas, yet it is not defined by them.
Because it is the cause of the jewel of the Dharma, it is considered like an obtained mine of jewels;
because it is the cause of virtue, it is considered like an obtained cloud.

All phenomena are Buddhahood because Buddhahood is not distinct from suchness and is characterized by its purity; yet, there is no phenomenon whatsoever that exists by way of an imagined intrinsic nature. Furthermore, Buddhahood consists of pure qualities (*śukladharma*), for the perfections and other wholesome factors have undergone a transformation into that very state.
Nor are they indicated by those [phenomena], because the perfections and so forth are not established as having the nature of perfections and so forth; this is the characteristic of non-duality.

Its power (anubhāva) consists in being like a mine of jewels and like a cloud, because it is the source of the jewels of the Dharma and of the crops of virtue within the fields of the mental continuums of those to be trained.

Buddhahood is either the collection of all dharmas or, alternatively, it is devoid of all dharmas; it is like a vast and great mine of the jewels of Dharma because of the emergence of the extensive and great jewels of Dharma. It is like a cloud for living beings because it is the cause for the production of the great white harvest of reality. Through its giving, it is like a rain of the water of Dharma that is extensively and well-applied, inexhaustible among all creatures. (AMsa 9.6)
By this third verse, he points out that very same meaning:

it resembles a mine of jewels because it is the cause for the emergence of the vast and extensive jewel of the Dharma; it is like a cloud because it is the cause for the production of the great white harvest of living beings;
and it bestows upon all creatures a great, well-ordered, and inexhaustible rain of the water of the Dharma—this should be understood as the analysis of the words here.

There are five verses concerning the unsurpassed nature of that very Buddhahood as a refuge: For Buddhahood is indeed a protection at all times from the entire multitude of afflictions, from all misdeeds, and even from birth and death. (AMsa 9.7)
By this, he demonstrates the nature of being a refuge in brief, for the purpose of protecting against the defilements of afflictions, karma, and birth:
"From all calamities, from the miserable states, from lack of skillful means, from the view of a self-identity, and from the inferior vehicle—it is therefore the supreme refuge. (AMsa 9.8)
By this second [verse], [the Buddha's power is shown] through the detailed protection from calamities and so forth.

Among these, "protection from all calamities" refers to such things as when, through the majesty of the Buddhas, the blind regain their sight, the deaf their hearing, those with distracted minds attain composure, and fears are pacified.
It provides protection from the miserable states because those who have fallen into them are liberated by the Buddha’s radiance, and it establishes others so that they do not go there.
It provides protection from [wrong] means because it rouses one from the views of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
It provides protection from the view of a self-identity (*satkāya*) because it brings about final nirvana through the two vehicles.
It is the protection from the Lesser Vehicle for those of indeterminate lineage by leading them to the single path of the Great Vehicle;
it is held to be the incomparable refuge, that supreme state of Buddhahood which provides protection against birth, death, all afflictions, and evil deeds.
It is the means of protection for all who have fallen into various fears, and for those who have entered the lower vehicles and the various miserable realms of pervasive suffering.
By this third verse, he demonstrates, through that very same meaning, the incomparable excellence and unsurpassed nature of that very state of being a refuge:
That which possesses a perfectly complete body through the qualities of a Buddha; that which knows how to lead sentient beings into the True Dharma;
and that which has reached the further shore through compassion for all the world—that Buddhahood is the supreme refuge to be sought here. (AMsa 9.10)
By this fourth [verse], he demonstrates the reasons why that is such an unsurpassed refuge:
because its nature is perfectly complete with the qualities of a Buddha, such as the powers (*bala*) and the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*);

and with respect to the fulfillment of one's own welfare, because of the knowledge of the means for training sentient beings in the true Dharma; and with respect to the fulfillment of the welfare of others, because of having reached the further shore of compassion.
From the beginning of time, Buddhahood has been the great refuge for all sentient beings;
it is held to be the means for turning away from all calamities and for the attainment of prosperity.

By this fifth verse, he shows in brief for how long a time, for how many sentient beings, and for what purpose it constitutes a refuge. "For what purpose" means for the turning away from all calamities and for the attainment of prosperity.
There are six verses concerning the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).

Buddhahood is the transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti), endowed with the most excellent qualities of pure dharmas; it is attained through the path of non-conceptual wisdom that is utterly pure and has a vast object, once the seed of the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable—which has followed [the mind] continuously for an extremely long time—has come to an end through all the extensive modes of abandonment. AMsa_9.12.

By this, the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*) is elucidated through the separation from the seeds of the discordant factors (*vipakṣa*) and through the possession of the perfection of the remedies (*pratipakṣa*).
And as for how that [transformation] is attained, it is through the acquisition of two kinds of paths:
through the acquisition of the path of perfectly pure supramundane knowledge (*lokottarajñāna*).
And because of the attainment of the path of knowledge whose object is the infinite knowable attained subsequent to that [realization].
"For a superior duration" means for a beginningless time.
"By all the most extensive modes of abandonment" refers to the various stages (*bhūmi*).
Established therein, that Tathāgata gazes upon the world as if standing atop a great mountain;
he takes delight in tranquility and feels compassion for beings who delight in sin—what need is there to mention others?
By this second verse, he demonstrates its distinction from other transformations of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
For one established therein, like a person standing upon a great mountain peak, beholds the world situated at a vast distance;
and having seen it, he feels compassion even for the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, let alone others.

The transformation of the Tathāgatas is held to be activity, upward movement, non-activity, the basis, cessation, and recurrence; it is both dual and non-dual, equal and distinguished, and all-pervading in nature.
By this third verse, he demonstrates its tenfold classification:
for that transformation of the Tathāgatas is "proceeding" (*pravṛtti*) because it proceeds for the sake of others;
it is "exalted proceeding" (*udvṛtti*) because it is a superior proceeding due to its excellence among all phenomena.
Non-occurrence with respect to the cause of affliction;
"basis" indicates that very basis which is the result of transformation;
and cessation through the turning away from afflictions is "cessation."
Because it is ultimate, its activity is extensive; thus, it is "non-returning" (āvṛtti).
Through the activity of manifesting both perfect awakening and final nirvāṇa, its activity is dual.
Because it does not abide in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa, its activity is non-dual in terms of the conditioned and the unconditioned.
The activity [of the Buddha] is equal to that of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas by virtue of the commonality of liberation;
it is distinguished by its inequality with respect to the Buddha-qualities such as the powers and the fearlessnesses;
and it is all-pervading because it has reached the instruction of all vehicles.
Just as space is always all-pervading and constant, so too is that [the Tathāgata] always all-pervading and constant;
just as space is omnipresent among the multitudes of forms, so too is that omnipresent among the multitudes of sentient beings.
By this fourth verse, he demonstrates the omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*) of Buddhahood, which has that [nature] as its intrinsic essence (*tatsvabhāva*),
through a summary and an explanation based on the analogy with space, by means of the first and second halves [of the verse].

The omnipresence of Buddhahood among the multitudes of sentient beings should be understood as its arrival at all sentient beings by way of being their very self (*ātman*), due to its perfect accomplishment (*pariniṣpatti*).
Just as the reflection of the moon is not seen when a water vessel is broken,
so too the form of the Buddha is not seen among corrupt sentient beings.
By this fifth [verse], although [the Buddha] is omnipresent, he establishes through an analogy that the image of the Buddha is not seen among sentient beings who have become unfit vessels:
"Just as fire blazes in one place and then subsides in another."
The same should be understood regarding the Buddhas: their manifestation and non-manifestation.

By this sixth verse, he establishes—through the analogy of the kindling and extinguishing of a fire—that when there are beings to be trained by a Buddha, the Buddha appears because of his arising; and when they have been trained, he is no longer seen because of his final nirvana. There are four verses regarding the effortless and uninterrupted performance of the Buddha’s work.
Just as the production of sound occurs from musical instruments that have not been struck,
so too does the emergence of the teaching occur from the Jina without effortful application.
Just as a jewel displays its own radiance without effort,
so too do the Buddhas display their activity without exertion.
By these two verses, it is shown that he accomplishes the work of a Buddha effortlessly, through a similarity to the power of a gem and the sound of a drum that have not been struck:
"Just as worldly activities are seen to proceed without interruption in space,
so too do the deeds of the Victors proceed without interruption in the outflow-free realm."
Just as in space there is always the cessation and arising of activities,
so too in the untainted realm (anāsrava-dhātu) there is the arising and passing away of the Buddha's work.
By these two [qualities], there is also the state of never ceasing the Buddha-activity, because the work of a Buddha is uninterrupted.

Just as in space, even though worldly activities are uninterrupted, there is likewise the arising and passing away of various successive activities; such is the case regarding the profundity of the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*). There are sixteen verses on this.
Although it is undifferentiated by priority or posteriority and free from all obscurations,
suchness— considered to be Buddhahood— is neither pure nor impure.
It is not pure because it is characterized by a sequence of prior and subsequent states;
yet it is not impure because, subsequently, all obscurations are purified through the removal of stains.
This occurs when emptiness is thoroughly purified through the attainment of the path of selflessness.
Because they have attained the pure self, the Buddhas have reached the state of the greatness of the self.
And therein, in the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), the supreme self (*paramātman*) of the Buddhas is taught.
What is the reason?
Because its nature is the supreme selflessness (*agra-nairātmya*).

The supreme selflessness is purified suchness (*viśuddhā tathatā*), and that is the self (*ātman*) of the Buddhas in the sense of being their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). When that [suchness] is purified, the Buddhas obtain the pure self, which is the supreme selflessness.

Therefore, because they have obtained the pure self, the Buddhas have attained the greatness of the self (*ātmamāhātmya*); with this underlying intention, the supreme self is established for the Buddhas in the uncontaminated realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*).
Buddhahood is said to be neither existence nor non-existence;
therefore, regarding the question of the nature of the Buddha, the method of the undeclared (avyākṛta) is held to be appropriate.
For that very reason, Buddhahood is not said to be an existence,
because its nature consists in the non-existence of both persons and phenomena, and because Buddhahood has that as its essence;
nor is it said to be a non-existence, because it possesses the characteristic of suchness.

Therefore, regarding questions concerning the existence or non-existence of a Buddha— such as whether the Tathāgata exists after death or does not exist— this is considered the method of the undeclared (*avyākṛta*).
Just as the cessation of heat in iron or the clearing of a visual impairment in sight,
so too in the Buddha’s knowledge of the mind, neither existence nor non-existence is praised.

Just as the subsiding of heat in metal and the subsiding of cataracts in vision are neither "existence"— because heat and cataracts are characterized by non-existence— nor "non-existence"— because they exist by way of their characteristic of subsiding— so too, the subsiding of passion and ignorance, which stand in the place of heat and cataracts, within the mind and wisdom of the Buddhas is praised as neither existence, because it is manifested by their absence, nor as non-existence.
Because they exist through each respective characteristic of liberation,
there is neither oneness nor multiplicity among the Buddhas in the immaculate realm;
for, like space, they are bodiless, yet they follow the sequence of their former bodies.
In the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*) of the Buddhas, there is no oneness according to their former bodies,
nor is there multiplicity due to the absence of a body, like space.
Within the Buddha-qualities such as the powers (*bala*), awakening (*bodhi*) is like a mine of jewels.
They are considered to be like great clouds for the crops of the world's virtue.
Because it is completely filled with merit and wisdom, it is considered like the full moon;
and because it produces the light of knowledge, it is considered like the great sun.
(MSA 39) These two verses concerning the likeness to a jewel-mine and a cloud, and the likeness to the full moon and the great sun, have their meaning already explained.
Just as immeasurable rays are intermingled within the orb of the sun, [so too are the Buddha's qualities].
They always act with a single purpose and illuminate the world.
Just as the Buddhas in the untainted realm (anāsrava-dhātu) are considered immeasurable,
performing their activities in unison with a single purpose, they are regarded as creating the light of primordial wisdom (jñāna).
By the first [verse], through the analogy of mixed rays having a single function, he demonstrates their commonality of activity;
the single-functionality of the rays should be understood as their having the same effects of ripening and drying.
By the second [verse], he shows their mixed single-functionality in the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) regarding activities such as emanations (*nirmāṇa*).
Just as from the emission of a single ray all rays are emitted from the sun,
so too should the emission of the knowledge of the Buddhas be understood.
By the simultaneous emission of all rays of light, it demonstrates the simultaneous activity of the wisdom of the Buddhas.
Just as there is no sense of "mine" in the operation of the sun's rays, likewise there is no sense of "mine" in the operation of the Buddhas' wisdom. (MSA 9.32)
Just as the world is illuminated all at once by the rays of the sun, which possess the brilliance of a single pearl,
so too is the entire object of knowledge illuminated simultaneously by the wisdoms of a Buddha.

The two verses have their meaning understood respectively through the absence of the sense of "mine" and through the illumination of the world as an object of knowledge. Just as it is held that the rays of the sun are obscured by clouds and other such veils, so too is the nature of the mind.
In the same way, the obscuration of the Buddha-knowledges is the depravity of sentient beings.
Just as there is an obscuration of light rays by clouds and so forth due to their lack of brilliance,
so too there is an obscuration of the Buddhas' wisdom in sentient beings due to their being unfit vessels, because of the extreme prevalence of the five corruptions (*pañcakaṣāya*).
Just as the variegated or non-variegated appearance of dye on a cloth depends upon the quality of the dust [upon it].
Likewise, through the power of penetration, there is variety or lack of variety in the knowledge of those liberated.
Just as the variegation of colors on a cloth occurs due to a particular kind of dye, while in some cases there is no such variegation,
so too, due to the specific power of the application of former vows and conduct, there arises a variety of knowledge within the liberation of the Buddhas.
The liberation of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas is undifferentiated;
however, regarding the profound, stainless realm, its characteristics, its state, and its activity— this is said of the Buddhas, like painting the sky with colors.
Thus, the threefold profundity of the Buddhas in the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*) has been explained:
profundity of characteristics by means of four verses,
and profundity of state by means of the fifth verse, because of not abiding in either unity or plurality.
The profundity of activity is explained through ten aspects.

Furthermore, that profundity of characteristics is taught with reference to the characteristic of purity, the characteristic of the supreme self, the characteristic of the indeterminate, and the characteristic of liberation.

The profundity of activity consists of the activity of being the locus for the jewels such as the factors conducive to enlightenment, the activity of maturing sentient beings, and the activity of reaching the ultimate consummation.

This has been taught with reference to the activity of teaching the Dharma, the activity of performing deeds such as emanations, the activity of the engagement of gnosis, the activity of non-conceptuality, the activity of gnosis in its various forms, the activity of the non-engagement of gnosis, and the activity of the distinction of gnosis within the commonality of liberation.

This exposition of the differentiations of profundity in the uncontaminated realm— which, due to its lack of conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), is like space— should be understood as being like painting pictures in the sky with colors.
Although suchness is undifferentiated for all, when it has attained purity, it is the state of a Tathāgata; therefore, all embodied beings possess that as their embryo (tadgarbha).

Suchness is undifferentiated in all, and the Tathāgata has that very purity as his intrinsic nature; therefore, it is said that "all sentient beings possess the embryo of the Tathāgata. There are eleven verses concerning the analysis of mastery.
By means of their mastery, the [mastery] of the Śrāvakas overcomes that of worldly beings;
by means of the mental stage belonging to the Pratyekabuddhas and Buddhas, the [mastery] of the Śrāvaka is overcome.
It does not approach even a fraction of the sovereign power of a bodhisattva;
it does not approach even a fraction of the sovereign power of a Tathāgata.
By means of these two verses, he demonstrates the sovereignty (*vibhutva*) of the Buddhas through the excellence of their preeminent power:
"The sovereignty of a Buddha is held to be immeasurable and inconceivable;
it proceeds in whatever [place], toward whatever [object], in whatever manner, to whatever extent, and at whatever time. (AMsa 9.40)
By this third [verse], through the distinctions of its modes and its profundity, he explains how it is immeasurable and how it is inconceivable:
for whose sake it proceeds, in which world-system, by what such modes, whether to a small or great extent, and at what time.
With the remaining verses, he demonstrates the different types of mastery (*vibhutva*) according to the different modes of mental activity (*manovṛtti*):
"Upon the transformation of the five sense-faculties, supreme mastery is attained; when all [faculties] function toward all objects, there arises the twelve hundred qualities. (AMsa 9.41)
Upon the transformation of the five sense faculties, two kinds of supreme mastery are attained:
[mastery] over the functioning of all five sense faculties with respect to all five types of objects,
and therein, the arising of twelve hundred qualities for each [faculty].
Upon the revolution of the mind as well, supreme mastery is attained,
in the non-conceptual and perfectly pure gnosis that accompanies that mastery.
When the mind undergoes revolution, supreme mastery is attained in the non-conceptual, perfectly pure gnosis that accompanies mastery;
accompanied by this, all gnosis of mastery proceeds.
Upon the revolution of the apprehension of objects, supreme mastery is attained.
For the sake of purifying the field, indeed, in order to manifest enjoyments according to one's wish.

Upon the transformation of the object and the transformation of the grasping, one attains supreme mastery over the purification of the field, by which one manifests enjoyments according to one's wish;
and there is non-obstruction at all times regarding all activities of knowledge.
Upon the revolution of conceptual construction, supreme mastery is attained at all times without obstruction regarding all forms of knowledge and actions.
Upon the revolution of the basis, supreme mastery is attained:
the non-abiding nirvana of the Buddhas in the immovable, stainless state.

Upon the revolution of the basis (*pratiṣṭhā-parāvṛtti*), the supreme mastery of the Buddhas—non-abiding nirvana—is attained within the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*). Upon the revolution of sexual desire (*maithuna-parāvṛtti*), supreme mastery is attained:
namely, dwelling in the bliss of a Buddha and beholding one's consort without defilement.
Upon the transformation of sexual intercourse, in the two states of the Buddha’s blissful abiding, and in the vision of one's spouse without defilement,
supreme mastery is attained through the reversal of the perception of space.
And [the power of prayer] consists in the fulfillment of intended aims and in the manifestation of one's gait and form.
When the perception of space is overturned, there is the fulfillment of the two intended purposes by which one becomes a "Womb of Space" (*gaganagarbha*);
and through the manifestation of movement and form, one possesses mastery over space by traveling at will.
Thus, when there is an immeasurable transformation, immeasurable sovereignty is recognized.
Because of the performance of inconceivable activities within the stainless basis of the Buddhas.
In this manner, the transformation is immeasurable.
Furthermore, within that untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) of the Buddhas, immeasurable mastery and the performance of inconceivable activity should be understood.
Regarding the fact that this very Buddha serves as the cause for the maturation of sentient beings, there are seven verses.
When the world has increased its virtue, it proceeds toward supreme purity; and by not abandoning virtue, it proceeds toward the highest state through the increase of virtue.
Thus does the world, whether immature or mature, proceed in every direction according to the well-spoken teachings of the Victors; yet here, it is certainly not entirely so.
By this, he shows what kind of maturation serves as the cause:
for those who have accumulated roots of merit, it leads to the supreme state of liberation; and for those who have not accumulated roots of merit, it leads to the accumulation of roots of merit.
One who is unripe reaches the supreme state through the increase of virtue and proceeds toward maturation; one who is ripe reaches the supreme state through complete purification.
And thus it proceeds at all times, yet never comes to an end because of the infinity of the world.

Having practiced such a course of conduct that is difficult to attain, the steadfast ones—by virtue of their possession of supreme qualities—obtain the great awakening which exists in reality, which is eternal, stable, and a refuge for those without refuge;
this they obtain at all times and in all ways throughout the ten directions. This is a marvel in the world due to their practice of the excellent method, yet it is not a cause for wonder.

By this second [verse], it is shown that for matured Bodhisattvas, the maturation [of others] is neither marvelous nor non-marvelous. Having always and at all times—that is, constantly and without interruption—experienced that [maturation], he practices the path and practices according to the excellent method.

In some places he displays various Dharmas and the Wheel of Dharma through hundreds of diverse gateways; in some places he manifests the disappearance of birth, and in other places he displays the manifold conduct of living beings.
In one place he repeatedly manifests complete enlightenment, and in another, nirvāṇa; yet he does not waver from that state, and he accomplishes everything.
By this third verse, he demonstrates the state of being a causal sign (*nimittatva*) in the application of the means for maturing many [beings] simultaneously through various gates;
namely, how he disciplines sentient beings according to where they reside,
and his manifold conduct among people through the various types of birth stories (*jātaka*).
And he does not move from his station because of the untainted realm (anāsravadhātu).
It does not occur to the Buddhas: "This person has been ripened by me," nor "This embodied being is not yet ripe," nor "Furthermore, this one is being ripened now.
Yet, without any deliberate effort, the multitude of beings indeed reaches ripening through wholesome dharmas—constantly, in every direction, and on all sides, through the three gates.
By this fourth verse, he demonstrates that the cause for the application of that maturation occurs without deliberate effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
"The threefold gate" refers to the three vehicles (*yānatraya*).
Just as the sun, according to its own exertion, brings about the ripening of crops in every direction and everywhere through its widespread and pure rays of light; so too does the Buddha.

In the same way, the sun of the Dharma also brings about the ripening of the crops in every direction and on all sides through the spreading rays of the Dharma that consist of the methods for pacification.
By this fifth [verse], he demonstrates the simile of maturation without volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*):
Just as from a single lamp there arises a vast collection of lamps, immeasurable and incalculable, yet it does not undergo exhaustion;
so too, from a single Buddha there arises a vast collection of maturation, immeasurable and incalculable, yet it does not undergo exhaustion, nor does it ever return to exhaustion. (AMsa 9.54)
By this sixth [verse], maturation through succession is shown:
just as the great ocean does not reach satiety nor undergo increase, even as vast and clear waters enter it, so it is with the bodhisattva.
Likewise, the Buddha-element never reaches satiety or increase through the constant and continuous influxes of purification; this is a supreme marvel in this world. (AMsa 9.55)

By this seventh [verse], through the illustration of the ocean regarding the entry into liberation for those who are matured, there is shown the lack of satiety of the *dharmadhātu* because it provides space [for all phenomena], and its lack of increase because it is not surpassed by meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
There are four verses on the purification of the *dharmadhātu*:
"It is characterized by the purity of suchness, which is free from the two obstructions regarding all phenomena."
It is characterized by the inexhaustibility of mastery over the knowledge of things and its objective support.
This is one verse concerning the meaning of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*):
it is characterized by the purification of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena from the two obscurations— the afflictive and the cognitive—
and it is characterized by the inexhaustible mastery over both the [ultimate] reality and the knowledge that takes it as its object.
The realization consists in the cultivation of the knowledge of suchness in every respect;
its fruit is the inexhaustibility in every way of bestowing the two [benefits] upon all sentient beings.
This second verse is undertaken with reference to the meaning of the cause and the meaning of the result.
The cultivation of the knowledge of suchness in every respect is the cause for the purification of the dharmadhātu.
"In every respect" means by way of all the various approaches to the teachings (dharmaparyāyamukha).

Its fruit is the inexhaustibility of bestowing both benefit and happiness upon all sentient beings in every way; its activity consists of the application of the emanations of body, speech, and mind through skillful means; and it is endowed with the two immeasurables: the gateways of meditative concentration and mnemonic formulas (dhāraṇī). // AMsa_9.58 //
This third verse begins with the subject of action (*karman*) and yoga (*yoga*).

The threefold emanation of body and so forth is "action" (*karman*); "yoga" is the endowment with both the gateways of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇī*), as well as the two immeasurable accumulations of merit and gnosis (*puṇya-jñāna-saṃbhāra*).
It functions through distinct modes by way of the [three bodies]: the essential (*svābhāvika*), the enjoyment (*sambhogika*), and the emanation (*nairmāṇika*).
This pure realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is proclaimed as belonging to the Buddhas.
This is the fourth verse concerning the meaning of "function" (*vṛtti*):
it possesses distinct functions by way of the functions of the essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*), the enjoyment body (*sāṃbhogikakāya*), and the emanation body (*nairmāṇikakāya*).

There are seven verses on the classification of the Buddha-bodies: The essential body, the enjoyment body, and another, the transformation body—these are indeed the divisions of the bodies of the Buddhas; the first, however, is the basis for the other two. (AMsa 9.60)
The bodies of the Buddhas are threefold:

the essential body (*svābhāvika-kāya*), which is the *dharma*-body characterized by the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*); and the enjoyment body (*sāṃbhogika-kāya*), by means of which one enjoys the Dharma within the circles of assemblies.

The emanation body (*nairmāṇika*) is that by which one performs the welfare of sentient beings through emanations. The enjoyment body (*sāmbhogika*) is distinct across all realms with respect to its retinues, fields, names, bodies, and activities for the enjoyment of the Dharma. (AMsa 9.61)
Therein, the enjoyment body (*sāṃbhogika-kāya*) is differentiated in all world-systems by its assemblies, circles, buddha-fields, names, bodies, and activities of enjoying the Dharma;

yet it is uniform and subtle. That which remains is considered the essential nature body (*svābhāvika-kāya*). It is the cause for mastery over enjoyment, appearing as enjoyments according to one's wish.
The nature body (*svābhāvikakāya*) of all Buddhas is equal because it is without distinction;
it is subtle because it is difficult to know.
It is connected with the enjoyment body (*sāmbhogikakāya*), and it is the cause for the mastery of enjoyment, so that one may manifest enjoyments at will.
The immeasurable emanation of the Buddha is considered the nirmāṇakāya;
in both [the sambhogakāya and the nirmāṇakāya], the accomplishment of the two purposes for the two [types of beings] is established in all its aspects.

The emanation body (*nairmāṇika-kāya*) of the Buddhas consists of immeasurable varieties of Buddha-emanations. The enjoyment body (*sāṃbhogika*) is characterized by the perfection of one's own welfare, while the emanation body is characterized by the perfection of the welfare of others.
Thus, the perfection of these two aims is established respectively in the two bodies: the enjoyment body and the emanation body.
Through the constant manifestation of craftsmanship, birth, great enlightenment, and parinirvāṇa,
this emanation body of the Buddha is a great illusion and a great skillful means for liberation.

Furthermore, that emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) should be understood as characterized by the fulfillment of the welfare of others, because it serves as a great means for liberation through the constant demonstration of arts such as playing the lute for the sake of those to be trained, as well as through the demonstrations of birth, perfect enlightenment, and nirvāṇa.
The collection of the bodies of the Buddhas should be understood by means of three bodies;
that which includes their own basis and the welfare of both self and others is demonstrated through these three bodies.
It should be understood that the entirety of the bodies of the Buddhas is comprised within these three bodies.
By means of these three bodies, the welfare of oneself and others, together with their basis, is demonstrated;
for two [of these bodies] are characterized by the accomplishment of the welfare of self and others, while the other two are based upon them, as previously stated.
They are considered equal in terms of their basis, their intention, and their action;
their permanence is found in their nature, their non-interruption, and their continuity.

Furthermore, these three bodies of all Buddhas are, respectively, without distinction in three respects: by way of their basis, because the *dharmadhātu* is indivisible; by way of their intention, because there is no separate intention among Buddhas;
and by way of their activity, because they share a common activity.
Within these three bodies, a threefold permanence should be understood, respectively, by which the Tathāgatas are said to possess eternal bodies.

Eternity by nature belongs to the *svābhāvika* [body], because it is eternal by its very essence; eternity through non-interruption belongs to the *sāmbhogika* [body], because the sharing of the Dharma is never severed; and eternity through continuity belongs to the *nairmāṇika* [body], because even upon its disappearance, manifestations appear again and again.

There are ten verses on the classification of the Buddha-knowledge: Mirror-like wisdom is immovable; the threefold wisdom rests upon it—namely, the wisdom of equality, the wisdom of discernment, and the wisdom of accomplishing activities. (AMsa 9.67)

The wisdom of the Buddhas is fourfold: mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣājñāna*), and all-accomplishing wisdom (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*). Mirror-like wisdom is immovable; the other three wisdoms are dependent upon it and are mobile.
Mirror-like wisdom is without "mine-ness," undivided, and ever-present.
It is unconfused regarding all objects of knowledge, yet it is never directed toward them.
The mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna) is without "mine-ness" and is undivided spatially; it is ever-present temporally;
it is unconfused regarding all objects of knowledge due to the perpetual absence of obscurations; yet it does not face toward those objects because it is formless.
Because it is the cause of all cognitions, it is like a great mine of wisdom.
And that [enjoyment-buddhahood] arises from the emergence of reflections of gnosis.
Because it is the cause of all types of those knowledges, such as the knowledge of equality and so forth, it is like a mine for all knowledges.
Furthermore, because the reflection of the wisdom of that Enjoyment-body Buddha arises therein, it is called the mirror-like knowledge (*ādarśajñāna*).
The knowledge of equality toward sentient beings is considered stainless due to the purity of cultivation;
this knowledge of equality is held to be entered into a tranquility that is non-abiding.

The knowledge of equality that was attained by the Bodhisattva at the times of clear realization is intended as the "knowledge of equality" when, through the purification of its cultivation, it has entered non-abiding nirvana for one who has attained awakening.
It is considered to follow all times through great loving-kindness and compassion,
and it manifests the image of the Buddha to sentient beings according to their respective inclinations.

It is accompanied by great loving-kindness and compassion at all times, and manifests the image of a Buddha to sentient beings according to their respective inclinations— since some sentient beings see the Tathāgata as blue in color, others as yellow, and so forth; and it is the wisdom of discernment, which is always unimpeded regarding all objects of knowledge.
And it is indeed like a treasury of dhāraṇīs and meditative absorptions (samādhis).
It displays all sovereign powers within the circle of the assembly,
cuts through all doubts, and rains down the great Dharma.
Discriminative wisdom is as described in the verse.
Wisdom in the performance of duties acts for the benefit of all sentient beings throughout all realms by means of various, immeasurable, and inconceivable emanations. (AMsa 9.74)
The knowledge of the performance of duties consists in accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings through immeasurable and inconceivable emanations of various kinds in all world-systems.

That inconceivable Buddha-emanation should be understood in every respect as being characterized by the completion of tasks through their various distinctions of number and fields at all times. (AMsa 9.75)
Furthermore, that emanation of the Buddha should be understood as always and in every way inconceivable,
by reason of the diversity of its activities, its numbers, and its fields;
and because of its sustaining power, its equanimity of mind, and its correct illumination of the Dharma.
And from the performance of duties, there arises the emergence of the four types of gnosis.
In that regard, "retention" refers to the retention of the teachings heard;
"equanimity of mind" toward all sentient beings arises from the equality of self and others.
The remainder has already been explained.
There is a verse concerning the non-duality and non-distinctness of the Buddhas:
"Because of the distinction of lineages, because of not being in vain, because of completeness, and also because of beginninglessness..."
Because there is no distinction, there is neither a single Buddhahood nor a plurality within the stainless basis.
That there is only one Buddha is not accepted.
For what reason?
Because of the diversity of lineages (*gotra*).
For sentient beings belonging to the lineage of the Buddhas are infinite;
that only one among them has attained perfect awakening, while others will not attain it—
whence is this known?
Furthermore, the accumulations of merit and wisdom of other bodhisattvas would be rendered futile because they would not attain full awakening; yet such futility is not tenable.
Therefore, on account of this non-futility, there cannot be only one Buddha, nor could there be the complete fulfillment of the welfare of sentient beings.
This is also untenable because no one would be established in the state of Buddhahood by that single Buddha.

Furthermore, there is no such thing as a "primordial Buddha" (ādibuddha), because Buddhahood is impossible without the accumulations (saṃbhāra), and those accumulations are impossible without another Buddha. Thus, even on account of beginninglessness, a single Buddha is not tenable.
Nor is multiplicity accepted for Buddhas, because in the untainted realm (anāsrava-dhātu) the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) is undifferentiated.
There are four verses concerning the entry into the means for attaining Buddhahood.
That which is non-existence is itself the supreme existence;
and non-apprehension in every respect is considered the supreme apprehension.
That which is non-existence by way of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is itself the supreme existence by way of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

And that which is the absolute non-apprehension of the imagined nature is itself the supreme apprehension of the perfected nature. Cultivation is considered supreme for those who do not perceive [an object] within cultivation.
The attainment of others is desired, as is the attainment for those who perceive it.
That very non-apprehension of cultivation is the supreme cultivation;
that very non-apprehension of attainment is the supreme attainment.
For those who perceive their own gravity, that [non-apprehension] is the long-lasting sign of their vigor.
For conceited bodhisattvas, awakening is seen to be far away.
And those who perceive its gravity and magnitude as endowed with marvelous qualities,
and who perceive a long duration for its full realization,
do not perceive a sign as an objective support for the mind.

And thinking, "We shall attain Buddhahood by exerting our own vigor," for those conceited Bodhisattvas who thus perceive objects, awakening is said to be far away because of their state of grasping at signs.
For those Bodhisattvas who are free from conceptual construction, it is taught that awakening is attained when they perceive all this, as it has been described, as mere conceptualization.

For those who perceive that all this is mere conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātra*), because they do not even conceptualize that very state of being "mere conceptual construction," the Bodhisattvas who are free from conceptualization (akalpa) are said to have effectively attained awakening at the stage of attaining the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*). Regarding the fact that Buddhas do not act with a single common purpose (*naikakāryatva*) among one another, there are four verses:

Rivers that have not entered the subterranean realm (pātāla) have separate bases and separate waters; they possess little water, their functions are distinct, and they serve as a minor source of enjoyment for the living beings dependent upon them.
And once they have entered the ocean, they all become based on a single foundation and consist of one great body of water;
having a unified purpose, they are always a source of great enjoyment for the multitude of living beings that depend upon the waters.

Those who have not yet entered into Buddhahood are wise ones whose bases are divided, whose views are divergent, whose understanding is meager, and whose activities are performed individually; they are always available for the benefit of limited beings. (AMsa 9.84)
And having entered into Buddhahood, they all possess a single basis and a single great awakening;
their activities are unified and they are always a source of great enjoyment for the multitude of great beings.
In that regard, the rivers have distinct bases because their respective receptacles are distinct;
they perform functions with individual purposes because they carry out their tasks separately;
and they are "enjoyed by the few" because they are enjoyed by only a small number of beings.
The remainder has already been explained.
There is a verse regarding the encouragement toward Buddhahood:
"Thus, because the stage of Buddhahood is endowed with incomparable pure qualities and is the cause of benefit and happiness," [it should be sought].
Because it is a mine of inexhaustible, supreme, and auspicious bliss, one of virtuous mind deserves to attain the thought of enlightenment.
The perfection of the welfare of others [is achieved] through the attainment of one's own goal by virtue of being endowed with the incomparable, stainless Dharma,
and because Buddhahood is the cause of benefit and happiness. Furthermore,
it is distinguished as a sublime state of bliss because it is a source of faultless, supreme, and inexhaustible happiness.
The wise person, by embracing that vow, is able to take up the undiminished thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
This concludes the ninth chapter, on Awakening, in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
(MSA 50)
The tenth chapter. The summary verse:
The beginning, accomplishment, refuge, lineage, and likewise the production of the thought [of awakening].
The welfare of oneself and others, the meaning of reality, spiritual power, maturation, and enlightenment.

And this section on enlightenment (bodhy-adhikāra) is to be followed from the beginning up to the chapter on enlightenment (bodhi-paṭala). There are two verses concerning the analysis of the characteristics of the different types of resolute belief (adhimukti-prabheda-lakṣaṇa-vibhāga):
It is that which is born and unborn, the grasper and that which has become the grasped, received from a friend, [received] from oneself, and that which is erroneous.
One is unerring and another is manifest; one proceeds from sound, while others are seeking and examining.
That which has arisen is past or present;
that which has not arisen is future.
The internal apprehending [consciousness] is that by which one resolves upon an object.
That which has become an object of apprehension is external; it is resolved upon as the objective support of the vehicle.
That which is received from a friend is coarse;
that which [arises] from one's own self is subtle.
That which is erroneous is inferior because of its mistaken resolve;
that which is non-erroneous is tranquil;
and that which is manifest is proximate because its conditions are present.
That which is not face-to-face is distant due to its opposite nature;
that which functions through sound consists of hearing,
while that which seeks consists of reflection.
Resolute belief (adhimukti) consists of that which is based on vision and that which consists of cultivation; it is characterized by discernment.
It is removable or not scattered, scattered or not scattered by opposing factors (vipakṣa); it is inferior or sublime, veiled or unveiled;
it is appropriate or inappropriate, accumulated or unaccumulated, firmly established, and far-reaching. // AMsa_10.3 //
That which is susceptible to being carried away is weak; that which is interspersed with opposing factors is middling;
that which is not interspersed with opposing factors is superior.
It is inferior in the other vehicle;
it is sublime in the Great Vehicle;
it is obscured and hindered regarding the attainment of excellence.
"Unobstructed" means being free from hindrances;
"properly applied" means due to practice that is constant and respectful; "improperly applied" means being devoid of those qualities.
It is "endowed with accumulation" because it is suitable for realization; it is "without accumulation" because of the opposite;
and it is "firmly established" because it has entered the stages.
[The obstacles] regarding the remaining distant stages:
there are three verses concerning the hindrance to resolute belief (adhimukti):
"Excessive lack of mental attention (amanasikāra), laziness (kauśīdya), and error in yoga."
A bad friend, immaturity regarding what is auspicious, and improper mental attention.
For that which has arisen, the obstacle is a preponderance of non-attention;
for that which has not yet arisen, it is laziness; for that which has become the grasped and the grasper, it is the confusion of yoga due to attachment in that very same way;
and for that which has been received from a friend, it is a bad friend because of causing a perverted grasp.
The weakness of the roots of virtue arises from lack of conviction in one's own self.
The obstacle to non-erroneous [realization] is improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), because it is its opposite.
Furthermore, there is negligence (*pramāda*) and limited learning (*alpaśrutatva*), as well as being satisfied with meager study and reflection.
And likewise, conceit regarding mere tranquility is considered a lack of mastery.
The obstacle to the [level of] "facing" is negligence, because that level is produced by non-negligence.

The obstacle to the [level of] "conduct through sound" is limited learning, due to not hearing sūtras of definitive meaning. The obstacles to the [level of] "seeking" are contentment with mere learning and contentment with limited reflection.
Being satisfied with mere reflection and pride in mere tranquility;
lack of mastery over what is to be removed and what is interspersed;
lack of revulsion, as well as revulsion, obscuration, and lack of application—these are the obstacles.
And lack of accumulation should be understood as an obstacle to resolute belief.
For the inferior [faith], there is no revulsion toward saṃsāra; for the sublime, there is revulsion;
and for the unobstructed, there is non-returning.
The lack of application toward that which is appropriate,
and the failure to accumulate that which has been gathered, constitute obstacles.
There are five verses concerning the benefits of resolute belief.
Great merit, freedom from regret, great joy, and great happiness;
non-wastage, stability, and likewise the attainment of excellence.
The clear realization of the Dharma, the supreme attainment of one's own and others' welfare,
and the swift acquisition of the superknowledges— these indeed are the benefits arising from resolute belief.
When [the thought] has arisen and is present, the merit is great;
when it is past, there is no regret because of the absence of remorse.
When there is both the grasping subject and the grasped object, great mental well-being arises through the application of meditative concentration;
when it is produced by a spiritual friend, there is no loss;
and when it is one's own resolute conviction, there is stability.
In the stage of error, in that which is present before one, and in those consisting of hearing and so forth, up to the middling stage, there is the progression toward distinction;
in the superior stage, there is the clear realization of the Dharma;
and in the inferior stage, there is the attainment of one's own aim.
In the sublime [perfection], the attainment of the welfare of others is supreme.

In those [perfections] that are unobstructed, endowed, accumulated, and so forth—belonging to the white side—the benefit is the swift acquisition of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*). For those possessed of desire, it is like a dog; for those with meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), it resembles a tortoise.
For those seeking their own benefit, it is like a servant; for those seeking the benefit of others, it is like a king.
Just as a dog afflicted by suffering is constantly unsatisfied and hungry; just as that tortoise is huddled within a hole in the water;
just as a servant moves about with a body perpetually trembling;
and just as a king dwells exercising power over the realm of other kings.
Likewise, one should always understand the distinction made by various forms of resolute belief regarding the purpose of the tasks performed for oneself, others, and those who abide in desire;
having recognized the supremacy of the Mahāyāna here according to the rule, the steadfast person should always and intensely choose that very [Mahāyāna] in this world.

Furthermore, the resolute belief (*adhimukti*) of those possessed by desire is like a dog; that of those who have attained worldly meditative concentration (*laukika-samādhi*) is like a tortoise; that of those intent on their own welfare is like a servant;
and that of those intent on the welfare of others is like a king.
Having established this very point through another [scriptural] passage, he encourages them to take up resolute belief in the Mahāyāna.
Verses on the Refutation of Laxity in Resolute Faith:
Since immeasurable beings who have become human attain perfect enlightenment at every moment, one should therefore not tolerate laxity.
For three reasons, dissolution is not logical:
because those who have become human beings attain enlightenment;
and they attain it eternally.
And they attain immeasurable [merit]. There are two verses concerning the distinction of the merit of resolute belief (*adhimukti-puṇya-viśeṣaṇa*):
"Just as one generates merit by giving food to others..."
But he who eats by himself does not have such a great arising of merit.
That which is spoken of in the Sūtras is obtained from the Dharma taught for the sake of others;
however, it is not obtained from the Dharma taught for one's own sake.
Just as merit arises for one who gives food because it is directed toward the welfare of others,
but not for one who eats it himself because it is directed toward his own welfare;
likewise, from the Mahāyāna Dharma taught based on the welfare of others, a great arising of merit is obtained as described in those various sūtras.
But not from the Dharma of the Śrāvaka vehicle, which is taught based on one's own self-interest.
Regarding the acquisition of the fruit of resolute belief, there is this verse:
"Thus, the wise person, having always generated great resolute belief toward the vast path and the great, irresistible Dharma,"
He attains vast and constant merit, its further increase, peerless qualities, and the state of a great being.
In whatever way and by whatever kind of resolute belief one grasps a particular result:
within the vast Mahāyāna Dharma, a wise person, through an irreversible and exalted resolute belief, grasps a threefold result— the increase of extensive merit,
the increase of that very resolute belief itself, and Buddhahood, which is the state of great-souledness possessing incomparable qualities caused by that [belief].
In the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, the tenth chapter is the "Chapter on Devotion.
The eleventh chapter, the "Chapter on the Search for the Dharma," contains four verses concerning the search for the objective support (*ālambana*).
The three baskets, or two, are intended by way of summary through nine reasons;
they bring about liberation through [the processes of] perfuming, awakening, pacifying, and penetrating.
The three baskets (*piṭakatraya*) are the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma.
These same three become two by way of the distinction between the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) and the Supreme Vehicle (*agrayāna*):
namely, the Śrāvaka Piṭaka and the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.
Furthermore, for what reason are those three, or those two, called "piṭaka"?
It should be understood that they are so called because of their inclusion—that is, because they include all objects of knowledge.
For what reason are there three?

The Sūtra is [taught] for nine reasons; as an antidote to doubt, it is taught so that whoever is uncertain regarding a particular meaning may attain certainty about it. The Vinaya is [taught] as an antidote to the pursuit of the two extremes: by prohibiting the enjoyment of what is blameworthy, which is the extreme of devotion to the pleasure of sensual desires, and by permitting the enjoyment of what is blameless, which is the extreme of devotion to self-mortification.
The Abhidharma is [taught] as an antidote to the dogmatic adherence to one's own views, because it illuminates the characteristics of phenomena without error.

Furthermore, the teaching of the three trainings is accomplished through the Sūtra: the accomplishment of higher ethics and higher mind through the Vinaya, because one who possesses ethical discipline is free from remorse, and through freedom from remorse, one attains meditative concentration;
and the accomplishment of higher wisdom through the Abhidharma, because of the discernment of the meaning of things without error.
Furthermore, the teaching of the Dharma and its meaning is accomplished through the Sūtra.
The accomplishment of the Dharma and its meaning occurs through the Vinaya, because it brings about the mastery of those two by means of the discipline that subdues the afflictions.
Skill in the definitive determination of the discussion regarding the Dharma and its meaning occurs through the Abhidharma.
For these nine reasons, the three baskets (piṭakas) are established.
And that [knowledge] is for the sake of liberation from cyclic existence.
How, then, does it liberate?
It liberates through the processes of perfuming, awakening, pacifying, and penetrating.
Through hearing, by way of mental impression; through reflection, by way of awakening;
and through cultivation, by way of pacification through tranquility (śamatha).
Through penetration by means of insight (vipaśyanā),
the Sūtra, Abhidharma, and Vinaya are considered to have four types of meaning in brief;
through knowledge of these, the wise one attains the state of omniscience (sarvākārajñatā).

Furthermore, these Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma each have four meanings in brief; through the knowledge of these, a bodhisattva attains omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), whereas a śrāvaka attains the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) by understanding the meaning of even a single verse.
It is called *sūtra* because it indicates [the truth] by way of its basis (*āśraya*), its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), its phenomena (*dharma*), and its meaning (*artha*).
Furthermore, it is called Abhidharma because it is directed toward [the truth], because it is repeated, and because it leads to the overcoming [of the afflictions].
How does each [term] have a fourfold meaning?
