It is called a *sūtra* because it indicates the basis (*āśraya*), the moment (*kṣaṇa*), the dharma (*dharma*), and the meaning (*artha*).
Among these, the "basis" refers to the place where it was taught, by whom it was taught, and for whom it was taught.
The characteristic consists of the characteristic of conventional truth and the characteristic of ultimate truth.
Dharmas refer to the aggregates, sense bases, elements, nutriments, dependent origination, and so forth.
Meaning refers to the underlying intention.
Abhidharma should be understood as such because it is directed toward [the goal], because it is frequent, because it overcomes, and because it leads to attainment.
Abhidharma is the dharma directed toward Nirvana, because it teaches the truths, the factors conducive to enlightenment, the gates of liberation, and so forth.

Abhidharma is the frequent dharma, because it provides extensive explanations of each individual dharma through various classifications, such as those with form and those without form, or those that are visible and so on.
It is called Abhidharma because it overcomes; that is, it overcomes the doctrines of others through formal debates and legal procedures.
It is called Abhidharma because by means of it the meaning of the Sūtras is thoroughly understood.
And it possesses the nature of Vinaya because of its treatment of offenses, their origination, their cessation, and the methods for emerging from them.
[This is taught] by way of the person, the designation, and the detailed determination [of these]. // AMsa_11.4 //
It should be understood by way of transgression, origination, emergence, and renunciation.
Among these, transgression consists of the five classes of offenses.
The origination of offenses is due to ignorance, negligence, abundance of afflictions, and lack of respect.
Emergence [from an offense] is by way of intention, not by means of punitive action.
There are seven kinds of deliverance.
Confession;
the acceptance of disciplinary measures such as those imposed on one to whom the training has been given (*śikṣādattaka*);
and the re-illumination [of the rule] through a further explanation when a precept has already been prescribed.
Relaxation [of the offense] occurs through ignorance, because the training rule has been relaxed by the entire Saṃgha.

Transformation of the basis occurs when there is a change of sexual characteristics for a monk or a nun, whereby the offense becomes non-common [to the other gender]. Thorough investigation is a specific form of investigation by means of the summaries of the Dharma.

And there is the attainment of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-pratilambha*) through the vision of the truths, because of the attainment of the Dharma when even minor and very minor offenses cease to exist. Furthermore, the Vinaya should be understood through four kinds of meanings: first, from the perspective of the person (*pudgala*), referring to the one depending upon whom a training rule is prescribed.
By way of designation (*prajñapti*), when an offense has been reported by an individual, the Teacher assembles the community and proclaims the training rule (*śikṣā*).

By way of detailed exposition (*pravibhāga*), there is the analysis of that recitation (*uddeśa*) once the training rule has been proclaimed. And by way of determination (*viniścaya*), there is the definitive assessment of how an offense occurs therein, or how it does not constitute an offense.
Regarding the search for the attainment of the object of focus, there are three verses:
The object of focus is considered to be the dharmas, both internal and external; it is twofold.
Attainment occurs through the two meanings of the two, and through the non-apprehension of the two. (AMsa 11.5)
... external, internal, and both external and internal.

Among these, that which functions as the grasper, such as the body and so forth, is internal; that which functions as the grasped is external; and the two suchnesses of those very [two] are the [internal and external].
Therein, the attainment of the two objects—internal and external—is by means of the twofold sense, respectively.

If one perceives the object of the grasper as non-different from the object of the grasped, and the object of the grasped as non-different from the object of the grasper, then the attainment of the suchness (*tathatā*) of both together— the internal and external objects— should be understood to arise from the non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) of those very two,
through the sustained concentration (*pradhāraṇā*) of one who has gained confidence in the meaning as it was explained by means of mental discursive thoughts (*manojalpa*).
Because of the manifestation of meaning, because of discursive thought, and because of the mind's abiding upon the name.
The attainment of the objective support of the Dharma occurs through the three types of knowledge, beginning with that derived from hearing;
and the threefold attainment of the objective support previously mentioned is based upon that.

Furthermore, the attainment of the objective support of the Dharma occurs through three types of knowledge consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation. In that regard, for one who has clarity regarding the meaning as it was taught, there is the attainment [of the Dharma] through knowledge consisting of hearing, by means of mental verbalizations (*manojalpa*)— that is, by means of conceptual constructions (*saṃkalpa*)— while the mind is concentrated and by means of its sustained application.
"Of one who is serene" means of one who is resolved and certain. "From sustained attention" means from discernment.
Through sustained attention to the appearance of an object arising from verbal expression, its attainment occurs by means of that which consists of reflection (*cintāmayī*).
If one perceives that this object appears solely from mental discourse (*manojalpa*) and nothing other than mental discourse— as stated in the section on "attaining the twofold objective"—

then its attainment should be understood as occurring through the knowledge consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya-jñāna*), by means of the mind's abiding in the name, due to the non-apprehension of duality, as stated in the section on "attaining the twofold objective. For this very reason, the aforementioned threefold attainment of the objective should be understood as being based upon the attainment of the objective that is the Dharma (*dharmālambana*).

In the search for mental attention (*manasikāra*), there are five verses: One belongs to the three realms, another performs its function; one has a basis accompanied by obstruction, and another establishes resolute conviction (*adhimukti*); and another produces intense desire.

The basis is twofold, being either deficient or complete; it consists of both that with discursive thought and that without discursive thought, as well as that which is associated with gnosis and has the nature of the secret essence of yoga.
This [object] is both unified and differentiated;
it is fivefold and sevenfold, and its thorough knowledge is fivefold.
The thirty-seven aspects pertain to cultivation;
this [path] has the two paths as its intrinsic nature, possesses two benefits, and is receptive.
The preparatory, the sovereign, the limited, and that which is vast in nature—
this attention (manaskāra) of yogins is considered to be of all types.

Mental attention is of eighteen kinds: that which is determined by the realm, that which performs its function, that which is distinguished by its basis, that which establishes resolute conviction, that which generates desire, that which is dependent on meditative concentration, that which is associated with knowledge, that which has a combined object, that which has a distinct object, that which is determined by thorough knowledge, and that which has entered into the modes of cultivation.

The mental engagement consisting of the nature of the path of calm abiding and special insight; the mental engagement of benefit; the receptive mental engagement; the preparatory mental engagement; the mental engagement of mastery; the limited mental engagement; and the extensive mental engagement.
Among these, that which is determined by realm is that which is determined by the lineage of the śrāvakas and so forth.
That which performs the function is that which possesses the accumulated provisions.
That which is distinguished by its basis is that which has as its basis either the household life with its constraints or the life of renunciation free from constraints.
That which establishes resolute conviction is that which is accompanied by the recollection of the Buddha.
That which generates desire is accompanied by conviction;

that which relies on meditative concentration is accompanied by the preparatory and fundamental concentrations, as well as by [the states of] mere vitarka and vicāra, and by the absence of vitarka and vicāra.

That which is associated with knowledge is the secret essence of yoga (*yogopaniṣad*) accompanied by yoga; furthermore, it consists respectively of that consisting of hearing (*śruta-maya*), that consisting of reflection (*cintā-maya*), and that consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*).

The [yoga] with a combined object (*saṃbhinnālambana*) is fivefold, having as its objects: the discourses (*sūtra*), the summaries (*uddāna*), the verses (*gāthā*), the aphorisms (*nipāta*), and whatever has been memorized and taught.

The [yoga] with a distinct object (*vibhinnālambana*) is sevenfold: having as its objects the name (*nāman*), the phrase (*pada*), the phoneme (*vyañjana*), the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*), material phenomena (*rūpi-dharma*), and immaterial phenomena (*arūpi-dharma*).
Furthermore, therein, that which has material phenomena as its object is that which has the body as its object;
that which has immaterial phenomena as its object is that which has feeling, mind, and mental factors as its objects.

That which is determined by full comprehension (*parijñā-niyata*) refers to the object to be fully comprehended, the meaning to be fully comprehended, the full comprehension itself, the fruit of full comprehension, and the realization thereof.
In this context, the object to be fully comprehended is suffering; the meaning to be fully comprehended is its very impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness;
and the full comprehension is the path.
The fruit of full comprehension is liberation;
the realization of that is the knowledge and vision of liberation.
One who has entered the modes of cultivation cultivates four modes and cultivates thirty-seven modes.

In that regard, cultivation is fourfold: cultivation of the aspect of the selflessness of persons, cultivation of the aspect of the selflessness of phenomena, cultivation of the aspect of vision, and cultivation of the aspect of knowledge.
Therein, cultivation is thirty-sevenfold:

cultivation of the aspect of the unattractive, cultivation of the aspect of suffering, cultivation of the aspect of impermanence, and cultivation of the aspect of selflessness, within the applications of mindfulness.

In the context of the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), there is cultivation in the mode of acquisition, cultivation in the mode of practice, cultivation in the mode of elimination, and cultivation in the mode of the antidote.
There is cultivation of mental attention that serves as the antidote to contentment when one generates desire;
and there is cultivation of mental attention that serves as the antidote to distraction and doubt when one exerts effort and initiates vigor, respectively.
The cultivation of the aspect of concentration as an antidote to restlessness occurs when one applies the mind;
the cultivation of the aspect of concentration as an antidote to laxity occurs when one exerts the mind.
These should be understood respectively within the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

For one whose mind is stabilized, there is the cultivation of the aspect of conviction regarding supramundane attainment; just as there is the cultivation of the aspect of conviction, so too are there the cultivation of the aspect of exertion, the cultivation of the aspect of non-forgetfulness of the Dharma, the cultivation of the aspect of mental stability, the cultivation of the aspect of discernment, and [the cultivation] with respect to the faculties (*indriya*).
These same five, when their opposites have been eliminated, constitute the mental applications (*manaskāra*) with respect to the powers (*bala*).

In the case of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), there is the cultivation of the aspect of the manifestation of perfect awakening; therein, the cultivation of the aspects of investigation, enthusiasm, joy, flexibility, and stability of mind, as well as equanimity.

There is the cultivation of the aspect of certainty regarding attainment; the cultivation of the aspect of guarding the ground of preparation; the cultivation of the aspect of the attainment of others;

the cultivation of the aspect of entering the morality dear to the noble ones (*āryakānta-śīla*); the cultivation of the aspect of the practice of a refined way of life; and the cultivation of the aspect of the repeated practice of the path previously cultivated and attained.

Regarding the limbs of the path (*mārgāṅga*), there is the cultivation of the aspect of not forgetting the sign of the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthitinimitta*), and the cultivation of the aspect of the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*) through abiding in the signless (*animitta*).
There is no specific explanation regarding the nature of the path as the cultivation of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
The mental attention of benefit (*anuśaṃsamanaskāra*) is twofold: that which removes coarseness (*dauṣṭhulya*) and [that which brings about] the attainment of the fruit.
And there is the removal of the signs of views.

The receptive [mental application] is that which receives instruction from Buddhas and Bodhisattvas within the stream of the Dharma. There are five types of preparatory mental application regarding the domain of meditative concentration.

The application of discerning enumeration is that by which one discerns the enumeration of names, phrases, and phonemes within the sūtras and other texts. The application of discerning occurrence is that by which one discerns two types of occurrence: the occurrence of limited measure in the case of phonemes, and the occurrence of unlimited measure in the case of names and phrases.
The application of discerning conceptual construction is that by which, based on a dyad, one discerns the conceptual construction of a dyad.

Based on the conceptualization of names, there is the conceptualization of objects; based on the conceptualization of objects, there is the conceptualization of names. That which is non-conceptual is the syllable.
There is the application consisting of sequential observation, by which one observes that the engagement in grasping an object is preceded by the grasping of a name;
and there is the application consisting of penetration.

Furthermore, that [penetration] should be understood as being of eleven kinds: by way of penetrating adventitiousness; by way of penetrating the signs of manifestation; by way of penetrating the non-apprehension of objects; by way of penetrating the non-apprehension of apprehension; by way of penetrating the *dharmadhātu*;

by way of penetrating the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*); by way of penetrating the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*); by way of penetrating the inferior disposition; and by way of penetrating the noble and magnanimous disposition.

Through the penetration of the establishment of the Dharma as it has been realized, and through the penetration of the established Dharma, the mental application of mastery (*vaśavarti-manaskāra*) is threefold: perfectly pure regarding the obstructions, perfectly pure regarding the obstructions of afflictions and the knowable (*kleśa-jñeyāvaraṇa*), and perfectly pure regarding the accomplishment of qualities. There are two verses concerning the search for the reality of phenomena (*dharma-tattva*).
Reality is that which is eternally devoid of duality, the basis of error, and absolutely impossible to express in words; it is of a non-proliferated nature.
It is to be known, abandoned, and purified, and is considered by nature to be stainless, its purification from afflictions being like that of space, gold, or water. (MSA 11.13)
Reality is eternally devoid of duality; it is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because it is absolutely non-existent in the form of the characteristics of the grasped and the grasper.
It is the basis of delusion, for by means of it, that [imagined nature] is conceptualized.
The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is inexpressible and consists of the absence of conceptual proliferation (*aprapañca*).

In this regard, the first reality is to be fully known, the second is to be abandoned, and the third is to be purified; it is pure by nature from adventitious defilements. For that which is pure by nature, its purification from afflictions is like [the purification of] space, gold, and water. Indeed, space and the others are not impure by nature.
Nor is it maintained that their purification does not result from the removal of adventitious stains.
Indeed, there exists nothing else in the world apart from that [reality], yet the entire world remains utterly deluded regarding it.
How has this manner of worldly delusion arisen—that one is intent upon what is non-existent while completely abandoning what is real?
Indeed, there is nothing else whatsoever in the world apart from this dharmadhātu characterized in such a way, because the dharma-nature is non-different from the dharma.
The remainder has already been explained.
There are fifteen verses on the investigation of reality as being like an illusion:
"Just as an illusion is described, so is the unreal imagination (abhūtaparikalpa) described;
just as that which is produced by illusion, so is the error of duality described. (AMsa 11.15)

Just as a magical illusion consists of wood, clods of earth, and so forth, which are causes of delusion and are manipulated by a mechanical device, so too should the unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*)—the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)—be understood.

Just as the forms of elephants, horses, gold, and so on, produced by that magic, appear within that illusion as if they were real entities, so too within that unreal imagination, the delusion of duality appears in the form of the grasped and the grasper; this should be understood as the aspect of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Just as its non-existence in that [object] is accepted as the ultimate truth (paramārtha),
so too its perception is accepted as conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya).

Just as the absence of "elephant-ness" and so forth exists in that which is produced by illusion, so too is the non-existence of the imagined dual characteristic accepted as the ultimate reality within that dependent nature.
Just as that illusory creation is perceived as having the form of an elephant and so forth, so too is the unreal imagination perceived as conventional truth.
And just as, in the absence of that [elephant], the manifestation of its cause is apprehended; [so too is the dependent nature apprehended in the absence of the imagined].
Likewise, upon the revolution of the basis, that which was unreal imagination is attained [as transformed].

Just as when the illusory creation has ceased, the reality of its cause— the wood or other material— is perceived, so too, upon the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), because of the absence of the delusion of duality, the true reality of the unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*) is perceived.
Just as the world, being undeluded regarding that cause, would act according to its desire.
Upon transformation, the husband likewise becomes a self-controlled ascetic, free from attachment and acting according to his will.

Just as the world, being unerring regarding its cause—such as wood and so forth—acts according to its desire and is independent, so too the Noble One, having undergone the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) and being free from error, acts according to his will and is independent.
Its appearance exists there, yet its substantial reality is not found;
therefore, existence and non-existence are predicated of illusions and the like.
This verse has its meaning already explained:
"Therein, existence is not non-existence, and non-existence is indeed existence."
And the non-distinction between existence and non-existence is established in the case of illusions and the like.
Therein, existence is not non-existence; that which has the appearance of such [an elephant] is not non-existent.
And non-existence is indeed existence; that which is the non-existence of "elephant-ness" and so forth is not non-existent.
Furthermore, no distinction is established between those two—existence and non-existence—in the case of illusions and the like.
For that which is the existence of its form there is precisely the non-existence of elephant-ness and so forth;
and that which is the non-existence of elephant-ness and so forth is precisely the existence of its form.
Thus, the appearance of duality exists here, yet its substantial reality is not found;
therefore, both existence and non-existence are predicated of form and the other aggregates.
Likewise, here in the unreal imagination (abhūtaparikalpa), there is the appearance of duality, but the existence of duality does not exist.
Therefore, both existence and non-existence are predicated of form and the other [objects], which have the nature of unreal imagination.
Therein, existence is not non-existence, nor is non-existence simply existence.
And the non-distinction between existence and non-existence is established with respect to form and the other [sense objects].
Therein, existence is not non-existence,
nor is non-existence simply existence; rather, it is the appearance of duality.
That which is the non-existence of duality and the lack of distinction between existence and non-existence is predicated of form and the other aggregates;
for that very existence of appearance is itself the non-existence of duality.
It is intended for the purpose of negating the appearances of superimposition and denial,
and also for the purpose of negating the proceeding by means of the Hīnayāna.
But for what purpose is this absolute nature of existence and non-existence, as well as their lack of distinction, asserted?
It is asserted, respectively,
for the purpose of negating the appearances of superimposition and denial.
And it is for the purpose of preventing departure via the Hīnayāna:
for having realized the non-existence of non-existence, one does not engage in superimposition;
and having realized the existence of existence, one does not engage in denial.
And having understood the lack of distinction between those two, one does not tremble at existence; therefore, one does not depart by means of the Hīnayāna.
The cause of error and the error itself are held to be the representation of form (*rūpa-vijñapti*);
and the representation that is non-material (*arūpin*) would not exist [as such] due to the non-existence of the other. (AMsa 11.24)

The representation of a sign (*nimitta-vijñapti*) which arises from the error regarding form (*rūpa-bhrānti*) is accepted as the representation of form (*rūpa-vijñapti*), which is designated by the term "form.
However, that error regarding form is itself a formless representation (*arūpiṇī vijñapti*).
Because the representation of form would not exist [without that error], the other—the formless representation—would also not exist.
Because of the absence of a cause,
the duality is illustrated by the delusion of grasping at the form of an illusory elephant;
therein, the duality does not exist in the way it appears, yet the duality is nonetheless perceived.
The duality is taught due to the error of grasping at the reflection and the skeleton;
therein, the duality does not exist in the way it appears, yet duality is nevertheless perceived.

The duality of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject is illustrated by the error of perceiving the form of an illusory elephant; therein, just as the duality does not exist yet the duality is nevertheless perceived,
so too for one who attends to a reflection or a skeleton, the duality is illustrated as before, arising from the error of grasping that [reflection or skeleton].
Because they exist in such a way and do not exist in such a way, due to the distinction between existence and non-existence,
those phenomena characterized by delusion are both existent and non-existent, like illusory things.
Those phenomena which have the characteristic of delusion and possess the nature of the discordant factors are both existent and non-existent, and are like an illusion.
For what reason?
Because they exist as such through their state of being unreal mental construction (*abhūtaparikalpa*).

Because they do not exist in that way by way of being apprehended object and apprehending subject, and because existence and non-existence are indistinguishable in those two respects, they are both existent and non-existent, and even illusion has such characteristics; therefore, they are like illusions.
Because they do not exist in that way... [and so on].
Because they exist as such and because they do not exist,
those remedial factors which have been taught as being like an illusion are without defining characteristics.

Even those remedial dharmas taught by the Buddha, such as the applications of mindfulness and so forth, are indicated to be without characteristics and like illusions. Why? Because they do not exist in the way they are grasped by the foolish, nor do they exist in the way they have been taught.
Thus, because they do not exist in the way they were demonstrated by the Buddha— such as the descent into the womb, birth, renunciation, and perfect enlightenment—
they appear despite being without characteristics and non-existent; therefore, they are like an illusion,
just as one illusory king is defeated by another illusory king.
Those who perceive all phenomena as being without a self are the sons of the Victors.

Those factors that are remedial are comparable to a phantom king, because they exercise sovereignty over purification in the abandonment of affliction; those factors that are afflictive are also comparable to a king, because they exercise sovereignty in the production of affliction.
Therefore, the defeat of the afflictions by those counteractive factors should be viewed as the defeat of a king by a phantom king.
And through that knowledge, Bodhisattvas become free from pride regarding both sides.
There is a verse for the purpose of illustration:

Like an illusion, a dream, a mirage, and a reflection; like a flash of lightning and an echo; comparable to the moon's reflection in water, and again equal to a magical creation—six, six, two, and again six, and two are considered as such, and three each: indeed, the conditioned phenomena (saṃskāras) have been taught here and there by the Buddhas, the supreme awakened ones.
As for that which was said by the Blessed One— that phenomena are like an illusion, up to being like a magical creation— therein,
phenomena like an illusion are the six internal sense bases (*āyatana*),
because they appear in such a way despite the non-existence of a self, a living being, and so forth.
The six external sense bases are like dreams, because their enjoyment lacks any real substance.
The two categories of phenomena—mind and mental factors—are like mirages, because they produce delusion.
Furthermore, the six internal sense bases are like reflections, because they are the reflections of prior karma.

The six external sense bases alone are like reflections, because they are shadows of the internal sense bases, arising through their dominant influence. "Six are considered pairs" means that the six are regarded as being in pairs.
The dharmas of the teaching are like echoes.
The dharmas based on meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are like the reflection of the moon in water, because concentration, being clear, takes the place of water.
They are like magical emanations (*nirmāṇa*) in their undertaking of intentional rebirth in existence, because all their activities and applications are free from affliction.
Regarding the investigation of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), there is this verse:
Unreal imagination is neither real nor unreal, and it is indeed non-conceptual; it is neither conceptual nor non-conceptual—all that is to be known is thus described.
Unreal imagination (*abhūtakalpa*) is that imagination which is not conducive to supramundane knowledge (*lokottarajñāna*).
That which is neither real nor unreal is that which is conducive to it, up to the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
Non-imagination (*akalpa*) is suchness (*tathatā*) and supramundane knowledge.
It is neither conceptual construction (*kalpa*) nor non-conceptualization; it is mundane knowledge obtained subsequent to supramundane [realization].
And all that which is to be known (*jñeya*) is just this much.
There are two verses concerning the investigation of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*).

From their own constituent elements, conceptual constructions arise as manifestations of duality; they are devoid of the substance of duality, yet they proceed with the activity of ignorance and the afflictions.
"From its own constituent element" means from the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which is the causal factor of existence.
"Appearing as a duality" means appearing as the grasped and the grasper.
"Together with ignorance and the afflictions, these function"—thus they are called those whose functioning is accompanied by ignorance and afflictions.
"Free from the two substances" means free from the substance of the grasped and the substance of the grasper.
In this way, affliction is to be investigated.
The attainment of a specific object occurs through the application of abiding in one's own realm.
For these very [appearances] proceed as non-dual manifestations, like a hide or a reed.
"Attainment of the specific object" refers to that previously mentioned acquisition of the dharma as an object.

"By means of application to the stationing in one's own realm" means that one's own realm is the suchness (*tathatā*) of conceptual constructions; "stationing" therein is because the mind is stationed upon the name;
and "by means of application" means by way of repeated practice.
Through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), for one whose basis has been transformed (*parāvṛttāśraya*), those very same conceptual constructions proceed as manifestations of non-duality,
like leather and like an arrow-shaft.
For just as that very same leather becomes soft through the removal of its hardness;
Just as that very arrow becomes straight by means of heating it with fire, so too,

through the cultivation of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), when liberation of mind and wisdom is attained, for one whose basis has been transformed (*parāvṛttāśraya*), those very same conceptual constructions no longer proceed with the appearance of duality; in this way, purification (*vyavadāna*) is to be sought.
There are two verses concerning the investigation of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*):
The mind is held to manifest as a duality, appearing as passion and so forth; likewise, it appears as faith and so forth. There is no separate entity that is either defiled or wholesome.
It is held that mind-only itself appears as a duality: the appearance of the grasped and the appearance of the grasper.
Likewise, it is held that this very same [mind] appears as the afflictions such as passion, or as wholesome dharmas such as faith.
However, there is no afflicted dharma characterized by passion and so forth, nor any wholesome dharma characterized by faith and so forth, that exists apart from the appearance of those [objects];
just as there is nothing characterized by duality apart from the appearance of duality.
Thus, the mind proceeds with variegated appearances and variegated forms.
Thus, it is held that there is an absence of the appearance [of objects], but not an absence of phenomena;
in that regard, mind itself is the reality, and it proceeds as a manifold appearance.
Successively, there is the appearance of attachment, or the appearance of aversion, or the appearance of other such factors;
and simultaneously, there is the appearance of various forms, such as the forms of faith and so forth.
This "appearance" (ābhāsa) is the presence or absence [of these factors] within the mind during its afflicted or wholesome states.
But it is not [the case] for wholesome phenomena (*dharma*), because apart from their appearance, they lack that characteristic.
There are eight verses regarding the investigation of characteristics;
with one verse there is the summary, and with the remaining ones there is the detailed explanation.

The objective, the characteristic, and the indication itself have been fully elucidated by the Perfectly Awakened Ones through their various classifications for the sake of favoring sentient beings. (AMsa 11.36)

By this, the summary is given: that mind which is accompanied by views, its state therein, and its lack of transformation—this is the object of definition in brief; however, it is immeasurable in its detailed divisions.
In this context, "mind" refers to consciousness and form;
"view" refers to mental factors;
and "state" refers to factors dissociated from the mind.
Unchangingness refers to the unconditioned, such as space and so forth, because its representation proceeds eternally in that manner.
Thus, in brief, the fivefold object of characterization is immeasurable in its detailed divisions. [The three natures are:
the sign of the perception of an object according to how it is expressed in speech, the latent predisposition for that, and...
Therefore, the manifestation of objects is also the imagined characteristic.
The characteristic is, in brief, threefold: the imagined characteristic and so forth.

Among these, the imagined characteristic is threefold: the sign (*nimitta*) of the perception of an object according to how it is expressed; the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) for that expression; and the object that appears from that predisposition even to those unskilled in linguistic convention, even without the perception of an object according to how it is expressed.

In this context, the mental perception of an object according to its verbal expression is the "perception of an object as it is spoken" (*yathājalpārthasaṃjñā*). Its objective support is the "sign" (*nimitta*). Thus, both that which is imagined and the cause from which it arises—the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*)—are intended here as the "imagined characteristic" (*parikalpitalakṣaṇa*).
This refers to the appearance of an object according to its name, and the appearance of a name according to its object.
For the imagined characteristic has non-conceptualization as its cause.

Another formulation is as follows: "according to the name and the object" (*yathānāmārtha*) means the manifestation of the object and the name; "the manifestation according to the name and the object" (*yathānāmārthaprakhyānatā*) means that if the object manifests according to the name, or the name manifests according to the object—this is the object of unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*), which is the imagined characteristic (*parikalpitalakṣaṇa*). For this much alone is imagined, namely, either the name or the object.
The imagination of the unreal, which appears in a threefold and threefold manner and is characterized by the grasped and the grasper, is indeed the characteristic of the dependent nature.
It has a threefold and a threefold appearance; thus it is "that which has a threefold-threefold appearance.
Among these, the threefold appearance consists of the appearance of words, the appearance of objects, and the appearance of bodies.
Furthermore, there is a threefold appearance: the appearance of mind (*manas*), apprehension (*udgraha*), and conceptualization (*vikalpa*). "Mind" is that which is always afflicted;
"apprehension" refers to the five bodies of consciousness (*pañca-vijñānakāya*).
Conceptual construction is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Among these, the first threefold appearance has the characteristic of the grasped (*grāhya*),
and the second has the characteristic of the grasper (*grāhaka*).
Thus, this unreal imagination (abhūtaparikalpa) is the characteristic of the dependent nature (paratantra).
That which is both non-existence and existence, the equality of existence and non-existence,
the unpeaceful yet peaceful, and the non-conceptual— this is the characteristic of the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna).

Furthermore, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*) is suchness (*tathatā*). For it is the non-existence of all imagined phenomena (*parikalpita*), yet it is not a non-existence because it exists as the absence of that [imagined nature].
It is the equality of existence and non-existence because there is no distinction between those two—existence and non-existence.
It is both unpeaceful due to adventitious secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and peaceful due to its natural purity (*prakṛti-pariśuddha*).
And it is non-conceptual because it is not within the sphere of conceptualization due to its lack of proliferation (*niṣprapañcatā*).

By this, the threefold characteristic of suchness is fully elucidated: its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), its characteristic as affliction and purification, and its characteristic as non-conceptuality.
Thus, the threefold characteristic has been explained.
Taking the motionless dharma as an object, there is thorough mental attention,
the abiding of the mind in the realm [of reality], and the vision of the meaning of existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, the stage of yoga characterized by signs (*lakṣaṇā yogabhūmi*) is fivefold:
the basis (*ādhāra*), the foundation (*ādhāna*), the mirror (*ādarśa*), the light (*āloka*), and the support (*āśraya*).
Among these, the "basis" is the outflow-dharma (*niṣpandadharma*); that which was taught by the Buddha as his realization is the outflow of that realization.
Application is appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manaskāra*).
The mirror is the mind’s abiding in the realm (*dhātu*), which is concentration (*samādhi*); this is what was previously described as "abiding in the name.

Illumination is the vision of objects according to their existence or non-existence; it is supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-prajñā*) by which one sees what exists as existing and what does not exist as non-existent, exactly as it is.
The basis is the revolution of the basis;
it is the attainment of equality therein, for the noble lineage is stainless.
It is considered to have the characteristic of being equal, distinguished, and neither deficient nor excessive. (AMsa 11.43)
The attainment of equality occurs within the untainted realm (anāsravadhātu), the noble lineage (āryagotra), together with other noble ones;
and that stainless noble lineage of the Buddhas is equal to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas by virtue of the equality of liberation.
It is distinguished by five distinctions:
by the distinction of purity, due to the purification of the afflictions along with their latent tendencies;
and by the distinction of complete purity, due to the complete purity of the field.
By way of the distinction of body, through being the *dharmakāya*;
by way of the distinction of enjoyment, through the uninterrupted engagement in the enjoyment of the Dharma within the circles of assemblies;
and by way of the distinction of activity, through the performance of deeds for the benefit of sentient beings via emanations such as dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven.
Furthermore, there is no decrease when the side of affliction ceases, nor any increase when the side of purification arises; this fivefold stage of yoga is its characteristic (*lakṣaṇā*),
for in this way that which is characterized (*lakṣya*) is characterized.

There are six verses concerning the search for liberation: The transformation of the appearance of objects, the body, and the [sensory] bases is the untainted realm (*anāsravo dhātu*), resulting from the transformation of the seeds; and it is the omnipresent foundation. (AMsa 11.44)
"From the transformation of the seed" means from the transformation of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
The transformation of the consciousnesses that manifest as objects, places, and bodies is the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*), which is liberation.
And that is the omnipresent basis, pertaining to both Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

There are four kinds of mastery: over the activity of the mind, over the grasping [of objects], over conceptualization, and indeed over non-conceptualization; as well as over the field, over gnosis, and over action. (MSA 11.45)
The meaning is: through the revolution of the mind (*manas*), the grasping (*udgraha*), and the conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Mastery (*vaśitā*) becomes fourfold, respectively, in regard to non-conceptuality, the field, gnosis, and action.
Furthermore, that fourfold mastery exists on the three stages beginning with the Immovable (*acalā*).
In one [state] there are two kinds, while in the other there is considered to be a single mastery each.
And this fourfold mastery should be understood as existing within the three stages beginning with the Immovable (Acalā).
On the single stage of the Immovable, it is twofold:
[mastery] regarding non-conceptuality, because there is no conceptualization through volitional effort; and [mastery] regarding non-manifestation.
And regarding the field, it is through the purification of the Buddha-field.

On each of the other stages, there is one mastery: on the stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī*), there is mastery over knowledge due to the attainment of the specific analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*);
and on the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), there is mastery over action because of the unimpeded nature of the activities of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*).
Having understood the two kinds of selflessness here, and having known that [selflessness] as it exists in the world to be equal, the wise one enters reality by way of grasping.
Then, from the mind abiding therein, even that [reality] does not appear; that non-appearance is liberation, the supreme cessation of apprehension.
There is another formulation of liberation:

having understood the two kinds of selflessness pertaining to the three realms of existence, and having known that twofold selflessness equally— namely, the absence of an imagined person and the absence of imagined phenomena, but not through absolute non-existence— the bodhisattva [attains liberation].

One enters into reality by means of grasping [the fact] that this is mere representation (*vijñaptimātra*), thinking, "This is merely a grasping. Then, because the mind abides in that reality of mere representation, even that mere representation no longer appears as reality to the mind.
Liberation is the non-apprehension of that [object], which is the supreme disappearance of apprehension due to the non-apprehension of both the person (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*).
For when there is a basis and the accumulation [of merit and wisdom] is present, seeing it as mere name, one sees indeed that mere name; and seeing that, one no longer sees even that. (MSA 11.48)
Another sequence:
"the support" refers to what is heard; "from the equipment" means because one has acquired the previous equipment for one who has gathered the equipment;

"when the support exists" refers to appropriate mental attention (*yonisomanaskāra*), wherein one perceives [phenomena] as mere names—that is, as mere verbal designations devoid of objective referents.
For one sees "mere name," that is, mere representation (*vijñaptimātra*), on the grounds that the four formless aggregates are merely names.
Seeing that, one no longer sees even that [representation], because when the object is absent, its representation is not seen. This non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) is liberation.
This mind, accompanied by the latent dysfunctions (*sadauṣṭhulya*), is bound by the snare of the view of self.
But its cessation is considered to result from abiding within the internal.
Another way [of explaining] this mind is that it proceeds through births accompanied by *dauṣṭhulya*. By stating "bound by the view of self," he shows the cause of *dauṣṭhulya*;
because it is bound by two kinds of views of self, it is therefore "accompanied by *dauṣṭhulya*."
"But cessation [occurs] through its abiding within itself" means that because that mind remains in the mind alone, there is no apprehension of an object.
Regarding the investigation into the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), there are two verses:
"Because of non-existence by way of its own self, and because of the non-abiding in intrinsic nature."
And because it is like a grasping and because that [object] does not exist, the absence of intrinsic nature is asserted.
The absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) of phenomena is due to their being dependent on conditions, because they do not exist by themselves.

It is the absence of intrinsic nature because they do not exist through their own self, since those things that have ceased do not arise again with that same self. It is the absence of intrinsic nature because of the non-abiding of intrinsic nature, due to momentariness. This threefold absence of intrinsic nature should be understood as following upon the three characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
And because of the absence of that [grasping], there is the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*); "because of the absence of that" means because of the absence of intrinsic nature.

Just as the grasping at intrinsic nature by the foolish—whether as permanent, blissful, pure, or by some other imagined characteristic (*parikalpitalakṣaṇa*)—that intrinsic nature does not exist; for that reason also, the lack of intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dharmāṇām*) is asserted.
Established by way of being devoid of intrinsic nature, they are successively dependent;
[they are] non-arising, non-ceasing, primordial peace, and parinirvāṇa.
(MSA 68) ... By virtue of being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), there is non-arising and so forth.
For that which is without intrinsic nature is unarisen; that which is unarisen is unceasing; and that which is unceasing is quiescent from the beginning.
"That which is primordially peaceful is by nature in a state of parinirvāṇa"— through these successive supports of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*),
non-arising and the other [characteristics] are established by way of this lack of intrinsic nature.
This is the noble verse concerning the pursuit of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*).
Regarding identity, otherness, specific characteristics, itself, and then change,
as well as affliction and distinction— patience regarding these is called the non-arising of dharmas.
The receptivity toward the non-arising of the eight [types of] phenomena is the "receptivity to the non-arising of phenomena" (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*).
First, regarding cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), there is no such thing as its initial arising.

Regarding identity and difference among preceding and succeeding [moments], it is not the case that those very same phenomena which arose previously arise again within cyclic existence, because they do not arise in that same state.
Nor [does it apply] to others, because there is no arising of a previously non-existent mode;
for the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) within the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) never arises at any time,
nor does the dependent nature (*paratantra*) arise by itself.

Regarding change: for the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*), there is indeed no arising of change. Regarding affliction: when affliction has been abandoned, those who have attained the knowledge of destruction do not see the arising of affliction again.
Regarding excellence: for the bodies of the Buddha-qualities (*buddhadharmakāya*), there is indeed no arising of excellence.
Thus, the patience regarding these phenomena that are not subject to arising is called "the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena.
There are seven verses on the search for the single vehicle:
because of the equality of the selflessness of phenomena and liberation, and because of the difference in lineages...
And because of the attainment of two intentions, because of emanation, and because of the ultimate limit, there is the single vehicle (ekayāna).

There is the single vehicle (ekayānatā) because of the equality of the dharma, since the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) of the śrāvakas and others is undifferentiated—this being so on the grounds that the "vehicle" is that which is to be traveled; there is the single vehicle because of the equality of selflessness, since the absence of self (ātmābhāvatā) is common to the śrāvakas and others—this being so on the grounds that the "vehicle" is the traveler; and there is the single vehicle because of the equality of liberation, this being so on the grounds that the "vehicle" is that which goes.
The single vehicle (ekayānatā) exists due to the distinction of lineages (*gotrabheda*):

because those of the indeterminate śrāvaka lineage attain deliverance by means of the Mahāyāna, it is called a "vehicle" (*yāna*) in the sense that they go by means of it. Furthermore, the single vehicle exists due to the attainment of two kinds of intention: because Buddhas have attained the intention of self toward all sentient beings, and because śrāvakas who are fixed in that lineage [attain the intention of others].

Because of their previous conduct in accumulating the requisites for enlightenment, they have attained a disposition fixed upon non-self; because they have obtained the conviction that the continuum [of the Buddha and themselves] is undivided, they obtain a specific portion of the Tathāgatas' favor through the power of the Buddhas.
Thus, by attaining a single-minded disposition, the Buddhas and their śrāvakas are of one vehicle (*ekayānatā*) due to this oneness.

There is the single vehicle by way of emanation (*nirmāṇa*), as it has been said: "I have attained final nirvāṇa through the Śrāvaka vehicle many hundreds of times," because such an emanation is displayed for the sake of those to be trained.
There is also the single vehicle by way of the ultimate limit (*paryanta*), because there is nothing further to be traveled; it is called a vehicle in that sense.
Thus, Buddhahood itself is the single vehicle, according to various sūtras.
In that sense, the state of a single vehicle (ekayānatā) is to be understood; it is not, however, that the three vehicles do not exist.
For what purpose, then, was the state of a single vehicle taught by the Buddhas with various underlying intentions?
It was for the sake of attracting some and for the sake of sustaining others.
For the perfectly awakened Buddhas have taught that there is a single vehicle for those who are not fixed [in their destiny].

"For the sake of attracting some" refers to those of the śrāvaka lineage who are indeterminate; "and for the sake of sustaining others" refers to those of the bodhisattva lineage who are indeterminate.
The indeterminate śrāvaka is of two kinds: according to whether the goal of the vehicle has been seen or not yet seen.
He has seen the truth, he is free from passion, and even though not yet free from passion, he is of mild temperament.
Furthermore, the śrāvaka who is not fixed [in his destiny] should be understood as being of two kinds:

one who has seen the goal of the vehicle and has realized the truths but departs by means of the Mahāyāna, and one who has not seen the goal of the vehicle and has not realized the truths but departs by means of the Mahāyāna. Moreover, the one who has seen the goal is either free from passion for sensual pleasures or not free from passion for sensual pleasures.
And that [person] should be understood as being gentle and slow in progress;
these two types of those who have seen the truth were mentioned,
and they both [possess this quality] because of their dedication of the attained Noble Path toward further existences.
They are endowed with a birth characterized by inconceivable transformation.
And those two, having seen the goal because they have attained the Noble Path,
should be understood as being endowed with a birth resulting from inconceivable transformation (*acintyapariṇāmikī*),
since the transformation of that Noble Path into a birth is indeed inconceivable; therefore, it is called "resulting from inconceivable transformation."
By the power of their vows, one takes birth [in the world],
while the other, through the yoga of non-returning, proceeds by means of emanations.
Of these two, one who is not free from passion takes rebirth according to his wish by the power of his vow;
the other [does so] through emanations by the power of the yoga of non-returning (*anāgāmitā*).
Because they both delight in nirvāṇa, they are considered to be of slow progress.
Again and again, through the application of the activity of one's own mind.

And because both of them delight in nirvāṇa, they are considered to be of slow progress, since they attain full awakening only after a very long time due to the frequent manifestation of their own śrāvaka-mind, which is accompanied by world-weariness.
Having failed to achieve his goal while born in a world without a Buddha, he exerts himself for the sake of meditative concentration;
then, seeking an emanation body, by relying upon it, he attains supreme enlightenment.

Furthermore, one who has seen the truths but is not yet free from passion—being a learner (*śaikṣa*) who has not yet accomplished his purpose—if born in a time devoid of a Buddha, applies himself to meditation with the aim of emanation.
Relying upon that emanation, he gradually attains supreme enlightenment.
It was with reference to him, abiding in these three stages, that the Blessed One spoke in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.

Having been a śrāvaka, one becomes a pratyekabuddha, and then again a buddha. And as in the analogy of fire: when one is in the state of having previously seen the truths, at a time devoid of a Buddha, one personally generates meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), abandons the birth-body (*janmakāya*), and assumes a transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), and when one attains supreme enlightenment (*bodhi*).
Regarding the search for the fields of knowledge, there is this verse:
"Without applying himself to the fivefold field of knowledge, the supreme noble one can by no means attain omniscience.
Thus, for the sake of refuting others, for the sake of assisting them, or for the sake of his own understanding, he indeed applies himself to those fields.
The fields of knowledge are fivefold:
the inner science, the science of logic, the science of grammar, the science of medicine, and the science of arts and crafts.
This demonstrates that for what purpose these should be sought by a bodhisattva.
For the sake of attaining omniscience, he seeks everything without distinction;
however, for the sake of refuting others who lack faith in them, he specifically seeks the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*) and the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*).
Furthermore, for the sake of benefiting others who desire them, he seeks the science of medicine (*cikitsāvidyā*) and the science of arts and crafts (*śilpakarmasthānavidyā*).
The inner science (*adhyātmavidyā*) is for the sake of personal realization.
Regarding the search for the nourishment of the elements (*dhātupuṣṭi*), there are thirteen verses.
Those mental orientations (*manasikāra*) associated with the perfections (*pāramitā*) which serve to fulfill the perfections and lead to the nourishment of the elements are taught by these stanzas.
Satisfaction in perceiving the causes, mindfulness of that basis,
the desire for a common fruit, and resolute conviction according to one's awakening.
These, moreover, range from the mental application of satisfaction in perceiving the cause up to the mental application of ascertaining oneself as supreme.
Among these, first of all, there is the mental application of satisfaction in perceiving the cause.

A bodhisattva established in the lineage (*gotrastha*), perceiving within himself the lineage of the perfections (*pāramitā*), brings about the nourishment of the element (*dhātu*) of the perfections through the joy of finding their cause.

Since one established in the lineage generates the mind set on unexcelled perfect enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*), immediately following this is the mental application (*manasikāra*) of mindfulness of that basis (*niśraya*).
For that bodhisattva, perceiving the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) as the very support for the perfections within himself, reflects thus: "These perfections will certainly reach fulfillment."
For indeed, we possess the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).

For one who has generated the thought of awakening, there is the mental application of desiring a common fruit when engaging in the practice of the perfections for the sake of oneself and others; this is because one forms the intention: "May the fruit of these perfections be shared with others, or may it not be otherwise."

One who applies himself to the welfare of both self and others penetrates the reality of the meaning of non-affliction as the means; therefore, immediately following this is the mental attention consisting of resolute conviction according to awakening (*yathābodhādhimucyanā-manasikāra*).
This sequence should be understood to apply everywhere:

because one forms the volitional construction (*abhisaṃskaraṇa*) that "just as the perfections were fully awakened to by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, will be fully awakened to, and are being fully awakened to, so do I resolutely believe."
Delight through the fourfold majesty, the determination to overcome weariness, and the fourfold practice regarding the discordant factors and their antidotes. (MSA 11.62)

The mental application of rejoicing in the manifestations is the rejoicing in seeing four kinds of manifestations: the abandonment of opposing factors, the maturation of the accumulations, the benefiting of oneself and others, and the bestowing of the fruit of ripening and the fruit of outflow in the future. The mental application of firm resolve regarding tirelessness concerns the maturation of sentient beings and one's own Buddha-qualities; it arises from the formation of a firm resolve that is untiring despite all the misconduct of sentient beings and all falls into suffering.
For the sake of attaining supreme enlightenment,
there is the mental attention toward the fourfold practice regarding both the adverse factors and their remedies: namely,
the confession of the adverse factors such as stinginess and the like, and the rejoicing in the remedies such as generosity and the like.
There is the entreaty of the Buddhas for the sake of teaching the Dharma that has them as its sovereign object,
the dedication of those [roots of merit] toward awakening,
serene confidence, waiting expectantly, and the desire to give to others.
The armor, the vow, and the mental attention of rejoicing.

Regarding the attainment of the power of resolute belief (*adhimukti*), there is the mental application of serene confidence toward the teachings and meanings that have the perfections (*pāramitā*) as their predominant subject. Regarding the search for the Dharma, there is the mental application of receiving [the teaching], by way of grasping that very same Dharma through the practice of non-rejection. Regarding the ten [recitations], there is the mental application of the desire to give, for the sake of illuminating the Dharma and its meaning for others.
With reference to practice, there is the mental attention of armor, because of donning the armor for the sake of fulfilling generosity and the other perfections;
the mental attention of aspiration, for the sake of gathering the conditions necessary to attain their fulfillment;
and the mental attention of rejoicing, because of rejoicing with the thought, "O, may I correctly accomplish [the path] through the practice of generosity and the rest."
These three very same mental attentions (manasikāra) are to be applied within the instruction and admonition (avavādānuśāsanī):
the mental attention to action conjoined with skillful means, because one attends to the practice of giving and so forth in all its modes through intentional thoughts;
and constant eagerness once power has been attained regarding the sixfold giving and so forth, which is wealth.
In ripening, in worship, in service, and in compassion.
The mental application of eagerness is fourfold:
regarding the attainment of capacity in the sixfold giving, beginning with the gift of giving and ending with the gift of wisdom;
likewise in the sixfold [perfections] beginning with ethical discipline.
Through the perfections themselves, one brings beings to maturity by applying the means of attraction;
and in worship, one performs it through giving with the worship of material gain and honor,
and through the remaining perfections with the worship of practice.
One should understand that there is the mental application of zeal toward serving the five kinds of spiritual friends who provide instruction on the perfections without error;
and there is the mental application of compassion through the four immeasurables, being friendly by bestowing gifts and so forth,
and feeling compassion for sentient beings when encountering their stinginess and other such faults.
Joy arises from being endowed with generosity and the other perfections; equanimity arises from the resolute conviction that they are free from affliction;
and there is shame regarding what was not done or what was poorly done, as well as remorse and delight in the [proper] object.
The perception of [others] as enemies, weariness, and the mental state of composing and expounding [the Dharma].

With reference to the quality of shame (*hrī*), there is the mental application of modesty (*lajjā-manaskāra*): it is the sense of shame regarding gifts and so forth that have not been performed, or those performed incompletely or incorrectly; and for one who feels such shame, this leads to non-attachment through the purpose of engaging in what is right and desisting from what is wrong, which functions as a form of remorse (*kaukṛtyāyate*).

With reference to steadfastness (*dhṛti*), there is the mental application of delight (*rati-manaskāra*): because of holding the mind without distraction upon the objective supports of giving and so forth.
There is also the mental application of indefatigability (*akheda-manaskāra*).

The mental application of exertion (*vyāvasāyika-manasikāra*) arises from regarding weariness in the practice of giving and so forth as an enemy. The mental application of composition (*racanā-manasikāra*) arises from the formative activity of composing treatises associated with the perfections.

The mental application of manifestation (*udbhāvanā-manasikāra*) begins with world-knowledge (*lokajñatā*), arising from the formative activity of manifesting that very treatise in the world according to the capacity of the recipients.
Generosity and the other perfections are the refuge for awakening, not Īśvara and the like,
because of the direct experience of both faults and virtues in these two.

The mental application of reliance is for the sake of attaining awakening, relying on generosity and the other perfections rather than on Īśvara and the like; the mental application of analytical knowledge arises from the realization of the faults and virtues of stinginess and its opposite, generosity; there is joy in recollecting the accumulation [of merit] and the vision of its great significance; and there is aspiration for yoga, for non-conceptuality, for its maintenance, and for the arrival of favorable conditions. (AMsa 11.67)

The mental application of joy through recollecting accumulation is so called because it demonstrates the accumulation of the provisions of merit and wisdom through the accumulation of giving and the other perfections. The mental application of demonstrating great significance is so called because it demonstrates that giving and the others have the purpose of attaining great enlightenment by way of their cultivation as factors conducive to awakening.
Furthermore, the mental application of aspiration is of four kinds.
The mental application of longing for yoga arises from the longing to cultivate the yoga of calm abiding and special insight;
the mental application of longing for non-conceptuality arises from the longing for skillful means in order to fulfill the perfections;
and the mental application of longing for steadfastness arises from the longing to uphold the meaning of the teachings that have the perfections as their primary subject.
The mental application (*manaskāra*) consisting of the desire to attain the conditions [for enlightenment] arises from the formative activity of right vows.
There is the vision of power in the emergence from the seven kinds of false grasping;
and there is also the fourfold perception of what is marvelous and what is not marvelous. (11.68)
The mental engagement that observes the power to eliminate the seven types of false grasping.
There are seven kinds of false grasping: grasping at what is non-existent as existent;
grasping at what is defective as possessing qualities; and grasping at what possesses qualities as being devoid of qualities.
Regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), there is the false grasping at permanence and pleasure;
regarding all phenomena (*dharma*), there is the false grasping at a self (*ātman*); and regarding *nirvāṇa*, there is the false grasping at it being non-peaceful.
As their antidotes, the three concentrations on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) and the four summaries of the Dharma (*dharmoddāna*) are taught.
Regarding the marvelous, there is mental attention consisting of four kinds of perceptions:

the perception of magnificence toward the perfections, the perception of their long duration, the perception of being independent of recompense, and the perception of being independent of karmic maturation.
Regarding the non-marvelous as well, there is likewise fourfold mental attention.
There are four kinds of non-marvels: because the perfections bring about the fruit of Buddhahood when they possess both magnanimity and duration;

and because, when these two alone exist, one establishes a mind of equality toward oneself and others; and because, even when receiving honors and so forth from those superior to oneself, such as the Śrāvakas, there is no expectation of a return favor...
Equanimity toward all sentient beings, a magnanimous vision, returning the virtues of others, and uninterrupted praise of the Three Jewels.
...the mental application of aspiring for the confidence [of others] through the engagement in virtues such as giving toward others;
the mental application of aspiration because of aspiring for three states regarding sentient beings:
the culmination of the perfections, the culmination of the bodhisattva stages, and the removal of the obscurations of sentient beings.
Uninterrupted mental attention consists in the formative application (*abhisaṃskaraṇa*) of not allowing the time for [the practice of] giving and so forth to pass by;
it consists in the volition (*cetanā*) of not remaining in a state of inferiority through the performance of what has been taught by the Buddha.
Through the decrease or increase of that [volition], there is neither lack of joy nor exultation toward sentient beings. (MSA 11.70)
The mental application of correct practice arises from non-erroneous execution, because one does not direct the mind toward remaining on this side [of the goal].
The mental application of non-delight arises regarding those who are declining in generosity and so forth;
the mental application of joy arises regarding sentient beings who are increasing in generosity and so forth.
There is no lack of interest in cultivation that is merely superficial or counterfeit;
there is no mental engagement of acquiescence, but rather a longing for that which is predicted and fixed [in the stage of certainty].
The mental application of lack of interest pertains to the cultivation of counterfeit perfections; the mental application of interest pertains to the genuine ones.
The mental application of non-acceptance arises from the formative effort to subdue opposing factors such as stinginess.

The mental application of aspiration is twofold: the mental application of aspiration for obtaining the prophecy of the fulfillment of the perfections, and the mental application of aspiration for obtaining the state of being fixed on the stages of the perfections.
In the future, there is the volition of conduct through seeing [the Buddhas], and the observation of equality.
Furthermore, because of the practice in the supreme dharmas and because of the determination of oneself as supreme, there is retention.

The mental application of conduct based on future vision is so called because, having gone from one state of existence to another, a bodhisattva performs the necessary formative acts. The mental application of observing the equality of giving and the other perfections is for the sake of resolving to practice the perfections continuously together with other bodhisattvas.
The mental application of determining one's own preeminence arises from seeing oneself as the principal [agent] through the engagement in the supreme dharmas of the perfections.
These ten virtuous mental applications, which follow upon the ten perfections,
always serve to nourish the element (dhātu) of the bodhisattvas.
Thus, the verse of conclusion has its meaning already explained.
Regarding the distinction of the search for the Dharma, there are two verses:
"The wise one's great search is held to be due to nourishment and to the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*)."
For them, [the transformation] is indeed with remainder and likewise without remainder, as well as that which pertains to mastery.

For Bodhisattvas, aspiration is considered to be without body, having attained a light body, and having a fulfilled body; it is characterized by great respect, subtle pride, and being free from pride.
The search is of thirteen kinds: by way of nourishment, through the nourishment of faith in what has been heard; and by way of resolute intention, through the stream of the entrance to the Dharma.
The first is with separation, belonging to those who have attained the state of mind;
the second is without separation; and the third is sovereign, belonging to those who possess mastery.
That which consists of hearing and reflection is "without body" because it is devoid of the Dharma-body;
that which consists of cultivation is "with body" on the stage of practice through resolute belief; and that which is "light-bodied" pertains to the seven [subsequent] stages.
The body is fully perfected in the remaining stages; it is characterized by great respect on the stage of practice through resolute belief, and by subtle pride in the seven [stages].
In the remaining [stages], they are emanations.
Regarding the investigation into the nature of the cause of the Dharma, there is this verse:
"In the realms of form and formlessness, the Dharma is the cause of characteristics; likewise, it is the cause of health and the absence of illness."
In sovereignty, through the superknowledges, and in their inexhaustibility for the wise.
In the realm of form (*rūpa*), it is the cause of the marks (*lakṣaṇa*);

in the formless (*arūpa*), it is the cause of health because it pacifies the disease of the afflictions (*kleśa*); it is the cause of sovereignty through the superknowledges (*abhijñā*); and it is the cause of their inexhaustibility because even in the nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*) there is no interruption.
Therefore, it is said in the *Brahmaparipṛcchāsūtra*:

Endowed with four qualities, Bodhisattvas seek the Dharma: with the perception of it as a jewel, in the sense that it is difficult to find; with the perception of it as medicine, in the sense that it pacifies the disease of the afflictions (*kleśa*); with the perception of it as wealth, in the sense that it is never lost; and with the perception of it as Nirvana, in the sense that it pacifies all suffering.
For the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are like jewels because they produce beauty; therefore, because they are the cause of those marks, there is the perception of the Dharma as a jewel.
Because it is the cause of health, there is the perception of it as medicine; because it is the cause of supernormal powers and mastery, there is the perception of it as wealth;
and because it is the cause of that which is inexhaustible, there is the perception of it as nirvāṇa, in the sense of being free from fear through the exhaustion [of suffering].
Regarding the investigation of conceptual construction, there is this verse:

The conceptualizations of non-existence and existence, of superimposition and denial, of unity and plurality, and of specific qualities, as well as the conceptualizations of adherence to names according to their literal meaning— these must be completely abandoned by the sons of the Conqueror.
A bodhisattva must avoid ten kinds of conceptual construction.
Regarding the conceptual construction of non-existence, as its antidote, it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā*: "In this regard, a bodhisattva, being truly a bodhisattva..."
The conceptualization of existence is that for which he says, as its antidote,
"He does not perceive a bodhisattva," and so forth;
the conceptualization of superimposition is that for which he says [as its antidote]:
"Form, Śāriputra, is empty of intrinsic nature"— this refers to the conceptualization of negation (*apavāda-vikalpa*), for which he states the remedy:
"not by way of emptiness."
The conceptualization of oneness is that for which he says, as its antidote:

"That which is the emptiness of form is not that form. The conceptualization of difference is that for which he says, as its antidote: [that which is the emptiness of form is not other than that form].
Nor is form other than emptiness; form itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is form.
This refers to the conceptualization of specific characteristics, for which the antidote is stated:
"This which is called 'form' is merely a name."
The conceptualization of specific distinctions is that which he taught as the antidote when he said:
"For form, there is neither arising nor cessation, neither affliction nor purification.
The conceptualization of adherence to objects according to their names is that which he taught as the antidote when he said: [as follows].
"Fabricated names," and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding the conceptualization that clings to names as being consistent with reality, he says this as its antidote:
"The bodhisattva does not perceive any of those names; not perceiving them, he does not cling to them as being real. This is the intended meaning.
Thus, having applied intense effort with a virtuous mind and having realized the true nature of reality sought through the two [truths],
he becomes a constant refuge for all beings, filled with qualities like the ocean.

By this concluding verse, he demonstrates the threefold greatness of the search (*paryeṣṭi*): the greatness of skillful means through fierce vigor; and the greatness of the ultimate truth through the search for the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) consisting of both conventional and ultimate truths—where "truth" (*satya*) means reality (*tattva*);
and the greatness of the welfare of others by being a refuge for all beings.
And the greatness of its own purpose is due to its being completely filled with qualities like the ocean.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, on the Search for the Dharma, in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
(MSA 77)
The Twelfth Chapter: A Verse on the Prohibition of Stinginess Regarding the Teaching of the Dharma.
The wise, with joyful minds, constantly bestow upon suffering beings their lives and possessions—though acquired with great difficulty and lacking in essence—through various forms of sublime giving.

How much more so, then, the noble Dharma which repeatedly brings benefit to all beings in every way—never found before in times of distress, yet being bestowed abundantly by those who increase it and remain inexhaustible.

Bodhisattvas, out of compassion, constantly bestow through magnificent gifts even those enjoyments that are obtained with great difficulty and are devoid of essence, at the cost of their own lives; how much more so the Dharma, which increases rather than diminishes for those who give it away, whether it be obtained without difficulty or even with great effort.

Regarding the meaninglessness and meaningfulness of the Dharma, there are two verses: The Blessed One did not teach the Dharma at all, since it is to be personally realized; yet, by means of teachings established through appropriate reasoning, he drew people toward their own true nature (dharmatā).

Then, like great pythons characterized by compassion, those whose essence is mercy have caused them to enter, as if with a mouthful of saliva, into the vast, pure, common, and inexhaustible cavity of their own tranquility.
In this regard, the Buddhas are like pythons; their own tranquility is the opening of their mouth, which is the Dharma-body.
It is vast in its purity due to the purification of the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable, along with their latent tendencies.
It is common to all Buddhas and inexhaustible because it is ultimate.

Therefore, that cultivation which belongs to yogins is by no means purposeless; therefore, that teaching of the Sugata is by no means purposeless. If the goal were seen through mere hearing, cultivation would be useless; if one could enter into cultivation without having heard [the teachings], teaching would be useless. (MSA 12.3)

Therefore, the cultivation of yogins is not purposeless, because through its power they attain the dharma that is to be personally realized. Nor is the teaching purposeless, because by means of dharmas established through reasoning, it draws people toward their own true nature (*svadharmatā*).
Furthermore, he shows how cultivation or teaching may be purposeful with the following half-verse:
The remainder has already been explained.
Regarding the classification of teaching, there is this verse:
"The teaching of the supreme beings is [based] on scripture, on realization, and on mastery."
It also issues forth from the mouth, from forms, and from all space. // AMsa_12.4 //
