In that regard, [the teaching] by way of mastery refers to that which issues forth from all directions— from trees, musical instruments, and so forth— even for those who have entered the great stages (*mahābhūmi*).
The remainder has already been explained.
Regarding the perfection of teaching, there are two verses:
it is clear, dispels doubt, is authoritative, and reveals reality in two ways.
This should be understood as the perfect teaching of the bodhisattvas.
This verse is an exposition of four points, as stated in the *Brahmaparipṛcchā*:

"Endowed with four qualities, bodhisattvas bestow the great gift of Dharma: by way of upholding the true Dharma, by way of refining their own wisdom, and by way of performing the deeds of a true person."
And by way of teaching both affliction and purification:

for by the first [quality], the teaching becomes clear through great learning (*bāhuśrutya*); by the second, it removes doubt because, through possessing great wisdom (*mahāprājña*), one cuts through the doubts of others.
By the third [verse], it is acceptable because its activity is irreproachable;
by the fourth, it reveals reality—namely, the two kinds of reality characterized by affliction and characterized by purification—by means of the two truths respectively.
For the supreme beings, the teaching is sweet, free from intoxication, and never wearying.
It is clear, variegated, logical, conducive to understanding, free from worldly motives, and indeed universal.

In this second verse, it is "sweet" because of the absence of harsh speech when one is rebuked by another; it is "free from intoxication" because one does not succumb to pride when receiving praise or success; and it is "unwearied" because of the absence of laziness.
It is clear because it is free from the "teacher's fist" due to its complete teaching;
it is diverse because it is non-repetitive;
and it is logical because it is not contradicted by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
It is "communicative" because its words and syllables are well-understood; it is "disinterested" because it does not exceed the scope of pure faith;
it is "universal" because it pertains to all three vehicles.
Regarding the perfection of speech, there is this verse:
The speech of the Son of the Victor is undepressed, sweet, well-spoken, intelligible, and likewise clear;
it is appropriate, free from worldly motives, measured, and inexhaustible. (AMsa 12.7)
It is not dejected (*adīnā*) because it fulfills the assembly (*parṣatpūraṇāt*);
it is sweet (*madhurā*) and lovely (*valgu*).
It is well-spoken because its syllables are clearly articulated and well-explained; it is intelligible because its terminology is familiar;
and it is appropriate because it is worthy of being heard, conforming to the needs of those to be trained.
It is non-material, being independent of gain and honor in the world;
it is extensive, being free from opposition;
and it is limited, because of the absence of weariness in its duration.
The [explanation of] the meaning is inexhaustible.
Regarding the perfection of the phrasing, there are two verses:
because of the brief statement (*uddeśa*), because of the detailed exposition (*nirdeśa*), likewise because of conformity with the vehicle (*yānānulomana*), and because of its elegance (*ślākṣṇya*).
Because it is dependent, because it is appropriate, because it leads to liberation, and because it is concordant.
It is "logical" because it provides a summary through words and syllables that are consistent with valid cognition;
it is "coherent" because its detailed exposition does not contradict that summary;
and it is "conforming" because it accords with the vehicles, being non-contradictory with the three vehicles.
By virtue of being smooth, they are appropriate through the absence of harsh sounds;
by virtue of being intelligible, they are suitable because they lead to the understanding of the meaning;
and by virtue of being fitting, they are conformable because they accord with those to be trained.

It should be understood that this perfection of expression belongs in every respect to the supreme beings, because it leads to liberation, because it is auspicious, because it has nirvāṇa as its primary objective, and because it is conducive through the equipment of the limbs of the adept, being favorable to the noble eightfold path of the learner.
That voice of the Sugatas possesses sixty qualities, is inconceivable, and is indeed infinite.
That [speech] consisting of sixty aspects is inconceivable, which was taught as the sixtyfold speech of the Buddha in the *Guhyakādhipatinirdeśa*.
Furthermore, Śāntamati, the speech of the Tathāgata issues forth endowed with sixty aspects: it is smooth, soft, agreeable, delightful, and pure, and so forth.
In that regard, it is "smooth" because it supports the roots of virtue in the realm of sentient beings.
They are "soft" because they are pleasant to the touch even in regard to unwholesome phenomena; they are "agreeable" because their meaning is excellent;
they are "delightful" because their phrasing is excellent.
It is pure because it is obtained subsequent to the unsurpassed supramundane [wisdom];
it is stainless because it is dissociated from all afflictions, latent tendencies, and habitual propensities;
it is luminous because its words and phrases are clearly understood.
It is beautiful because it possesses the power and quality of destroying the views of the evil intellects of all non-Buddhist teachers;
it is worthy of being heard because its practice leads to definitive liberation;
and it is infinite because it cannot be refuted by any opposing disputants.
It is graceful because it is pleasing;
it is disciplined because it serves as the antidote to passion and other afflictions;
it is not harsh because it provides a pleasant means for the formulation of the training rules.
It is not harsh because it teaches the means of deliverance through the perfection of transcending those transgressions;
it is well-disciplined because it teaches the method of the three vehicles;
and it is pleasant to the ear because it is the antidote to distraction.
It brings refreshment to the body because it induces meditative concentration; it brings joy to the mind because its fruit is the induction of the gladness of insight;
and it brings satisfaction to the heart because it cuts through doubt.
It generates joy and bliss because it removes false certainties; it is free from burning anguish because there is no regret regarding one's practice;
and it is to be fully understood because it serves as the basis for perfected knowledge consisting of hearing.
It is to be known as such because it is the basis for perfected knowledge consisting of reflection (*cintāmayajñāna*);
it is perfectly clear because it is established through the Dharma without the "teacher's fist" (*anācāryamuṣṭi*);
and it is lovable because it inspires love in those who have attained their own goal.
It is to be celebrated because it is desirable for those who have not yet attained their own goal;
it is to be commanded because it correctly reveals inconceivable phenomena;
it is to be made known because it correctly teaches inconceivable phenomena.
It is "logical" because it is not contradicted by valid means of knowledge;
it is "conjoined" because it teaches disciples according to their fitness;
and it "abandons the fault of redundancy" because it is never fruitless.
It has the speed of a lion’s roar because it terrifies all non-Buddhist teachers;
it has the sound of a dragon’s voice because of its magnificence;
it has the resonance of a cloud’s thunder because of its profundity.
They possess the voice of the lord of nāgas because they are authoritative; the sound of the music of kinnaras because they are sweet;
and the cry of the kalaviṅka bird because they are constantly melodious.
It has the resonance of the voice of Brahmā because it reaches far;
it has the resonance of the voice of the jīvañjīvaka bird because it is an auspicious omen that precedes all accomplishments;
and it has the sweet sound of the lord of gods because it is not to be transgressed.
It has the sound of a drum because it precedes victory over all Māras and adversaries;
it is not haughty because it is unafflicted by praise;
it is not dejected because it is unafflicted by blame.
It penetrates all sounds because it enters into all grammatical forms and all characteristics;
it is free from corrupt words because they do not issue forth when mindfulness is lost;
it is unimpaired because it is present at all times for the sake of the tasks to be accomplished for those to be trained.
It is not dejected because it does not depend on gain or honor;
it is not depressed because it is free from fault;
it is joyful because it is untiring.
It is "extended" because it follows from skill in all branches of knowledge;
it is "entire" because it accomplishes every purpose of sentient beings;
it is "flowing" because its continuity is uninterrupted.
It is graceful because it manifests in diverse forms;
it fulfills all voices because it manifests as the cognition of many sounds from a single voice;
it satisfies the faculties of all sentient beings because it manifests as the cognition of one or many meanings.
It is irreproachable because it accords with its promise;
it is steady because it is applied at the appropriate time;
it is not fickle because it is performed without haste.
It resounds throughout the entire assembly because it is heard equally by assemblies both far and near.
It is endowed with the excellence of all aspects because it transforms the Dharma through all kinds of worldly examples and meanings. There are four verses regarding the greatness of this teaching.
Indeed, through speech consisting of well-composed words that resolve doubts by means of detailed instruction and analysis,
[the teaching] follows upon extensive practice for those who are "those who know the condensed" and "those who know the elaborated."
He declares it by means of speech;
he makes it known through well-joined phrases;
he establishes, analyzes, and elucidates it respectively through summary, detailed exposition, and the cutting away of doubts.
He makes manifest; "making manifest" refers to teaching accompanied by extensive practice for the purpose of providing the strength of certainty.
He teaches to those who understand through concise statements (*udghaṭitajña*), and he fully elucidates for those who understand through detailed exposition (*vipañcitajña*).
This teaching of the Buddhas is indeed pure by virtue of the three spheres;
furthermore, it should be understood as being free from the eight faults.

"Pure by way of the three spheres" means that [it is pure] in terms of the speech and words with which one teaches, as well as in terms of the modes such as the brief exposition (uddeśa) and so forth.
And for those who possess the knowledge of what is condensed and what is elaborated,
this very teaching should be understood as being free from eight faults in due order:
namely, laziness, lack of understanding, failure to provide an opportunity, and not having brought [the matter] to its conclusion.
The non-elimination of doubt and the failure to consolidate its removal.

Furthermore, those eight faults are: laziness, lack of full comprehension, failure to provide an opportunity [for questioning], incomprehensibility of the meaning, non-severance of doubt, non-firming of its removal—which means the lack of certainty—and weariness as well as parsimony; for these are considered to be the faults in discourse. Because they are absent, the teaching of the Buddhas is unsurpassed.
Weariness is that by which one does not teach repeatedly; and stinginess is the failure to reveal the teaching in its entirety. Regarding the perfection of the goal, there are two verses.
This sublime Dharma, because it is the cause of devotion, contentment, and wisdom,
has a twofold purpose, is easy to grasp, and teaches the holy life (brahmacarya) endowed with four qualities.
Unique to others, exclusive, fulfilling the destruction of the afflictions of the three realms,
and pure by nature as well as through the purification of stains— this is held to be the fourfold sublime conduct (*brahmavihāra*).
The Dharma is that which fully reveals the holy life (*brahmacarya*) endowed with four qualities;
it is excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, because it serves as the cause for devotion, satisfaction, and wisdom through hearing, reflection, and meditation, respectively.
In this context, devotion is resolve, conviction, contentment, and joy, arising from the discernment of reasoning once one has understood that [the goal] is attainable.
Intellect is the knowledge of things as they truly are for one whose mind is concentrated.
It has a twofold meaning; therefore, it is "well-meaning" (*svartha*) because of its connection with both conventional and ultimate truth.
It is "well-phrased" because its words and syllables are easily grasped, owing to the fact that its words and syllables are well-known.
It is the "fourfold holy life" (*brahmacarya*);
it is "exclusive" because it is not shared by others; it is "complete" because it fulfills the abandonment of the afflictions of the three realms.
It is "pure" because it is pure by nature due to being free from outflows (*anāsrava*);
it is "cleansed" because it is purified of stains through the purification of the mental continuum (*saṃtāna*) for those whose outflows are exhausted.
There are two verses regarding the analysis of intentional terminology (*abhisaṃdhi*).

The intentional terminology (saṃdhi) of introduction, another intentional terminology based on characteristics, the intentional terminology of the antidote, and also the intentional terminology of transformation. (AMsa 12.16)
Regarding the disciples, regarding intrinsic natures, regarding the discipline of faults,
and regarding the profundity of the expression— this is the fourfold intentional terminology (saṃdhi).
Those who perceive the essential in the insubstantial, who are firmly established in perversion,
and who are thoroughly afflicted by defilement, attain the unsurpassed awakening.
Thus ends [the section]. AMsa_12.17.
Four kinds of intentional terminology (*abhisandhi*) are to be understood regarding the Buddha's teaching:

the intentional terminology for introduction (*avatāraṇābhisandhi*), the intentional terminology for characteristics (*lakṣaṇābhisandhi*), the intentional terminology for remedies (*pratipakṣābhisandhi*), and the intentional terminology for transformation (*pariṇāmanābhisandhi*).
Among these, the intentional terminology for introduction is to be seen in relation to the *śrāvakas*.

The intention regarding characteristics (*lakṣaṇābhisandhi*) is to be seen in the three natures—the imagined and so forth—because of the teaching that form and other phenomena exist in order to introduce beings to the teaching and to prevent them from being terrified; it is seen in the teaching that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature, unproduced, and so on.

The intention regarding the antidote (*pratipakṣābhisandhi*) is to be seen in the subduing of faults, as will be stated in two verses concerning the benefits of the discourse on the Supreme Vehicle as the antidote to the eight obscurations.
The intention of transformation (pariṇāmanābhisaṃdhi) is to be seen in the profundity of the expression, as it has been said:
"Those who perceive the essence in what is essenceless, who find happiness in perversion,
and who are thoroughly afflicted by afflictions, attain supreme enlightenment."
This is the intended meaning here:

"Those who perceive the essential in the unessential" refers to those whose perception of the essential—that is, their perception of what is primary—is directed toward non-distraction; for distraction is the scattering of the mind.

And "firmly established in error" means they are firmly established in the error of impermanence and so forth—by way of the reversal of the grasping at permanence, pleasure, purity, and self—and are thus not subject to decline.
"And they are afflicted by affliction" means they are excessively exhausted by the fatigue of long-term exertion in difficult practices.
Regarding the analysis of the underlying intention, there is this verse:
"It should be understood as equality in another sense, and likewise again in another time."
And regarding the disposition of the person, the intention is fourfold.
The intention is fourfold.
The intention of continuity is that which was said: [Msa 83]...
"I myself was that Vipaśyin, the perfectly awakened Buddha at that time," because there is no distinction in the *dharmakāya*.

There is an intention regarding a different meaning when he says, "All phenomena are without intrinsic nature, unarisen," and so forth, because the meaning is not according to the literal expression. There is an intention regarding another time when he says:
The intention is that those who make a vow for Sukhāvatī will be reborn there after some time has passed.

Regarding the intention based on the dispositions of individuals (*pudgalāśayābhiprāya*): it is that he praises one particular root of virtue while censuring another, in order to gather those who are satisfied with only a small amount [of merit] into the vastness [of the Mahāyāna]. Taking up two verses that set forth the benefits of the Mahāyāna sūtras, he says:
Disrespect toward the Buddha and the Dharma, laziness, contentment with a mere trifle,
conduct characterized by passion and pride, remorse, and instability— these are the obstacles.
The obscuration of sentient beings, its antidote, the supreme vehicle, and the lack of conversation [with those who hold wrong views]:
from these, the abandonment of all faults that constitute obstacles occurs for them.
The wise one, the best of beings, who applies himself to memorizing these two verses either by their wording or their meaning, obtains ten kinds of benefit. *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* 12.21.
And at the time of death, there is nourishment of the entire realm, supreme joy,
birth according to one's wish, and the recollection of past lives in all circumstances.
Meeting with the Buddhas, hearing this supreme vehicle from them,
having faith along with understanding, the two gateways, and swift awakening.
Regarding "contempt for the Buddha and the Dharma," there are five verses.

In that context, "the division of those who are not fixed" refers to the separation from the Mahāyāna of those bodhisattvas who are not yet fixed [in their lineage]. "Not conversing about the Supreme Vehicle" refers to the teaching of the Mahāyāna.
The discourse on the counteragent to the obscuration of contempt for the Buddha is:
"At that time, I myself was the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin.
The discourse on the counteragent to the obscuration of contempt for the Dharma is:
"Having attended upon as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, the realization of the Mahāyāna arises"—
this is the discourse that serves as the antidote to the hindrance of indolence.
"Those who make a vow for Sukhāvatī shall be reborn there."
"By merely grasping the name of the Tathāgata Vimalacandraprabha, one becomes fixed in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
This is a discourse on the remedy for the inferior state of being satisfied with only a small amount [of merit].
In this regard, the Blessed One in some instances disparages giving and other virtues, whereas in others he has praised them.

The discourse on the remedy for the obscuration of one whose temperament is dominated by passion is that in which the Blessed One describes the splendor of the Buddha-fields. The discourse on the remedy for the obscuration of one whose temperament is dominated by pride is as follows:
Wherein the Blessed One describes the superior excellence of a certain Buddha;
this is the discourse on the remedy for the hindrance of remorse (*kaukṛtyāvaraṇa*).
"Those who shall act with even a single syllable of respect toward the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas will all go to the heavenly realms"—
this is the discourse on the remedy for the obstacle of indeterminate differentiation.
Furthermore, it is the teaching of the prophecy of the Great Śrāvakas' attainment of Buddhahood and the teaching of the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna).

The nourishment of the entire element (*dhātu*) consists in the nourishment of the element for the sake of sustaining the whole Mahāyāna, because through the removal of its obscurations, one attains resolute faith (*adhimukti*) throughout the entire Mahāyāna. There are two gateways: the gateway of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the gateway of mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇī*). It should be understood that there are two kinds of benefits in the present life and eight kinds in future lives, due to the gradual attainment of ever-higher distinctions.

Regarding the benefits of teaching, there is this verse: Thus, the Bodhisattva who possesses a happy rebirth, is untiring, compassionate, renowned, and endowed with knowledge of the proper method, becomes an excellent teacher; indeed, he shines among people through his teachings just like the sun.
Being a good speaker is due to five causes,
and the benefit is a radiance like that of the sun,
because one is highly esteemed for winning over the world.

There are five causes of being a good teacher by which one demonstrates without error: [teaching] repeatedly, with a mind free from worldly desire, with acceptable speech, and in accordance with those to be trained.
This concludes the twelfth chapter on Teaching in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
The thirteenth chapter follows.

There are six verses on the classification of practice: Having understood the two kinds of selflessness—of the person and of phenomena—the wise one should avoid the threefold [view] of falsity and correctness regarding these two. (AMsa 13.1)

Having understood reality as it is and having understood the Dharma, one becomes a practitioner of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānudharmapratipanna), a practitioner of proper conduct (sāmīcīpratipanna), and a follower of the Dharma; this he demonstrates.
In that regard, the knowledge of the selflessness of persons and phenomena is twofold, by way of the absence of the grasped and the grasper.
Having abandoned the two—falsity and correctness—there are three [to be cultivated].
The concentration on emptiness pertains to the non-existence of the imagined nature;

the concentrations on the wishless and the signless pertain to the existence of the dependent and perfected natures, respectively. These three concentrations are mundane, yet they are not false because they bring about supramundane knowledge.
It is not right [to claim] that [this knowledge] is supramundane, because it is mundane.
One who knows the meaning understands that all phenomena are like a raft;
one who knows the Dharma is so called for the sake of abandoning satisfaction with mere learning.
Thus, one who knows the meaning understands that all phenomena, such as the sūtras and so forth, are like a raft. By abandoning contentment with mere learning, he becomes a knower of the Dharma.
Having thus penetrated duality through the knowledge of an ordinary person, [he proceeds further].
Upon the perfection of that knowledge, one practices in accordance with the Dharma.

Having realized the two kinds of selflessness through these two types of knowledge belonging to ordinary persons—namely, the knowledge of objects and the knowledge of phenomena—he practices accordingly for the sake of perfecting that knowledge; thus he practices in accordance with the Dharma. Thereafter, he attains supramundane, unsurpassed knowledge.
On the initial stage, it is equal to all bodhisattvas who possess that same nature.
"Then he attains supramundane, unsurpassed knowledge," because there is no vehicle more distinguished than this.

"On the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā*), he is equal to all bodhisattvas who share that nature"— that is, with those belonging to that very stage— in this way he becomes one who has entered into proper conduct through equality with the bodhisattvas of that stage.
Having brought about the complete destruction of all afflictions to be abandoned through vision,
one applies oneself to the path of cultivation for the sake of abandoning the cognitive obscurations and attaining knowledge.
The meaning of the verse is clear:
"By means of non-conceptual knowledge that functions as a stabilizing factor,
one thus practices in accordance with the Dharma throughout the remaining stages."
By the remainder, he demonstrates the practice of the subsequent Dharma (*anudharmacāritva*).
This is by means of the non-conceptual knowledge that discerns the stages (*bhūmi*) and by being non-conceptual;
and "by one who moves together" means by one who moves in continuous connection, through mutual uninterruptedness.
By these two verses, the practice in accordance with the Dharma is shown.
Regarding the practice of heedfulness in application, there are four verses:
"Easy to obtain, well-supported, on good ground, with good companions..."
A suitable place is one that possesses good qualities, where a wise person takes up residence.
By means of four wheels—beginning with dwelling in a suitable locality—he demonstrates the practice of heedfulness (*apramādakriyā*).
Therein, by this verse, he demonstrates dwelling in a suitable locality:
it is "easily obtained" because the requisites for life, such as robes and alms-food, are acquired without difficulty.
It is well-established because it is not occupied by wicked people such as bandits and the like;
it is a good location because it is a land of health;
and it has good companions because its companions possess similar ethical discipline and views.
Good yoga [is practiced] because of the lack of much distraction and chatter during the day, and the lack of noise and such at night;
one who is learned, has seen the truth, is eloquent, compassionate,
and untiring— such a Bodhisattva should be known as a great true person.
By this second verse, he shows the true person (*satpuruṣa*).
This is because of his possession of the qualities of scripture and realization, eloquence, a mind free from worldly motives, and tirelessness.
He has taught that very cultivation which has its own object, is well-provisioned, well-steadied, and well-practiced.
And self-righteous exertion is characterized by well-applied practice for deliverance.
By this third [verse], he demonstrates his own state of right aspiration as comprised by wise attention (*yoniso-manaskāra*):

namely, by taking the true Dharma as one's object; by having well-accumulated the provisions; by cultivating the signs of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and so forth from time to time; by not being satisfied with a mere trifle; and by applying oneself continuously and with reverence when there is further work to be done.
For the attainment of joy, the occurrence of leisure,
health, meditative concentration, and analytical investigation, the cause is indeed merit performed in the past.
By this fourth [verse], he demonstrates the state of having previously performed merit through five kinds of causes:
as the cause of delight, because one takes pleasure in dwelling in a suitable locality;
and as the cause of birth in a favorable moment, because one obtains reliance upon a true person (*satpuruṣa*).
And because it serves as the cause for health, meditative concentration, and wisdom, one's own right aspiration is thereby accomplished.
Regarding the very departure from afflictions by means of the afflictions themselves, there are three verses:
"Since no phenomenon exists that is separate from the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*)."
Therefore, the Buddhas consider passion and the other afflictions to be the means of deliverance for them.
Regarding what was said by the Blessed One:
"I do not speak of an escape from passion other than through passion itself; likewise for hatred and delusion," he now demonstrates the underlying intention (*abhisaṃdhi*) therein.

Because there is no phenomenon that is separate from the *dharmadhātu*, since phenomena do not exist apart from their true nature (*dharmatā*); therefore, even the *dharmatā* of passion and so forth receives the designation "passion" and so on, and that [very *dharmatā*] is the escape from passion and so forth—such is the intended meaning therein to be understood. Because no phenomenon exists separate from the *dharmadhātu*.
Therefore, in the exposition of affliction, that consciousness is held by the wise to be [the basis].
Regarding what was said— that ignorance (*avidyā*) and awakening (*bodhi*) are one—
even there, in the explanation concerning defilement (*saṃkleśa*), that same underlying intention (*abhisaṃdhi*) applies:
ignorance would be the very nature of awakening (*bodhidharmatā*) through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).
Since one practices correctly with respect to those very [afflictions] such as attachment, one is liberated from them; therefore, that is their departure.

By practicing correctly (*yoniśas*) with respect to those very same [afflictions] such as passion and so forth, one is liberated from them; therefore, it is precisely when they are fully understood that they become the means of escape from them—this is the intended meaning here.
Regarding the avoidance of the mental orientations (*manasikāra*) of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, there are two verses:
"Indeed, for the Sons of the Conqueror (*jinaputra*), the intense suffering arising from dwelling in the abodes of hell is in no way an obstacle on account of sentient beings."
Driven by the virtues and faults of the state of tranquility, various virtuous conceptualizations are obstacles for those of the Lesser Vehicle, but they are [not so] for the wise.

Indeed, dwelling in the hells does not at all act as an obstacle for the wise toward pure and vast enlightenment at any time; however, the conceptualization [of one's own benefit] in another vehicle—which, though supreme in its own welfare, is cool—does act as an obstacle even to the abiding in supreme bliss.
Of these two verses, the second is the proof for the first;
both have their meaning already explained.
There are four verses concerning the refutation of fear regarding the absence of intrinsic nature and natural purity:

The non-existence of phenomena and their perception, as well as the state of being both without affliction and pure, should be known as being like an illusion and so forth, and likewise like space. (AMsa 13.16)
Just as in a painting that has been skillfully executed according to rule, there is no actual elevation or depression, yet they are seen;
likewise, in the construction of the unreal, duality is at all times and in every way non-existent, yet it is seen.
Just as when turbid water has been clarified, that clarity does not arise from elsewhere, but is merely the removal of impurities therein;
for this very same rule applies to the purification of one's own mind.
And it is held that the mind is always luminous by nature, yet it is defiled by adventitious faults;
for apart from the mind that is the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā), no other mind is established as being luminous by nature.

The non-existence of phenomena and the perception of phenomena are grounds for fear; likewise, the fact that the *dharmadhātu* is by nature free from affliction and yet becomes pure later on are grounds for fear for the foolish.
Establishing these points respectively through the similes of illusions and so forth, and through the simile of space, he thereby refutes such fear.
Similarly, he does so respectively through the simile of the lack of high and low in a painting, and through the simile of water that has been stirred up and then clarified.
With the fourth verse, he demonstrates the similarity of the mind to water:
just as water is clear by nature but becomes turbid through adventitious impurity, so too the mind is held to be luminous by nature but defiled by adventitious faults.
Furthermore, the natural luminosity of any other mind characterized by dependence (*paratantralakṣaṇa*) is not established apart from the mind that is the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatācitta*).
Therefore, in this context, it should be understood that "mind" refers precisely to the suchness (*tathatā*) of the mind.
There are four verses regarding the prohibition of offenses arising from passion.
The Bodhisattva’s great love for sentient beings penetrates to the very marrow, just as he would feel toward an only son; therefore, it is considered to always act for their benefit.
Because he acts for the benefit of sentient beings, he does not incur an offense born of passion;
however, hatred toward any sentient being is contrary to his true path.
Just as a female pigeon, exceedingly affectionate toward her own offspring, remains embracing them with her natural instinct,
so too does such hostility contradict [the presence of] compassion toward embodied beings who are like her own children.

Since loving-kindness exists, the mind of hostility is its opposite; since tranquility exists, the mind of affliction is its opposite. Since benefit exists, the mind of deceit is its opposite; since joy exists, fear is not its opposite.

That which is the bodhisattva’s love for sentient beings is intended here as "passion" (rāga); he prohibits any offense committed on their account because it serves as the cause for accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings.

He cites the example of the female pigeon because of her excessive passion; due to the intensity of her maternal affection, hostility toward living beings is incompatible with a compassionate bodhisattva.

For bodhisattvas, there is loving-kindness toward sentient beings, which consists of the pacification of their misfortunes, the giving of what is beneficial, and joy; these arise from the production of affection.
Precisely because of this loving-kindness and so forth, a mind of hostility is its opposite, as are the minds of causing misfortune and the like that precede it.
There are five verses concerning the distinctions in practice:

Just as a sick person applies himself to a good medicine, so does he apply himself to cyclic existence; and just as a physician applies himself to the sick, so does he apply himself toward sentient beings. (AMsa 13.24)
Just as one behaves toward a servant who has not yet been fully trained, and just as a merchant behaves toward his own person, so too does one behave toward merit in relation to sensual desires.
Just as a washerman applies himself to his work on a garment,
so does a father behave toward his young son without causing him harm.
One who desires fire applies himself to the lower kindling wood with persistence;
or, like a trustworthy person, one applies oneself to higher mental cultivation when it has not yet been accomplished.
Just as a magician proceeds toward his object of knowledge through wisdom,
so too is the practice of the bodhisattva considered to be in that same manner and toward that same object.
This explains that in what manner one practices and in what [state] one does so:
"in what manner" means as sick people [use] excellent medicines and the like;
"in what" refers to [practicing] within cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) and so forth, because one engages with cyclic existence after having applied thorough discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāya*).

Because, through compassion, one does not abandon sentient beings who are afflicted by the defilements; because one makes one's own mind free from self-interest; and because, through the perfections such as generosity, one leads to the increase of enjoyments in their respective order.
Because of purifying the actions of body and so forth,
because of not being provoked by the harm of sentient beings,
and because of constant application to the cultivation of the wholesome.
Because of not relishing meditative concentration and because of non-perversion regarding the objects of knowledge,
there is a verse concerning the purification of the three spheres of practice.
Thus, constantly possessing noble vigor and being well-engaged in the ripening and purification of the two,
he proceeds by stages to the unsurpassed accomplishment with a supremely pure and non-conceptual intellect.

Thus, by means of non-conceptual knowledge of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyajñāna*), the absence of conceptualization regarding the practitioner, the object to be practiced, and the practice itself should be understood as the purity of the three spheres (*trimandalapariśuddhi*).
"Engaged in the ripening and purification of the two" refers to [the ripening and purification] of sentient beings and of oneself.
The thirteenth chapter on Practice in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
The fourteenth chapter, the Analysis of Instruction and Admonition, consists of fifty-one verses.
Having emerged from incalculable eons while increasing his resolute faith,
he is filled with wholesome qualities just as the ocean is filled with waters.
"Increasing resolute conviction" means leading it to its superior stage.
The rest has been explained.
Thus, having accumulated the equipment, the Son of the Conqueror is pure from the beginning.
Being well-discerning and of a disciplined mind, one applies oneself to meditative cultivation.

He is "pure from the beginning" because he has purified the bodhisattva vows and because he has straightened his view in the Mahāyāna by grasping the meaning without error. He is "well-knowing" because of his great learning. He is "of a disciplined mind" because he is free from hindrances.
Then, within the stream of dharma, he receives from the Buddhas extensive instruction for the sake of attaining the vastness of tranquility and primordial wisdom.
The meaning of the verse is clear.

Thereafter, regarding the Dharma consisting of the sūtras and so forth, which reveals that non-dual reality, the practitioner should first fix his mind upon the names of the sūtras and the rest. *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* 14.4.
Thereafter, he should proceed gradually through the various divisions of the words;
he should investigate their meanings and reflect upon them internally and thoroughly.
Having ascertained those meanings, he should further synthesize them within the Dharma;
thereafter, he should form a firm resolve for the realization of that meaning.
Regarding the Dharma consisting of the *sūtras*, *geya*, and so forth, one should first fix the mind upon the names of those [texts], such as the *Daśabhūmika* and others.
By these three verses, six types of mental engagement (*citta*) are taught.

There are six types of mind: the fundamental mind (*mūlacitta*), the following mind (*anucaracitta*), the investigative mind (*vicāraṇācitta*), the determinative mind (*avadhāraṇācitta*), the synthesizing mind (*saṃkalanacitta*), and the aspirational mind (*āśāsticitta*).
Among these, the fundamental mind is that which takes as its object the names of phenomena such as the sūtras, having either heard instruction or formulated it by oneself.
For example: "impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self," and so forth, when not yet reflecting properly (*yoniśas*).
The *anucaracitta* (concomitant mind) is that by which one follows the distinctions of the words of the sūtras and so forth, having taken them as objects by name.
The *vicāraṇācitta* (investigating mind) is that by which one investigates both the meaning and the phrasing.
Therein, one examines the meaning through four modes: by counting (*gaṇanā*), by weighing (*tulanā*), by investigating (*mīmāṃsā*), and by scrutinizing (*pratyavekṣaṇā*).
Among these, counting is the grouping together, such as: "form consists of ten bases and a portion of one [base]," or "feeling consists of the six groups of feeling," and so forth.
Weighing is the grasping of the specific measure of a quantified phenomenon, free from both superimposition and denial.
Investigation is the examination of the means of valid cognition; it is discernment;
it is the observation of an object that has been calculated, weighed, and investigated.
One examines the phoneme through two aspects:
by way of its having meaning when combined with all [other phonemes], and by way of its being devoid of meaning when isolated.
The mind of ascertainment is that by which one ascertains the sign of that which has been followed or examined in such a manner.
The synthesizing mind (*saṃkalanacitta*) is that which, having condensed the object previously examined within the root-mind, proceeds in a form that is unified and integrated.

The aspiring mind (*āśāsticitta*) is that which, accompanied by desire (*chanda*), proceeds for the sake of whatever purpose one is engaged— whether for the fulfillment of those [aims], or for the sake of the fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*), or for the sake of entering the stages (*bhūmi*), or for the sake of attaining excellence.
For it is mind alone that exists as the appearance of an object; there is no object other than mind. Whether one knows "mind-only" or does not know it, mind alone is the object and nothing else.
Thus, the sixfold mind is established as the object. One should seek and investigate this through a continuous stream of mental discursive thoughts.
And one should also investigate with mental attentions that are non-discursive and of a single flavor.
The path of calm abiding (śamatha) for this [practitioner] should be known as the condensed names of the dharmas;
the path of insight (vipaśyanā) should be known as the investigation of their meanings.
Furthermore, the path of union (yuganaddha) should be understood as the synthesis of those two;
one should seize the mind when it is sluggish and again pacify it when it is agitated.
When [the mind] has attained tranquility, one should maintain equanimity toward that object;
then, one should again apply it continuously and with reverence to everything.
By these four verses, eleven modes of mental attention (*manaskāra*) are taught:
that with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*),
and that without applied thought but with sustained thought only (*avitarka-vicāramātra*).
It is without applied thought and without sustained thought;
it is the mental application of tranquility and the mental application of insight.
The mental application of the yoked pair; the mental application of the sign of calm abiding;
the mental application of the sign of equanimity.
There is continuous mental attention and respectful mental attention;
having bound the mind to the object, one should not allow it to be distracted from its forward momentum.
Having quickly recognized distraction, one should again apply oneself to that [object].
The wise person should withdraw the mind within themselves higher and higher;
thereafter, they should delight the mind in meditative concentration by perceiving its virtues.
One should pacify aversion toward that [object] by seeing the fault in distraction;
likewise, one should pacify covetousness, dejection, and other such states when they have arisen.
Then, through that practice, the practitioner further attains a state of mind that flows spontaneously,
first with effort and subsequently without effort.
By these four verses, the means for stabilizing [the mind] has been taught through the nine modes of mental abiding:
one places the mind, settles it, fixes it, closely places it, tames it, pacifies it, thoroughly pacifies it, makes it one-pointed, and composes the mind—these are the nine modes.
Then, having obtained a slight pliancy of body and mind...
Furthermore, he who possesses mental attention (manaskāra) should be known as one who increases those very [qualities] again and again.
By virtue of its increase and far-reaching nature, it attains the fundamental state;
purifying that state for the sake of the superknowledges, it reaches supreme flexibility.

Through the accomplishment of the superknowledges (abhijñā) within meditative absorption (dhyāna), he travels to world-systems for the sake of making offerings to immeasurable Buddhas and for the purpose of hearing [the Dharma].
Having worshipped immeasurable Buddhas over the course of immeasurable eons,
he attains supreme flexibility of mind through that worship.
"Attains supreme adaptability in meditation"—this is how it should be connected.
"By immeasurable eons" means by those that have reached an incalculable number.
The meaning of the rest of these verses is already understood.
Then he obtains five benefits that precede [the higher stages] through his purity;
and from that, he becomes a vessel for unsurpassed purification.
For one who has begun with the total [perceptions], the body, in which the residual heaviness (*dausthulya*) is slight, dissolves moment by moment;
and both body and mind are filled on all sides with pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
He knows the appearance of phenomena in its entirety as undifferentiated;
in his complete purity, he perceives signs that are non-conceptual.
In every way, the wise one constantly effects the fulfillment and purification of the dharma-body; thus he undertakes the cause.
(MSA 93) Thereafter, one obtains five benefits that precede purification;
"of purification" refers to the stage of pure intention (*śuddhyāśaya-bhūmi*).
And through the attainment of these, one becomes a vessel for purity;
this is unsurpassed because there is no other vehicle higher than it.
Regarding the fulfillment and purification of the *dharmakāya*, there is fulfillment on the tenth stage (*bhūmi*) and purification on the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*).
Among these five benefits, it should be understood that three belong to the side of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and two belong to the side of insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Thus, this continues up to the worldly attainment;
thereafter, that bodhisattva, having become such, is concentrated in meditative equipoise (*samāhita*).
One does not perceive any objects as being separate from mental discourse.
For the sake of increasing the light of the Dharma, he exerts firm vigor;
and through the increase of the light of the Dharma, he abides in mind-only.
Then he perceives that all objects appear within the mind;
at that time, his distraction regarding the object of apprehension is abandoned.
Then, only the distraction of the subject remains for him;
at that time, he again quickly touches the immediate meditative concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*).
Beyond this are the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

A Bodhisattva who has become thus, with a concentrated mind, does not perceive any phenomena as being distinct from mental discourse (*manojalpa*)—whether they be called specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) or general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). Only mental discourse itself appears;
this is the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).
This is that light concerning which it was said in the *Kṣāranadī*:
"Light" is a designation for the receptivity to the contemplation of phenomena (*dharmanidhyānakṣānti*).
For the sake of increasing that very light of the Dharma, he exerts firm vigor through steadfast application.
This is his stage of the Summits (mūrdhāvasthā), and through the increase of the light of the Dharma, he abides in "mind-only" (cittamātra) because of the penetration that "this is mind.
Consequently, he perceives that all objects are merely manifestations within the mind itself.
There is no object other than the mind;
at that time, his distraction regarding the apprehended is abandoned,
and only the distraction regarding the apprehender remains.
This is his stage of patience (*kṣānti*);
and at that time, he quickly touches the immediate concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*).
This is his stage of the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
For what reason is it called "immediate" (*ānantarya*)? Because immediately after that, the distraction of the subject (*grāhaka-vikṣepa*) is abandoned;
for these stages, beginning with "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), follow in due order.

Thus, these are the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya), beginning with "heat" (uṣmagata). Furthermore, he attains a supramundane, unsurpassed, non-conceptual knowledge that is free from stains and dissociated from the two types of grasping.
From this point onward is the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
It is "disjoined from the two types of grasping" because it is disjoined from the grasping of the object (*grāhya*) and the grasping of the subject (*grāhaka*).
It is unsurpassed because it is the immediate succession of the vehicle;
it is non-conceptual because it is dissociated from the conceptualization of grasped object and grasping subject;
and it is free from stains because of the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned through vision.

By this, it is said that it is "dustless" and "free from stain. This transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti) is held to be his first stage (bhūmi). And through immeasurable eons, it attains complete purification.
The meaning of this verse is clear.
Furthermore, having realized the equality of the dharmadhātu at that time,
one then attains a state of mind that always regards all sentient beings as equal to oneself.
Regarding selflessness, the nature of suffering, what is to be done, and the absence of reward,
he maintains an even mind toward sentient beings, just like all other sons of the Conquerors.
And by penetrating the equality of phenomena through the selflessness of phenomena, one always attains a mind of equality toward all sentient beings by means of fivefold equality:
through the equality of selflessness and the equality of suffering, because there is no distinction between selflessness and suffering within the continuums of oneself and others.
By the equality of duty, because there is a commonality in the desire to abandon the suffering of both oneself and others;
and by the equality of non-reciprocity,
because one does not rejoice in receiving recompense from others as one would from oneself.
And by way of equality with other bodhisattvas, because he realizes in the same manner as they have realized;
he perceives the conditioned phenomena of the triple world as unreal conceptualization through perfectly pure knowledge in the sense of non-duality. (AMsa 14.32)
With extremely pure knowledge, because it is supramundane, he perceives the conditioned phenomena of the three realms as being merely unreal conceptualization;
and he perceives the existence of that non-existence as liberated from those who fall into dogmatic views.
For having attained the path of vision, it is then designated by that [name].
One perceives the existence of that very absence of the grasped and the grasper as the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), liberated from the afflictions to be abandoned by vision.
Having understood the emptiness of non-existence, and likewise the emptiness of existence,
and having understood the emptiness of intrinsic nature, one is called a "knower of emptiness."
And that bodhisattva is called "one who knows emptiness" because of his knowledge of the three kinds of emptiness.

The emptiness of non-existence is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because it lacks existence by way of its own characteristic. Likewise, the emptiness of existence is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), for it does not exist in the manner that it is imagined, even though it exists by way of its own characteristic. The emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because its very nature is emptiness.
The signless state (animittapada) should be known as the complete exhaustion of conceptual constructions (vikalpa),
and unreal imagination (abhūtaparikalpa) is indeed that which is the wishless (apraṇihita).
The signless state is to be known as the complete exhaustion of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).
The meaning is that the unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*) is the state and the objective support (*ālambana*) of non-resolution (*apraṇidhāna*).
Its acquisition is held to be constant together with that path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
O Son of the Victor, [this applies] to all the various factors conducive to enlightenment.

By means of that path of seeing, it should be understood that the Bodhisattva attains all the factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣadharmas), such as the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and so forth.

Having realized through wisdom that the world consists of nothing but conditioned formations (saṃskāra) and is devoid of self, yet is merely the growth of suffering, he abandons the view of self which is composed of what is useless, and takes recourse in the "Great Self-view" (mahātmadṛṣṭi) which possesses great purpose. (MSA 14.37)
One who possesses the view of self here without a [false] view of self, and who is deeply pained even without suffering;
who accomplishes the welfare of all yet has no expectation of being an agent, just as one who, having performed what is beneficial for oneself, expects nothing for himself.
He whose mind is liberated by supreme liberation, yet remains bound by firm and long-lasting bonds,
exerts himself and acts even while not seeing the end of suffering.
In this world, people are unable to bear even their own suffering; how much less can they bear the accumulated suffering of others?
They regard only their own single life as having passed away, remaining indifferent to it; the Bodhisattva, however, is the opposite of that.

The love, the affection, the application, and the tirelessness toward sentient beings that belong to the sons of the Conquerors—this is the supreme marvel amidst worldly existences; yet it is not at all a marvel, because there is no distinction between themselves and sentient beings.
With these five verses, the majesty of the bodhisattva who has attained the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) is elucidated.
The "view of self consisting of what is not beneficial" is the afflicted view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
The "great view of self" is the view of self that possesses great purpose, which consists in attaining a mind of equality toward all sentient beings.

For it is of great purpose because it is the cause for performing the welfare of all sentient beings; it is a view of self that, though devoid of the [false] view of self which consists of what is useless, is of great purpose because it is deeply pained by the suffering arising from the continuums of all sentient beings, even without the suffering born of its own continuum. It is one whose mind is liberated from those things to be abandoned by vision through supreme liberation and by means of the unsurpassed vehicle.

Bound by a firm and extensive bond that extends to the mental continuums of all sentient beings, he does not see the end of suffering because his own element is infinite like space; yet he applies himself to bringing about the end of suffering and indeed accomplishes it for immeasurable sentient beings.
However, the Bodhisattva is the opposite of that, for he is capable of bearing the suffering of all sentient beings condensed together, as far as it extends throughout the world.

That which is the Bodhisattva’s affection for sentient beings, his desire for their welfare and happiness, the application toward that end, and the lack of weariness in one whose mind is so engaged— all this is most wonderful in the worlds,
yet it is not at all wonderful because he regards sentient beings as equal to himself.
Thereafter, on the path of cultivation, in the remaining stages...
In this world, one applies oneself to the cultivation of the two kinds of knowledge.
That gnosis is non-conceptual and purifies the qualities of a Buddha;
the other [gnosis] is according to conventional designation and brings sentient beings to maturity.
And the departure from cultivation occurs upon the completion of two incalculable aeons; having reached the final cultivation, the Bodhisattva becomes one who is consecrated.
And having attained the diamond-like concentration, which is impenetrable by conceptual constructions,
one reaches the final transformation of the basis, which is free from all obscurations.
And one attains omniscience, the unsurpassed state,
abiding in which one acts for the benefit of all sentient beings.
By these, the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) is elucidated;
it consists of two kinds of knowledge:
the non-conceptual (nirvikalpa), by which one purifies one's own Buddha-qualities (buddhadharma).
And there is the mundane [wisdom] obtained subsequent to the supramundane, which exists according to its established order and by which one brings sentient beings to maturity.
Upon the completion of two incalculable eons, having reached the final cultivation that has gone to its conclusion, one is consecrated and attains the diamond-like samādhi.
It is called "diamond-like" in the sense that it is indestructible by conceptual constructions and latent tendencies.

Then one attains the final transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), which is stainless regarding all afflictive and cognitive obstructions, as well as omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) and the unsurpassed state. Abiding therein, for as long as cyclic existence lasts, one acts for the benefit of sentient beings by manifesting perfect awakening, nirvāṇa, and so forth.
How could such a vision of the Sage, who is so difficult to encounter, not be of great significance? For indeed, there can be no constant vision [of him].
Their minds are constantly and intensely nourished by the surges of serene faith arising from incomparable hearing [of the Dharma].
Constantly urged on by the Tathāgatas face-to-face, he remains well-established in the gateway of the Dharma;
as if being seized by the hair and dragged out from the abyss of faults, he is forcibly established in enlightenment.
Having completely overcome the entire world through utterly pure visions and non-conceptual awakenings,
he shines with great magnificence like the great sun, dispelling the profound darkness of the world.
(MSA 97) By these three verses, he demonstrates the greatness of instruction (*avavāda*).
For one who receives instruction in the stream of the entrance to the Dharma, there is constant vision of the Buddhas.
And from that comes the hearing of the incomparable Dharma;
because of this, there arises an extreme clarity of faith, and for one whose mind is nourished by the surges of that faith, the constant vision of the Buddhas becomes of great benefit.
The rest has its meaning already explained.

The Buddhas constantly bestow perfect praise upon one who is correctly engaged in their own welfare, and they offer censure to one engaged in envy; likewise, for those intent on stability and discernment, the Jinas here duly demonstrate all kinds of factors conducive to obstacles. By avoiding and cultivating these factors according to the yoga [prescribed] for the supreme being, there comes to be vastness within this teaching of the Sugata.
By this verse, he demonstrates the fourfold instruction:
with respect to higher ethics (*adhiśīla*), by means of bestowing praise upon the Bodhisattva who is correctly engaged in his own welfare;

and with respect to higher mind (*adhicitta*) and higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*), by teaching all types of factors—both those that are obstacles and those that are conducive—to one who is intent on stability and analytical investigation.
Having abandoned those obstacles and cultivated those favorable conditions respectively,
in this "yoga"— that is, in the cultivation of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*)—
he, having thus continuously fulfilled the accumulation of merit, attains a most vast meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of the mind.
Having received the great instruction from the best of sages, that supreme being becomes one who has reached the further shore of the ocean of virtues.
The summary verse has its meaning already explained.
This concludes the fourteenth chapter, on Instruction and Admonition, in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
The summary verse: Abundance of resolute belief, the seeking and teaching of the Dharma, correct practice, and likewise right instruction and admonition.
There are four verses on the classification of action accompanied by skillful means:
Just as the earth is everywhere the foundation for forests, living beings, mountains, and flowing rivers,
so too is the threefold action of the wise declared to be the universal basis for all virtues such as giving.
By this verse, he demonstrates the means of origination;
for every kind of wholesome action, such as giving and so forth— including the perfections and the factors conducive to enlightenment— is originated by the three types of karma.
"In the wise" means among the Bodhisattvas.
The mention of "forests" and so forth is for the purpose of illustrating objects that are enjoyed, whether unstable or stable.
[They are those] whose selves are exerted through extremely difficult deeds of various forms, extending over many eons.
For the sons of the Conquerors, there is here no submission to karma consisting of body, speech, and mind.
Just as one who seeks his own welfare would protect his own body from poison, weapons, great fires, and enemies,
so too should the Son of the Conqueror protect himself from the threefold karma and from the various inferior vehicles.
By these two verses, he shows the means for emerging [from the state of weariness].
It is because of emerging from weariness with the Mahāyāna and from falling into other vehicles, respectively; "sannati" (depression) has the meaning of "kheda" (weariness).

The similarity to poison and so forth [is established] because action associated with the Hīnayāna involves the dedication of the mind toward the Hīnayāna; because it results in the total severance of the roots of virtue in the Mahāyāna, preventing the arising of unarisen roots of virtue;
because it causes the destruction of roots of virtue already arisen; and because it acts as an obstacle to the attainment of the perfection of Buddhahood.
One who is always free from conceptual construction does not perceive the agent, the action, or the performance of the action in a threefold way.
Consequently, through the inclusion of those skillful means, that person’s action becomes infinite and reaches the further shore of purity.
By this fourth verse, he demonstrates the means for the purification of action;
because, through the complete purity of the mandala, there is the non-apprehension of agent, action, and activity.
"Infinite" means inexhaustible.
The fifteenth chapter of the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, titled "Action Accompanied by Skillful Means," is concluded.
The sixteenth chapter, concerning the "Compendium of the Classifications of the Perfections," begins with this summary verse:

Now, the enumeration, their characteristics, their sequence, their etymological explanation, and their qualities through practice; their classification, their synthesis, their opposites, their benefits, and their mutual determination—these are to be known. (MSA 16.1)
There are six verses on the classification of number:
Prosperity consists of the excellence of enjoyments, the excellence of the personal basis, the excellence of attendants, and the excellence of undertakings;
furthermore, it includes being free from the power of the afflictions and always being free from error regarding what is to be done.
Thus ends the first [section].
In that regard, through the four perfections, there is a fourfold prosperity.
Through generosity comes the perfection of wealth; through ethical discipline, the perfection of the physical body;
and through patience, the perfection of attendants.
For by practicing that [generosity], one becomes very dear to many people in the future;
through diligence, there is perfection in undertaking because of the success of all undertakings;
and by means of the fifth [perfection], there is freedom from being under the power of the afflictions, due to the suppression of the afflictions through meditative concentration.

Through the sixth [perfection], there is non-erroneousness regarding duties, because of the thorough knowledge of all tasks as they truly are. Thus is spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*). With respect to both lack of affliction therein and the undertaking of non-perverted duties, the six perfections are established.
One who is well-engaged in the welfare of sentient beings acts through generosity, non-injury, and forbearance.
Through the basis, the abiding, and liberation, one practices for one's own sake in every way.
Thus is the second [section].

A bodhisattva correctly engaged in the welfare of sentient beings accomplishes the welfare of sentient beings through the three perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, and patience—respectively, by means of relinquishment, non-harming, and the endurance of harm.
Through the three [remaining perfections]—by way of having a basis, by the stability of the mind, and by liberation—he practices every aspect of his own welfare.
Relying upon vigor, one practices meditation and wisdom in due order: by the concentration of the unconcentrated mind and by the liberation of the concentrated mind.
Thus, with respect to the welfare of others and the welfare of oneself, there are six perfections:
through non-affliction, non-harming, endurance of harm, and lack of weariness in action.
Through captivating and well-spoken words, there is the welfare of others; from this, one's own welfare [arises].
Thus ends the third [section].
Through generosity and the other perfections, the bodhisattva’s entire benefit for others is accomplished;
that is, by means of providing resources and removing obstacles for others, respectively.
By not harming others and by enduring harm;

by being untiring in acts of assistance; by attracting others through the power of miracles and so forth; and by cutting through doubts with well-spoken and eloquent words—through this altruism, the Bodhisattva’s own self-interest is accomplished.
Because others' tasks are one's own task and because of the attainment of great enlightenment,

there are six perfections (*pāramitā*) due to the commitment to the welfare of all others. Furthermore, there is lack of attachment to enjoyments, intense reverence for the two [truths], and tirelessness.
And yoga is non-conceptual; this is the equal and supreme vehicle.
Thus is the fourth:
through giving, the bodhisattva has no delight in possessions because of his lack of regard for them;
through the undertaking of ethical discipline, he possesses intense reverence for the bodhisattva trainings.
Through patience and vigor, there is non-exhaustion respectively in two respects: in suffering caused by sentient and non-sentient beings, and in the application to the wholesome;
and in meditative concentration and wisdom, there is non-conceptual yoga comprised of calm abiding and insight.
And because this constitutes the summary of the entire Mahāyāna, there are six perfections:
one is the path of non-attachment toward sense objects; another is for the restraint of distraction regarding the attainment of those [perfections];
another is for not abandoning and for increasing sentient beings; and another is for the purification of obscurations.
Thus ends the fifth [chapter].
In this context, generosity (*dāna*) is the path of non-attachment toward sense objects, because attachment to them is removed through the practice of relinquishment.

Ethical discipline (*śīla*) consists in the restraint of distractions that lead to the acquisition of those [objects]; for one who abides in the monastic vows (*bhikṣusaṃvara*), it ensures that no distractions regarding any worldly activities arise so as not to attain those sense objects.
Patience consists in not abandoning sentient beings because one is not distressed by the suffering involved in helping them all.
Diligence consists in the increase of the wholesome, since for one who has initiated diligence, that [wholesome] is attained accordingly.
Meditation and wisdom constitute the path for the purification of obstructions, because through these two, the obstructions of afflictions and the knowable are purified.
The "path" refers to the means.
Thus, because of the context of the path in all its aspects, there are six perfections;
and with reference to the three trainings, the six perfections were fully proclaimed by the Victors.
The first three are twofold according to the last two; among the three, there is one.
Thus ends the sixth [chapter].
Among those, the first three perfections constitute the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*), because they include their respective equipment and retinues.

For through generosity (*dāna*), one takes up ethical discipline (*śīla*) without regard for enjoyments; and once taken up, one protects it through patience (*kṣānti*) by not reviling in return when reviled, and so forth.

"Twofold" refers to the training in higher mind (*adhicitta*) and the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*); this [training] is subsumed by the latter two, namely meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), respectively.
It should be understood that among all three trainings, there is one perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), because vigor is the companion to them all.

There are six verses on the analysis of the characteristics: Generosity is free from its opposite, is accompanied by non-conceptual knowledge, fulfills all desires, and ripens sentient beings in three ways. (16.8)
The generosity of Bodhisattvas has four characteristics: it is free from opposing factors because of the abandonment of attachment;
it is accompanied by non-conceptual wisdom due to its application to the penetration of the selflessness of phenomena; and it fulfills all desires by giving whatever anyone wishes for.
The ripening of sentient beings is threefold: by means of generosity, one gathers sentient beings and establishes them in the three vehicles according to their respective capacities;
morality is free from its opposites and is accompanied by non-conceptual knowledge;
and likewise, the fulfillment of all desires is also threefold as a means of ripening sentient beings.
Patience is free from its opposites and is accompanied by non-conceptual knowledge;
it fulfills all desires and matures sentient beings in three ways.
Vigor is devoid of its opposite, accompanied by non-conceptual knowledge, fulfills all desires, and matures sentient beings; it is threefold. (MSA 16.11)
Dhyāna is free from opposing factors, accompanied by non-conceptual knowledge,
fulfills all desires, and matures sentient beings in three ways.
Wisdom is free from its opposites and has reached non-conceptual knowledge;
it fulfills all desires and matures sentient beings in three ways.
Just as the characteristic of generosity is fourfold, so too should it be understood for ethical discipline (*śīla*) and the others.
Their respective opposites, however, are immorality, anger, laziness, distraction, and faulty wisdom.

The fulfillment of all desires through ethical discipline and the other perfections occurs because they fulfill the desires of others by means of restraining all bodily and vocal actions, enduring offenses, providing assistance, and cutting through doubts.
The quality of ripening sentient beings consists in attracting them through ethical discipline and the other perfections, thereby ripening them within the three vehicles.
Regarding the analysis of their sequence, there is this verse:
"Because the latter arises based upon the former, they are taught in that order."
Also because of the state of being inferior or superior, and because of being gross or subtle.
These [perfections], beginning with generosity, are taught in sequence for three reasons:
because each subsequent one arises based upon the preceding one.

For one who is indifferent to enjoyments undertakes ethical discipline; being possessed of ethical discipline, one becomes patient; being patient, one exerts vigor; having exerted vigor, one produces concentration; and with a concentrated mind, one perceives things as they truly are.
Because the former is inferior and the latter is a state of excellence;
for giving is inferior while ethical discipline is superior, and so on up to meditation being inferior while wisdom is superior.
Furthermore, because the former is coarse and the latter is subtle.
For generosity is coarse because it is easy to enter and easy to practice;
ethical discipline is subtle because it is difficult to enter and difficult to practice.
In this way, it continues up to the point where meditative concentration is coarse and wisdom is subtle.
There is a verse in the section on etymological analysis:

"Because of the removal of poverty, the attainment of coolness, the destruction of anger, and because of the possession of excellence, the concentration of mind, and the knowledge of the ultimate truth, it is called [Buddha]. (AMsa 16.15)
It is called *dāna* because it removes poverty;

it is called *śīla* because it brings about coolness, for one who possesses it is free from the burning afflictions caused by sense objects; it is called *kṣānti* because there is an exhaustion of anger, since through it anger is exhausted;
and it is so called because it joins one with the supreme.
Vigor (*vīrya*) is from the application to wholesome phenomena (*kuśaladharma*). It is called meditation (*dhyāna*) because it holds the mind within.
It is called wisdom (*prajñā*) because by means of it one knows the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Regarding the classification of cultivation, there is this verse:
"Based upon the foundation of cultivation, as well as mental attention, intention, skillful means, and mastery, [the cultivation] of all [perfections] is explained. *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* 16.16.

The cultivation of the perfections is fivefold. Among these, that which is based on the substratum (*upadhi-saṃniśritā*) is of four aspects. Therein, that which is based on the cause (*hetu-saṃniśritā*) is the practice of application toward the perfections by the power of one's spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
That which is based on maturation is that which arises through the power of the excellence of one's physical form;
that which is based on aspiration is that which arises through the power of former vows;
and that which is based on analytical discernment is the repeated practice of application toward the perfections through the power of wisdom.
The cultivation of the perfections based on mental attention is fourfold:
[first] by means of mental attention consisting of resolute belief, for one who has resolute belief in the sūtras associated with all the perfections;
and [second] by means of mental attention consisting of relishing, for one who relishes the perfections already attained through the application of seeing their virtues.

The cultivation of the perfections based on intention is sixfold: [first] by means of the mental application of rejoicing, for one who rejoices in the giving and other virtues of all sentient beings in all world-systems; and [second] by means of the mental application of delighting, for one who delights in the future excellence of the perfections of oneself and of sentient beings.
It is by means of an insatiable intention, a vast intention, a joyful intention, an intention of benefit, an unstained intention, and a virtuous intention.

Among these, the bodhisattva’s insatiable intention regarding giving is as follows: even if a bodhisattva were to fill world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges with the seven precious jewels and offer them to a single sentient being in a single moment, and likewise offer as many of his own bodies as there are sands in the river Ganges; [he would still not be satisfied].
And in this manner, he would provide for them moment by moment for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges.
And just as he would do for one sentient being, so too would he provide for the entire realm of sentient beings who are to be ripened for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment by this same method.
Yet, the bodhisattva’s intention to give remains entirely unsatiated.
Such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s insatiable intention regarding giving;
and the bodhisattva does not let such a succession of gifts lapse for even a single moment, nor does he interrupt it until he sits at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa).
Such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s vast intention regarding giving;
and the bodhisattva becomes even more joyful while thus favoring those beings with his gift than those beings themselves are when being favored by that gift.
Such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s joyful intention regarding giving. Furthermore,
that bodhisattva regards those beings whom he thus benefits through giving as being more helpful to himself than he is to them.
"By virtue of their being a support for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment"—
such a disposition as this is what is meant by "disposition.
Furthermore, even after a bodhisattva has performed such vast merit consisting of giving toward sentient beings, he has no need for a return favor or for its karmic maturation.
Such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s stainless intention regarding the cultivation of the perfection of generosity:
that the bodhisattva rejoices in the maturation of even such a vast mass of giving for the sake of sentient beings, and not for himself.
Having made it common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s virtuous intention regarding the cultivation of the perfection of generosity.
In that regard, the bodhisattva’s insatiable intention concerns the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva, throughout body-forms as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, with a lifespan as long as the measure of aeons equal to the sands of the river Gaṅgā, were to experience a constant lack of all necessities while performing the four modes of conduct within a great trichiliocosm filled with fire, and were to cultivate even a single moment of the perfection of ethical discipline up to a single moment of the perfection of wisdom; [this would be far more meritorious than the aforementioned gift].
In this manner, whatever constitutes the aggregate of ethical discipline and whatever constitutes the aggregate of wisdom by which one awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—

one should cultivate the aggregate of ethical discipline up to the aggregate of wisdom; for the Bodhisattva’s intention in the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline, up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, remains truly insatiable.

Such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s insatiable intention regarding the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline, up to and including the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; that is,

the intention by which a bodhisattva does not slacken or interrupt that succession of cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline, up to the succession of cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, until sitting at the seat of awakening—
this kind of intention is the bodhisattva’s vast intention regarding the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline, up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
