Furthermore, a bodhisattva becomes even more joyful by means of that cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom while benefiting sentient beings,
than those very sentient beings who are being benefited.
Such an aspiration is the bodhisattva’s joyful intention regarding the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva regards those sentient beings as more beneficial to himself than he is to them—
those whom he benefits through the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, rather than benefiting himself—
on account of their being the support for his attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s beneficial intention regarding the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; and having performed such vast merit consisting of the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, the bodhisattva has no desire for recompense or for its maturation.

Such an intention as this—extending from the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom—is the bodhisattva’s unstained intention (*nirlepa-āśaya*).

In that regard, when a bodhisattva rejoices only for the sake of sentient beings in the maturation of the mass of merit consisting of the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, and having made it common to all sentient beings, dedicates it toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment; this is [the intention].
Such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s virtuous intention regarding the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
Cultivation based on skillful means is threefold in aspect,
by virtue of examining the purity of the three spheres through non-conceptual knowledge.
For indeed, that means is for the accomplishment of all mental attentions (*manasikāra*).
The cultivation of the perfections (*pāramitā*) based on mastery (*vibhutva*) is threefold: by way of mastery over the body; by way of mastery over objects; and by way of mastery over activity.
Through mastery over conduct and through mastery over teaching.
Among these, mastery over the body is as follows: (Msa 104)
The Tathāgata should be viewed as having two bodies: the essential (svābhāvika) and the enjoyment (sāṃbhogika).
Among these, the mastery of conduct (caryāvibhutva) is to be seen as the transformation body (nairmāṇika-kāya), by which he displays to all sentient beings a religious practice in every form.
Mastery of teaching is the absence of obstruction in teaching all aspects of the six perfections.
There are twelve verses on the summary of the classifications.
Each of the perfections, beginning with generosity, is distinguished by six meanings.
These six meanings are: essence, cause, fruit, function, endowment, and operation.
Regarding the distinctions of generosity, there are two verses.
The presentation of the meaning is rooted in volition;
it fulfills the two types of assistance through the excellence of enjoyments and the excellence of the personal existence.
Having fully understood that very gift as being endowed with non-avarice and consisting of the visible Dharma, material goods, and fearlessness, the wise person should practice it.
The nature of giving is the communication of wealth to recipients.
Its cause is the volition co-arising with non-greed and other [wholesome roots].
Its fruit consists of the perfection of enjoyments and the perfection of the personal existence (ātmabhāva) as comprised by longevity and so forth, as in the *Pañcasthāna-sūtra*.
Its function is the benefit of oneself and others, as well as the fulfillment of the equipment for great enlightenment.
Its activity consists in its application among those who are free from stinginess,
through the distinctions of bestowing the gift of the Dharma, material goods, and fearlessness in this very life.
There are two verses regarding the classification of ethical discipline (*śīla*):
It consists of six limbs and culminates in the cultivation of tranquility; it bestows a happy rebirth and stability;
it is established in peace and free from fear; and it is endowed with the equipment of merit (*puṇyasaṃbhāra*).
Ethical discipline, which is obtained through both convention and the nature of reality, exists in those who abide in restraint;
having thus fully understood ethical discipline, the wise person should bring it to perfection.

"Six-limbed" refers to its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). "Possessing the six limbs" means that one dwells endowed with ethical discipline (*śīla*) and so forth, up to training by undertaking the precepts (*śikṣāpada*). "Ending in the state of tranquility" refers to the cause (*hetu*).
Because it is undertaken with the intention of [attaining] nirvāṇa;
"bestowing a happy rebirth and stability" refers to the fruit,
because through ethical discipline one goes to a happy rebirth.
And because one attains stability of mind through the sequence beginning with freedom from regret,
it is said that "it is the foundation, peaceful, and fearless"— this refers to its function.
For ethical discipline (*śīla*) is indeed the foundation of all virtuous qualities.
It is peaceful because it calms the burning heat of the afflictions;
and it is fearless because it does not give rise to the fears, transgressions, and hostilities that have their causes in [actions such as] taking life.

"Endowed with the equipment of merit" refers to *yoga*, because it consists of the constant restraint of the actions of body, speech, and mind at all times. "Obtained through convention and through the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) exists among those who abide in restraint" is the explanation of its function; therein, that obtained through convention is comprised within the *prātimokṣa* restraint, while that obtained through the nature of reality is comprised within the meditative (*dhyāna*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) restraints. This is its functional differentiation, as it operates through these three types of differentiation.
"It exists among those established in restraint" refers to the conduct of proper behavior.
Regarding the classification of patience, there are two verses:
"The knowledge of endurance and acceptance arises from compassion and reliance upon the Dharma."
It is declared to have five benefits and to accomplish the welfare of both.
Among these, austerity is considered to be of three kinds when conjoined with intensity;
having thus fully understood patience, the wise person should bring it to perfection.
"Knowledge of endurance and acceptance" is the intrinsic nature of the threefold patience (*kṣānti*). This is because "endurance" (*marṣa*) refers to the endurance of harm,
corresponding respectively to the patience of enduring injury and the patience of reflecting on the Dharma, while "acceptance" (*adhivāsa*) refers to the patience of accepting suffering.
"Out of compassion and by relying on the Dharma" is the cause. Furthermore, reliance on the Dharma consists of the undertaking of ethical discipline and the mastery of what has been heard.
"It is said that there are five benefits" refers to the fruit;
as it is stated in the Sūtra:
"There are five benefits in patience."
He does not abound in enmity; he does not abound in divisiveness;
he abounds in happiness and gladness.
One dies without regret; after the dissolution of the body, one is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world among the gods.
And this action—namely, the endurance and acceptance [of suffering]—is said to accomplish the welfare of both, as has been stated.
"He accomplishes the welfare of both himself and another—he who, perceiving another to be angry, personally pacifies him there. Thus it is said.
"Endowed with the power of austerity" refers to yoga;
as it has been said:
"Patience is the supreme austerity."
Regarding those [patiences], "that" refers to the functioning based on the substratum (*ādhāra-vṛtti*), because they function within those who possess patience.
It is considered to be threefold, which refers to the functioning by way of differentiation (*prabheda-vṛtti*) according to the three types of patience as previously explained.
There are two verses concerning the differentiation of vigor (*vīrya*).
Right enthusiasm for the wholesome is firmly established upon faith and aspiration;
it increases qualities such as mindfulness and serves as the antidote to the afflictions.
Endowed with qualities such as non-attachment, that [vigor] is sevenfold in those [contexts];
having fully understood vigor alone, the wise person should cultivate it.
"Right enthusiasm for what is wholesome" is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The term "wholesome" is intended to exclude enthusiasm for other activities, and "right" is intended to exclude enthusiasm for the liberation of non-Buddhist outsiders (*anyatīrthika*).
"Established upon faith and aspiration" is its cause (*hetu*), for one who possesses faith exerts great vigor (*vīrya*).
"In the increase of qualities such as mindfulness" refers to the fruit;
for one who has initiated vigor, there arises the emergence of qualities such as mindfulness and meditative concentration.
"Being an antidote to the afflictions" refers to its function (*karman*), as it is said: "But one who has initiated vigor dwells in happiness, unmixed with evil and unwholesome states.
"Endowed with virtues such as non-attachment" refers to its application (*yoga*).
"In them" refers to those who have initiated vigor; this is the function of the basis (*ādhāravṛtti*). "Sevenfold" refers to the function of differentiation (*prabhedavṛtti*).

Furthermore, that vigor—which is both physical and mental—applied with continuity and with respect toward the three trainings, beginning with the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla*), is what is meant.
There are two verses concerning the distinctions of meditative absorption (dhyāna):

The stability of the mind within, established upon mindfulness and vigor, leads to the attainment of happiness, the superknowledges (abhijñā), and mastery over dwelling [in those states]. (AMsa 16.25)
Among all phenomena, meditation is preeminent, and it exists in three forms;
having thus fully understood meditation, the wise person should cultivate it.
The stability of the mind within is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Being established upon mindfulness and vigor is its cause (*hetu*),
because when there is no loss of the object of focus, one accomplishes meditative attainment by relying on vigor.
"For the sake of rebirth in happiness" refers to the fruit, because the fruit of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is rebirth in a state free from affliction.
"Mastery over the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) and the [divine] abodes" refers to its function (*karman*),
because through meditative absorption one gains mastery over the superknowledges.
And because of mastery over the noble, divine, and Brahma-abodes,
there is a connection with preeminence, as it is said: "the foremost among all phenomena."

"All phenomena have meditative concentration as their foremost" means that this exists within those who practice meditation; this is the function of the support. And that [concentration] is threefold: with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), without applied thought but with sustained thought alone (*avitarka-vicāramātra*), and without applied thought and without sustained thought (*avitarka-avicāra*).
It is without applied thought and without sustained thought;
furthermore, it is accompanied by rapture,
and it is accompanied by pleasure.
And it is accompanied by equanimity;
this is the functioning according to differentiation.
There are two verses regarding the differentiation of wisdom.
Right discernment is to be known as being established upon concentration;
it is taught as the livelihood of wisdom for the sake of complete liberation from affliction.
Among all phenomena, there exists a superior one, and it is threefold;
having thus fully understood wisdom, the wise person should bring it to perfection.
"Correct discernment of the knowable" is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
"Correctly" means not erroneously; this is for the purpose of excluding the correct discernment of worldly affairs.
"Established in meditative concentration" is its cause (*hetu*).
One whose mind is concentrated understands things as they truly are;
because it leads to complete liberation from affliction, this is the fruit.
For by means of that, there is complete liberation from affliction.
By means of mundane, supramundane-inferior, and great supramundane discernment;
"living by wisdom and teaching well" means that living by wisdom and teaching well are its functions,
for by these, those who live by supreme wisdom truly live.
"He teaches the Dharma correctly" means that he possesses supremacy with respect to all phenomena;
as it has been said:

"All phenomena have wisdom as their supreme [quality]"; the commentary states that "it exists in them in a threefold manner," because it operates within those possessing wisdom and through its threefold differentiation.
There is the mundane, the inferior supramundane, and the great supramundane.
Thus has been explained the differentiation of each of the perfections, such as generosity and the rest, according to their sixfold classification of meanings.
Regarding the analysis of the means of integration, there is this verse:
All pure dharmas— whether distracted, concentrated, or both—
should be known as being embraced by two, two, and two perfections respectively.
All pure dharmas are dharmas such as giving and so forth.

Among these, those that are distracted are subsumed by the first two perfections, because giving and the undertaking of ethical discipline (*śīla*) are not states of meditative concentration (*samāhita*).
Those that are concentrated are subsumed by the last two, because meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and wisdom according to reality (*yathābhūta-prajñā*) are states of meditative concentration.
Both [types] are associated with two, namely patience and vigor,
because those two exist both in a state of meditative concentration and in a non-concentrated state.
There are six verses concerning the analysis of their opposites.
Neither attached, nor attached, nor attached; indeed not attached is the giving of the Bodhisattvas—neither attached, nor attached, nor attached. (AMsa 16.30)
There are seven kinds of attachment that are the opposites of giving:

attachment to enjoyments, attachment to procrastination, attachment to contentment with only that much, attachment to partiality, attachment to seeking a return, attachment to karmic maturation, and attachment to the opposite side,
which arises because the latent tendencies for attaining those opposites have not been eradicated.
And there is the power of distraction.
Furthermore, that distraction is twofold:
distraction of mental attention due to longing for the Lesser Vehicle; and...
And there is distraction through conceptualization because of the conceptualization of the giver, the recipient, and the gift.
Therefore, because of being free from the seven kinds of attachment, the non-attachment of giving is said to be sevenfold:
"neither attached, nor attached, nor attached; not attached at all, and likewise with morality."
And it is not attached, not attached, and not attached for the Bodhisattvas.
The patience of Bodhisattvas is not attached, not attached, not attached; it is not characterized by attachment; it is not attached, not attached, not attached. (AMsa 16.32)
Neither attached, nor attached, nor attached, yet indeed attached is the vigor of the bodhisattvas; neither attached, nor attached, nor attached. (AMsa 16.33)
Neither attached, nor attached, nor attached; indeed not attached is the meditation of the Bodhisattvas—neither attached, nor attached, nor attached. (AMsa 16.34)
Neither attached, nor attached, nor attached; non-attachment is not wisdom.
Neither attached, nor attached, nor attached—such is the state of the Bodhisattvas.
Just as attachment to generosity has been described, so too should it be understood for ethical discipline up to wisdom.

However, here one should understand that attachment to immorality and so forth is the opposite of attachment to enjoyments; this is because attachment to the adverse factors arises from not having eradicated the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are the counterparts to those [virtues].
And there is distraction due to conceptual construction, arising from the imaginative construction of the three spheres as appropriate.
Regarding the analysis of the qualities, there are twenty-three verses:
"The sons of the Buddha have always renounced even their own lives upon encountering a seeker; out of compassion, they do not expect a return from others, nor do they pray for a desired reward."
And by that very giving, all people have been established in the three types of enlightenment; furthermore, through the embrace of wisdom, that giving has been made inexhaustible in the world.
Thus the meaning of the words is easily understood:
The sons of the Buddha have always undertaken the threefold morality consisting of restraint and exertion; heaven is not their desired goal, nor do they, upon reaching it, develop attachment to it.
By that very morality, all living beings are established in the three types of enlightenment, and through its integration with primordial wisdom, that morality is made inexhaustible in the world.

Ethical discipline is threefold: the ethical discipline of restraint, the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous qualities, and [the ethical discipline of acting for the benefit of sentient beings].
And the ethical discipline of acting for the welfare of sentient beings consists of one type, which has restraint as its nature,
and two types, which have exertion as their nature.

The sons of the Buddha have practiced forbearance, which is exceedingly difficult to perform, as well as all manner of injuries from men; yet this was not for the sake of heaven, nor out of incapacity, nor out of fear, nor even with a view toward receiving benefit.

By means of supreme forbearance, they have established all living beings in the three types of enlightenment; and furthermore, through the embrace of primordial wisdom, that forbearance has been made inexhaustible in the world.

Thus, by means of the supreme patience—namely, the patience of enduring suffering and the patience of forbearing the injuries of others, respectively—the sons of the Buddha have exerted incomparable vigor, consisting of both armor and application, in order to destroy the host of afflictions within themselves and to attain supreme enlightenment for the sake of others. By that very vigor, the entire multitude of living beings has been established in the three types of enlightenment; and furthermore, through the integration of wisdom, that vigor has been rendered inexhaustible in the world.
Thus, there is the vigor of armor and the vigor of application.

The sons of the Buddha have fully accomplished meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) consisting of manifold samādhis; having dwelt in every way in the most excellent joys of meditation, they out of compassion resort to inferior rebirths.
By that very meditation, all people are established in the three types of enlightenment; and furthermore, through its integration with wisdom, that meditation is made inexhaustible in the world.
Thus, "abounding in meditative concentration" means being comprised of the infinite meditative concentrations of the Bodhisattvas.

The sons of the Buddha have fully understood reality (*tattva*) and all that is to be known in every way; yet no attachment whatsoever has been produced by the Buddhas even toward *nirvāṇa*, so how could it be toward the conventional?

By that very knowledge, all people have been established in the three types of enlightenment; furthermore, through the embracing of sentient beings, knowledge has been made inexhaustible in the world. (AMsa 16.41)

Thus: reality (*satattva*) is the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) comprised within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), namely the selflessness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharmanairātmya*).

And that which is "to be known in every way" refers to the knowable (*jñeya*), which is differentiated by infinite distinctions of characteristics such as one's own conventions and so forth; and that which is "not to be known" (*ajñeya*).

The inexhaustibility of generosity and the other perfections through their being embraced by non-conceptual gnosis (*nirvikalpajñāna*) is due to their not being exhausted even in the nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*).
Furthermore, because wisdom embraces sentient beings through compassion, it does not abandon them.
Moreover, the summarized meaning of these six verses is indicated by the seventh verse:
"It is magnanimous, non-material, of great purpose, and inexhaustible."
For it should be understood that the fourfold quality belongs to generosity and the other perfections collectively.
Thus it is said. In this regard, by the first line, the loftiness of generosity and the other perfections is illuminated;
by the second, their non-material nature;
and by the third, their great purpose, because they accomplish the welfare of great beings.
By the fourth [verse], inexhaustibility is established; thus, through these verses, their fourfold quality should be understood:

"The compassionate giver, by virtue of his superior application, overcomes the satisfaction of seeing [the recipient] fulfilled, as well as the lack of satisfaction toward the petitioner, and even the latter's expectations. (AMsa 16.43)
For when a person who is a petitioner experiences joy upon seeing a donor, and then, having obtained what was desired, experiences the satisfaction that arises from the fulfillment of their wishes;
whereas dissatisfaction arises from not seeing [the donor] and from the non-fulfillment [of their wishes];
and there is also the hope regarding seeing him and the fulfillment of their wishes.
That [joy] arises more intensely in the Bodhisattva at all times from seeing supplicants and from fulfilling their desires;
whereas dissatisfaction arises from not seeing them and from not fulfilling [their desires].
Therefore, the compassionate giver surpasses all those [other givers] by virtue of his excellence;
for he is compassionate because he always renounces his life, enjoyments, and wife for the sake of sentient beings.
Since he rejoices to his heart's content in that renunciation, how could he fail to maintain it here? (MSA 16.44)
Abstention from those [things] is "abstention from them," namely from the lives, enjoyments, and wives belonging to others.
By this, he demonstrates the quality of the precept of abstaining from the three types of physical misconduct.
Disregarding [his own welfare], with an even mind, fearless, and giving everything for the sake of compassion;
How could a noble one speak falsehood for the sake of harming others?
By this, he demonstrates the quality of abstaining from false speech.
False speech might be uttered for one's own sake out of regard for one's body and life,
or for the sake of another out of affection for a beloved person.
Whether out of fear, such as fear of kings and the like, or for the sake of some material gain, for the purpose of profit;
whereas a bodhisattva is indifferent toward his own body and life.
He possesses an even mind toward all sentient beings by virtue of having a mind of equality with himself;
he is fearless because he has transcended the five fears;
and he is a giver of everything to those who ask because of his renunciation of all his possessions.
For what reason would he speak falsehood?
Because he desires the welfare of others, possesses compassion, and is deeply afraid of causing suffering to others;
and because he is well-engaged in the discipline of sentient beings, he remains far removed from the three faults of speech.

Since a bodhisattva desires the welfare of all sentient beings equally, how could he engage in slander for the sake of creating a rift between others? Furthermore, being compassionate and intent on removing the suffering of others,
and being exceedingly fearful of causing suffering to others, how could he speak harsh words for the purpose of producing pain in others?

Being correctly engaged in the discipline of sentient beings, how could he engage in frivolous speech? Therefore, he is very far removed from the three faults of speech— slander, harshness, and frivolous speech—
as he is compassionate, a giver of all things, and highly skilled in the arising of phenomena through dependent origination.
How could he endure every form of mental affliction?
Covetousness, malice, or wrong view— these, respectively,
constitute the quality of purity of morality for Bodhisattvas, due to their association with specific dharmas that are the antidotes to immorality.
For they always maintain the perception of benefit and joy toward those who harm them, and the perception of others' welfare toward those who suffer in constant misery.
When a compassionate person attains [this], what would there not be that should be forgiven?
For one who,

because of having always abandoned the perception of "other" and possesses an affection for others that is greater than for oneself, neither the perception of an injurer nor the perception of suffering arises.
For one who possesses compassion, vigor is not difficult to practice because of the performance of difficult deeds.
The Bodhisattva is compassionate.
In that regard, concerning the compassion of one who possesses compassion, the heroism that arises from performing difficult deeds for the sake of others is both not difficult and very difficult.
How is it not difficult?
Because the perception of "other" regarding others has been removed,
and because one always feels greater affection for others than for oneself,
how could this be very difficult to perform?
That energy which is thus free from the notion of "other" and possesses a love greater than for oneself is [superior].

For the meditation (dhyāna) of the three [vehicles] is considered to be of little happiness, self-centered, sluggish, subject to decline, perishable, and accompanied by delusion; it is the opposite for Bodhisattvas.
The meditation of worldly beings brings little happiness; that of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas brings happiness for oneself alone.
It is sluggish for worldly beings because it is attached to the view of a self-existent body (satkāya), and for the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas because it is attached to Nirvāṇa.
It is subject to decline for worldly beings, and it is perishable for the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas because it perishes upon entering the Nirvāṇa without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa).
For all [others], it is accompanied by delusion through their respective afflicted or unafflicted delusions;
for Bodhisattvas, however, meditative absorption is characterized by great bliss, brings happiness to both self and others, is non-attached, non-declining, inexhaustible, and free from delusion.
Just as darkness is dispelled by lamps, so too is the threefold knowledge [dispelled] by the [removal of] obscurations.
But the incomparable knowledge of the compassionate ones is like the rays of the sun.
Just as knowledge gained by groping with the hands in the dark has a limited scope, is not direct perception, and is indistinct, so it is for ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Just as knowledge gained by lamps in a small room is partial, is direct perception, yet not entirely pure, so it is for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Just as knowledge gained by the rays of the sun is all-pervasive, direct perception, and perfectly pure, so it is for Bodhisattvas.
For this very reason, that [giving] is incomparable;
through its basis, its substance, its motive, its dedication, its cause, its knowledge, its field, and its support, it is considered supreme. (MSA 16.52)
In that context, the basis is the bodhisattva.
As for the object: for the gift of material things (*āmiṣadāna*), the internal object is supreme;
for the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*), it is for those who are afraid of the miserable states and cyclic existence (*apāya-saṃsāra*).
That is fearlessness;
the Mahāyāna is the gift of Dharma;
the cause is compassion.
Dedication is the aspiration for the fruit of great enlightenment.
The cause is the latent impression from previous practice of the perfection of generosity.
Knowledge is non-conceptual, by means of which one gives a gift purified of the three spheres, through not conceptualizing the giver, the gift, or the recipient.
The field is fivefold:
one who is in need, one who is suffering, one who is without refuge, one who practices misconduct, and one who possesses virtues.
Among these four [latter types], each subsequent field is superior.
In their absence, there is the fifth:
the threefold basis upon which one gives,
namely, resolute conviction, mental attention, and meditative concentration.
Resolute belief (*adhimukti*) is as described in the analysis of cultivation (*bhāvanāvibhāga*) regarding the mental application of resolute belief (*adhimuktimanaskāra*).
Mental application (*manaskāra*) is as described in that same context regarding the mental application of relishing and rejoicing (*āsvādanābhinandanamanaskāra*).
Meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and so forth are as mastery (*vibhutva*) is described in that same context.
Thus, the supreme gift is that which has a supreme basis and so forth;
this should be understood as the exposition:

that which gives, that which is given, that by which it is given, that to whom it is given, from what it is given, by whose possession it is held, where it is given, and to what extent and in what manner—that is the gift.
Ethical discipline is considered supreme by reason of its basis, its substance, its cause, its dedication, its motive, its knowledge, its field, and its support. (MSA 16.53)
Vigor is considered supreme by reason of its basis, its substance, its cause, its dedication, its cause [of attainment], its knowledge, its field, and its support. (AMsa 16.54)
Dhyāna is considered supreme by virtue of its basis, its substance, its sign, its transformation, its cause, its knowledge, its field, and its support. (AMsa 16.55)
Wisdom is considered supreme by virtue of its basis, its substance, its cause, its transformation, its motive, its knowledge, its field, and its support. (AMsa 16.56)
The supreme object of ethical discipline is the bodhisattva vow;
that of patience is the lowly and weak who take one's life;
and that of vigor is the cultivation of the perfections and the abandonment of their opposites.
The *dhāna* consists of the bodhisattva samādhis;
the *tathatā* belongs to wisdom (*prajñā*);
and the *kṣetra* of all [perfections], beginning with ethical discipline (*śīla*), is the Mahāyāna.
The remainder is to be understood as before:
"A gift that brings happiness to a single being but causes harm for many eons would be dear to Bodhisattvas; how much more so its opposite. (MSA 16.57)

Even if the gift of Bodhisattvas were to bring happiness to only a single being while causing harm to themselves for many eons, it would still be dear to them because of their extraordinary compassion; how much more so when it brings happiness to many beings and confers benefit upon themselves for many eons?
For the sake of which embodied beings desire wealth, that very thing the wise bestow upon other embodied beings.
Wealth is sought by people for the sake of the body, yet that very same wealth is relinquished hundreds of times by the wise.
In this regard, the first half [of the verse] is explained by the second half:
"When the mind does not suffer even while casting off the body itself, what need be said regarding inferior wealth?"
Therefore, that joy of his is supramundane; because of that, it is further superior for him.
In this regard, it is shown that when his mind does not suffer even as he casts off his very body, that is his "supra-mundane" state.

Since he attains joy through that suffering, that [joy] is superior to it; thus, it is "superior to the supra-mundane. Even though he is a seeker, he does not find satisfaction through the acceptance of desired objects obtained according to his wish.
Just as here the wise one attains satisfaction through the gift of all things by means of the satisfaction of those who seek his aid, so too [does he attain it elsewhere].
"By those who have obtained what was desired and sufficient" means by those who have acquired what was intended and adequate.
"By the gift of all that exists" means up to the point of giving even one's own life.
A beggar does not regard himself as so wealthy as to possess such complete enjoyments as this.
Through the gift of all that he possesses, even though he is without wealth, the wise man regards himself as one who possesses wealth.
Even upon obtaining vast wealth, a seeker does not consider it a favor from the donor for the sake of his own gain;
rather, the wise person, having satisfied seekers here with excellent gifts according to the rule, conceives toward them the notion of a great favor, just as [the donor feels].
This is due to a particular quality of compassion.
The meaning of these two verses is clear:
embodied beings, their own sorrow dispelled and established in well-being, enjoy even vast wealth when it belongs to one [who acts thus].
Just as there is an abundance of spreading branches from a tree of enjoyments rich in supreme fruit on the path, no one other than the Bodhisattvas is such an enjoyer of excessive enjoyment.

Because he possesses both extensive distribution and excessive enjoyment, he is one who distributes extensively and enjoys excessively; and it should be understood that he is none other than a bodhisattva.
The remainder has its meaning already explained by way of the distinction of preeminence, the distinction of cause, the distinction of action, and the distinction of types and bases.
It is taught that diligence is to be fully understood through its classification as the antidote to the four obstructions.
(VI.6) Diligence is to be thoroughly understood through sixfold distinctions,
beginning with the distinction of preeminence.
By way of the distinction of its causes,
by way of the distinction of its modes, and by way of the distinction of its bases.
And by way of the distinction between the remedies for the four obstructions,
there follows the detailed exposition of this topic through the subsequent verses:
"Vigor is supreme among the collection of white [virtuous] qualities, because the attainment of them depends upon it."
Through vigor, there is immediately a very happy dwelling, as well as supramundane and mundane accomplishment.
"Vigor is supreme among the class of pure qualities" means that it is supreme among the entire class of all pure qualities; thus, the preeminence of vigor is indicated.
"Because, depending on it, there is the subsequent attainment of those [qualities]" indicates the reason for its preeminence, since the attainment of all wholesome dharmas is based upon vigor.
Through diligence, there is an immediately pleasant dwelling, as well as supramundane and mundane accomplishment; thus is its function indicated.
For by means of diligence, the supreme dwelling in happiness is attained in this very life, and all supramundane and mundane accomplishments are brought about.
Through diligence, the desired enjoyments of existence are obtained; through diligence, one attains powerful purity;
through diligence, having transcended the view of a self-identity, one is liberated; and through diligence, one awakens to supreme enlightenment.
Thus, by way of synonyms, the function of vigor has been indicated through the distinction between mundane and supramundane accomplishments (*siddhi*). Among these,
mundane accomplishment is considered "powerful" [in a relative sense] because it is not ultimate.
Furthermore, it is considered that vigor consists of decline and increase, that which is sovereign over liberation, and its opposite;
that which has entered into reality, that which is transformative, and another vigor is explained as being of great purpose.
The Buddhas proclaim all forms of vigor: first, the vigor of armor; then, the vigor of application properly exerted; and the vigor of non-despondency, imperturbability, and insatiability.
Such is the classification of its types.
Among them, the vigor of decrease and increase pertains to the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), specifically for the increase of wholesome dharmas in two of them.
The vigor that has liberation as its sovereign pertains to the faculties (*indriya*).

The faculties (*indriya*) exist in the sense that they exercise sovereignty over liberation; the powers (*bala*) exist in the sense that their opposites cannot crush them, as they overcome the opposing factors;
and they are established among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) for one who has entered into reality, because they are so designated on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
It is transformative because, among the factors of the path, it serves as the cause for the final transformation of the basis on the path of cultivation.
It is great-purpose vigor because its nature is that of a perfection (*pāramitā*), being dedicated to the welfare of both oneself and others.
It is armor-like vigor because one dons the armor for the sake of application.
The vigor of application is so called because of its application; the undaunted vigor because there is no despondency even regarding what is to be attained that is sublime;
and the unshakable vigor because it is not disturbed by sufferings such as cold, heat, and the like.
The vigor of non-contentment arises from not being satisfied with a meager attainment;
these very [forms of] vigor, such as the armor-like vigor and so forth, are mentioned in the Sūtra.

"One who possesses strength, possesses vigor, is energetic, possesses firm prowess, and does not cast off the burden regarding wholesome qualities" is said, respectively, to refer to inferior, middling, and superior vigor. Based on the persons engaged in the three vehicles, that vigor— due to the application of a dejected or extremely noble intention and intellect— is considered to have small benefit or great benefit.
Here, the distinction of vigor is taught by way of the distinction of its basis.
It should be understood that, based on those individuals engaged in the three vehicles, there is respectively inferior, middling, and superior vigor.
What is the reason?
This is due to the application of a sluggish or an exceedingly noble intention and intellect.

For the intention of the intellect is sluggish for those engaged in the two vehicles, because their concern is solely for their own benefit; it is exceedingly noble for those engaged in the Mahāyāna, because their concern is for the benefit of others.
For this very reason, energy is respectively of small benefit and great benefit, and superior in terms of one's own welfare.
One who possesses energy is not defeated by enjoyments; one who possesses energy is not defeated by the afflictions;
one who possesses energy is not defeated by weariness; and one who possesses energy is not defeated by failure to attain.
Thus, this is the classification of the antidotes to the four obstructions.
There are four kinds of obstructions to generosity and the other perfections by which one does not engage in them:
attachment to enjoyments, due to grasping after them; [the remaining three are likewise to be understood].
Attachment to afflictions arises from the persistent clinging to their enjoyment; weariness arises from becoming exhausted by the application and exertion in practices such as giving;
and attainment [of a limited result] arises from being satisfied with only a small measure of giving and so forth.
This fourfold vigor has been described according to the distinction of its respective antidotes.
There is a verse concerning the analysis of their mutual determination:
"Through mutual inclusion, through differentiation, through the dharma, and through the signs."
The definitive determination of the six perfections should be understood in every respect.
The determination [of their inclusion] is by way of mutual inclusion:
because through the gift of fearlessness there is the inclusion of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and patience (*kṣānti*), since by means of those two one grants fearlessness;
and because through the gift of the Dharma there is the inclusion of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), since by means of those two one gives the Dharma.
Because vigor belongs to both, it bestows fearlessness.
Through the ethical discipline (*śīla*) that gathers wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka*), there is a gathering of all [perfections] such as generosity (*dāna*) and the rest.
In this way, the mutual inclusion of patience (*kṣānti*) and the others should be applied accordingly.
The determination according to classification:

giving is sixfold, namely, the giving of giving, the giving of ethical discipline, and so on, up to the giving of wisdom; this is because one establishes ethical discipline and the other perfections within the mental continuums of others.
Determination by way of the Dharma:
those sūtras and so forth in which the meanings of generosity and so forth are observed,
and those sūtras and so forth among the teachings in which the practices of generosity and so forth are observed.
Their mutual inclusion should be understood as follows:
determination is by way of signs.
Generosity serves as the sign for ethical discipline and the other perfections.
Because one who is indifferent to enjoyments applies oneself to ethical discipline (*śīla*) and the other perfections;

for even ethical discipline—such as the undertaking of the monastic vows (*bhikṣusaṃvara*)—arises from the renunciation of all possessions, and for one established in ethical discipline, there is the application of patience (*kṣānti*) and the rest.
Furthermore, the undertaking of the ethical discipline that gathers virtuous qualities (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) is the cause of all the [perfections], beginning with generosity.
In this way, the mutual causality of patience and the other perfections should be applied accordingly.
Regarding the analysis of the articles of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), there are seven verses. There are four articles of attraction.

Generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful action, and consistency between words and deeds: therein, generosity, pleasant discourse, purposeful action, and shared purpose are intended [to be practiced] through teaching them, causing others to adopt them, and following them oneself.
Generosity is held to be the same as in the perfections (*pāramitā*); pleasant speech is the teaching of them; purposeful action is the instigation of others toward them.
Since the word "them" refers to the perfections, the meaning is the teaching of the perfections and the instigation of others toward the perfections.

Consistency of purpose (*samānārthatā*) is when one follows for oneself that very course in which one encourages another. Furthermore, for what purpose are these four bases of sympathy (*saṃgrahavastu*) maintained? For this [is] for the sake of others.

The means [of conversion] should be known as fourfold, according to the four bases of sympathy: that which bestows favor, that which takes hold, that which sets [others] in motion, and likewise that which follows along.
Generosity is the means of assistance,
because it produces physical benefit through the giving of material things;
pleasant speech is the means of grasping.
Because it causes one to grasp meanings that were previously uncomprehended or doubted,
beneficial conduct is the instigator; for it sets one in motion toward what is wholesome.
Consistency of purpose (*samānārthatā*) is that which conforms [to others].
For, having recognized the one who encourages (*samādāpaka*) as someone who acts exactly as he speaks, others follow him in whatever wholesome state they have been led to enter.
By the first [of these four means], there is the state of being a fit vessel; by the second, there is resolute conviction (*adhimucyanā*).
Practice is [taught] by the third [verse], and purification by the fourth.
Through the gift of material goods, one becomes a vessel for the Dharma by attaining a state of compliance.
Through pleasant speech, one gains conviction in that Dharma by means of explaining its meaning and cutting through doubts. Through purposeful conduct, one practices in accordance with the Dharma.
Through consistency of purpose (*samānārthatā*), one purifies that practice by means of long-term application;
this is the function of the bases of sympathy (*saṃgrahavastu*). The state of having four bases of sympathy is considered to be due to two types of gathering.
It is also [attained] through material gifts and through the Dharma, and through the Dharma by means of its objective support.

Furthermore, although the Blessed One has spoken of two other bases of sympathy— the gathering by means of material things and the gathering by means of the Dharma— these very four bases of sympathy are subsumed within those two.
In the first case, it is by means of gathering through material things;
in the remaining cases, it is by means of gathering through the Dharma.
Furthermore, those [gathering through the Dharma] are by means of the Dharma in its threefold form.
Through the dharma of the object, the dharma of practice, and the dharma of its purification, respectively,
the summary [of the path] should be known as inferior, middling, and superior; generally barren and non-barren, and indeed non-barren in every respect, according to the distinction of their aspects.

This is the classification of the types of gathering (saṃgraha). Among these, the inferior, middling, and superior gathering of Bodhisattvas toward those engaged in the three vehicles should be understood as corresponding respectively to the stage of practice through aspiration (adhimukticaryābhūmi), which is for the most part fruitless.
For those who have entered the [bodhisattva] stages, it is generally not fruitless;
on the eighth stage and above, it is entirely unfailing because the welfare of sentient beings is necessarily accomplished.
This method has been adopted by those engaged in attracting a following.
And for the accomplishment of all goals, it is praised as the means of happiness for everyone.
Whosoever are engaged in attracting a following, they all rely upon this very means, namely the four bases of sympathy (*saṃgrahavastu*).
For it is praised by the Buddhas as the most excellent and easy method for the accomplishment of all goals;
those who have been attracted, those who will be attracted, and those who are being attracted at present, are all gathered by means of these.
All of them are thus; and therefore, that path is for the ripening of sentient beings.
By this, he shows that in all three worlds, the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) constitute the single path for the ripening of all sentient beings,
because there is no other path. Thus,
with a mind constantly unattached to enjoyments, having reached the further shore of tranquility, self-restraint, and exertion, his self is firmly established.
Being free from conceptual construction regarding existence, its objects, and their signs, he becomes a gatherer of the multitude of sentient beings.

By this, he demonstrates the application of the means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) for a bodhisattva established in the six perfections as previously described; for by means of the perfections and the means of attraction, respectively, one accomplishes the welfare of oneself and others.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter on the Perfections in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
The seventeenth chapter: Seven verses on the classification of the worship of the Buddha.
Worship of the Buddhas, whether in their presence or in their absence, with robes and other offerings,
by one whose mind is deeply serene, serves to fulfill the two accumulations.
For one who possesses the vow that the birth of a Buddha may not be in vain,
the non-apprehension of the three is the perfected worship of the Buddha.
Another is for the sake of maturing immeasurable sentient beings;
another is by way of material things, by way of the mind, by way of resolute belief, and by way of the storehouse.
Another [type of compassion] arises from sympathetic concern and patience through its manifestation;
and [another] from the engagement with objects, awakening, liberation, and suchness.
Thus, by these four verses, worship is demonstrated through its basis, its object, its cause, its dedication, its motive, its knowledge, its field, and its support. (AMsa 17.5)
It should be understood as follows: therein, the basis consists of the Buddhas, whether manifest or unmanifest;
the object consists of robes and so forth;
and the sign consists of the mind accompanied by intense faith.
The prior vow is that the transformation [of merit] may become an arising [of Buddhahood];
knowledge is non-conceptual because of the non-apprehension of the worshiper, the object of worship, and the act of worship;
the field consists of immeasurable sentient beings.
It is for the sake of ripening that [the bodhisattva] applies himself to it, plants it in them, and provides its support;
furthermore, there is the support of material things (*upadhi*).

In this context, worship is performed by relying on material things such as robes and so forth, while it is performed by relying on the mind through the mental attentions of savoring, rejoicing, and delighting.

And by those aforementioned qualities, such as resolute belief (*adhimukti*) and so forth— namely, having resolute belief in the Mahāyāna Dharma, having generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*),
and having compassion for sentient beings— the term "repository" (*nidhāna*) is used here for "vow" (*praṇidhāna*) in accordance with the requirements of the verse meter.
It consists of enduring hardships through the practice of austerities,
the thorough engagement in the perfections,
and the correct mental attention toward the Dharma.
For that is the engagement with the object (*vastv-ābhoga*) because it is non-erroneous in its reality;
it is vision on the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) by virtue of right view.
For that is the awakening to the object (*vastv-avabodha*) due to the awakening to things as they truly are (*yathābhūtāvabodha*).

In terms of liberation, it is because of the liberation from afflictions for the śrāvakas; likewise, it is because of the attainment of great awakening [for the bodhisattvas]. This is the distinction of the modes of worship.
Furthermore, it is distinguished by way of the cause, by way of the fruit, and by means of both oneself and others.
And it is twofold: by way of gain and honor, and by way of practice.
Worship is considered to be small or great, and it is likewise accompanied by pride or free from pride; it is also regarded as such according to its application, its course, and its vow.
Thus, this is another classification of types based on the distinction of object and so forth.

In that regard, the past is the cause and the present is the fruit; the present is the cause and the future is the fruit. In this way, they should be understood as past, future, and present in terms of cause and fruit. That which belongs to oneself is internal, while that which belongs to others is external.
In terms of gain and honor it is coarse;
in terms of practice it is subtle.
It is limited when inferior and great when sublime.
Furthermore, that which is accompanied by pride is inferior, while that which is free from pride is sublime because of the non-conceptualization of the three spheres.
That which is to be practiced at another time is distant;
that which is to be practiced at that very time is near.
Furthermore, that which belongs to a future rebirth is distant;
that which belongs to an immediate [rebirth] is near.
Moreover, whatever worship one vows to perform in the future is distant; that which one has already resolved to perform is near.
Furthermore, it should be understood that what constitutes the supreme worship of the Buddhas? It is said:

Worship of the Buddhas is supreme by virtue of one’s own mind, through devotion to the Dharma, through intention, and through mastery; and through being embraced by non-conceptual means, and through entering into the state of having a single common purpose with all [Buddhas]. (AMsa 17.8)
Thus, by these five aspects, worship of the Buddhas with one's own mind should be known as supreme;
namely, through faith in the Mahāyāna Dharma associated with worship,
and through intention, by means of the nine intentions.
These consist of the intentions of relishing, rejoicing, and delighting;
the intentions of insatiability, vastness, joy, assistance, non-attachment, and goodness, which have been taught in relation to the cultivation of the perfections;
and, by way of mastery, through meditative absorptions such as the Gaganagañja and others.
[This is] by virtue of embracing the means of non-conceptual knowledge,
and by virtue of entering into the single task shared with all great bodhisattvas, because their activities are mutually blended and integrated.
There are seven verses in the section on the service of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Therein, by means of four and a half verses,
service is demonstrated through its basis, its object, its cause, its dedication, its motive, its knowledge, its field, and its support. (AMsa 17.9)

One should rely upon a friend who is self-controlled, tranquil, and thoroughly pacified; who is superior in virtue, diligent, and rich in scriptural knowledge; who has awakened to reality, is endowed with eloquence, compassionate by nature, and free from weariness.
Thus, such a person possessing these qualities is the basis for service:
"tamed" through the practice of ethical discipline by means of the restraint of the senses;
"calmed" through the practice of meditative concentration by means of internal tranquility of mind.
It is "tranquil" because it pacifies manifest afflictions through its application;
it is "superior in qualities," being neither equal nor inferior;
and it is "exertive," not indifferent toward the welfare of others.
"Rich in scripture" means not having heard little;
"awakened to reality" means through the realization of reality.
It is endowed with speech, meaning it is possessed of the faculty of eloquence;
it is compassionate in nature because its mind is free from worldly desire;
and it is devoid of weariness because it teaches the Dharma continuously and with due respect.
"One should serve a spiritual friend with honor, gain, and personal attendance, and through correct practice.
Regarding such service, however,
the wise one should approach a spiritual friend at the proper time with humility, possessing the very same intention toward the Dharma as the teacher does.
Thus, there are three kinds of signs:
the desire to understand and knowledge of the proper time.
And freedom from pride;
having no longing for honors or gains, he should dedicate them toward spiritual practice.
Thus, dedication is for the sake of practice through service, not for the sake of gain or honor.
And by practicing according to the instructions received, the wise one should thereby please his mind.
Thus, practicing according to the instructions is the cause for service,
because by means of it one pleases his mind.
Having attained skill in the three vehicles through wisdom, one should strive for the accomplishment of one's own vehicle.
Thus, through skill in the three vehicles, there is knowledge for the sake of maturing immeasurable sentient beings and for the accomplishment of a pure field. (AMsa 17.13)
Thus, there are two kinds of fields for that service:
immeasurable sentient beings and the completely pure Buddha-field,
because [the Dharma] is established among them after they have heard it.
And by one who abides therein,
endowed with the quality of being an heir to the Dharma and not entering [into friendship] for the sake of material things— that is a friend.
This is the basis for service.
Relying on being an heir to the Dharma, one should attend upon a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra),
and not as an heir to material things.
Hereafter, the distinction of the modes of service should be understood through one and a half verses.
For the sake of the cause, for the sake of the fruit, and by following the gateway of the Dharma, the wise one should cultivate a friend both externally and internally.

The wise one should serve a spiritual friend through the hearing of the teachings and through mental application; by means of a mind free from pride and equal toward all, and through the investigation of causes and fruits according to their distinctions as past and so forth—as previously explained—by following the gates of the Dharma; and externally as well, which constitutes the distinction between the internal and the external.

For the stream of the entrance to the Dharma is the following after the entrance to the Dharma; it is distinguished as gross and subtle in terms of what is heard externally from others and the application of yoga within the mind.
Hearing is indeed gross, while reflection and cultivation are subtle;
that very [cultivation] is the application of yoga within the mind.
"Because of application to a mind that is both equal and free from pride"—this refers to the distinction between the inferior and the sublime.
Furthermore, through [considering] the destination, the practice, and the vow, the wise one should rely upon a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
Thus, the distinction between "distant" and "near" should be applied as before.
Furthermore, what is the supreme service? This is the seventh verse:
"Supreme is the service of a true friend, by virtue of one's own mind, through the inclination toward the Dharma, through intention, and through masteries."
And by means of embracing the method of non-conceptualization, and by entering into the state where all [practices] have a single purpose.
Thus, as before.
There are twelve verses on the classification of the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*):
"The Brahma-like [states] are free from opposing factors and have reached non-conceptual knowledge."
Functioning with a threefold object, they bring sentient beings to maturity, O steadfast one.
The sublime abodes are the four immeasurables:
loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Furthermore, these should be understood as having four characteristics in the case of a bodhisattva.
By the abandonment of opposing factors, by the possession of the excellence of the counteragent,
and by the excellence of its activity, because it functions with respect to three kinds of objects.
For they have sentient beings as their object and phenomena as their object;
and because of the distinction of their activity,
namely, because they bring sentient beings to maturity.
Because they have sentient beings and phenomena as their objects:
furthermore, in which category of sentient beings or in which phenomenon do they operate? And when they are without an object, upon what object do they depend?

For the wise, these [applications of mindfulness] operate toward one who seeks happiness, one afflicted by suffering, one who is happy, and one who is afflicted; as well as toward the Dharma taught for those [states], and toward the suchness of that [Dharma].
Those having sentient beings as their object operate toward the entire range of sentient beings, from those seeking happiness up to those who are afflicted.
For instance, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) has the aspect of wishing for the union with happiness of sentient beings,
while compassion (*karuṇā*) has the aspect of wishing for their separation from suffering.

Sympathetic joy has the aspect of not being separated from happiness; equanimity has the aspect of bringing about the state of freedom from afflictions for those sentient beings amidst their various feelings;
those having the Dharma as their object take as their object the Dharma taught by him.
In those [states] where your dwellings were taught, they are without objective support (*anālambana*) because they are that very suchness (*tattathatā*);
for since they are non-conceptual (*avikalpa*), they are "without objective support" in the sense that they are as if without an object. Furthermore:
And because it has suchness as its object, because of the attainment of patience and purification,
because of two types of action, and also because of the destruction of the afflictions, loving-kindness is without objective support.
(MSA 122) It should be understood that loving-kindness without an object is characterized by these four reasons:
because it has suchness as its object.
On the eighth stage, through the attainment of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena,
it is purified by the nourishment of the element and by two types of action.
That loving-kindness which is comprised by the outflow of bodily action and by the destruction of the afflictions;
for it has been stated that the afflictions themselves are the object.

Because of the statement that "the objective support is cut off through the abandonment of the mental knots," they are both immovable and movable; they are relished by the wretched and are not to be known [by them]. Furthermore, those sublime abodes (brāhmya-vihāra) should be understood as being fourfold.
In this context, the "wavering" [attainments] belong to the category of decline because they are subject to retrogression;
the "unwavering" belong to the categories of maintenance or distinction because they are not subject to retrogression;
those that are "tasted" are afflicted, while those that are "untasted" are unafflicted.
"By the wretched" means by those who are greedy for pleasure and lack a magnanimous mind.

This is the classification of the divine abodes (brāhmyavihāra) according to their types, such as those conducive to decline and so forth. Furthermore, among these, "the Bodhisattvas are established in the immovable states which are free from attachment."
Those that are unstable, nor even those that are relished;
those whose nature is unconcentrated, those that are weak or middling, and those belonging to inferior stages;
those with inferior intentions, and those that are similar—these are indeed inferior, whereas otherwise they are superior.
This is the distinction between the weak and the intense.
Among these, the six types of weak [faculties] are by nature unconcentrated;
all [the others], even when concentrated, are likewise [weak].
Those who are weak or middling;
those who belong to a lower stage when compared to the higher bodhisattva stages;
and those whose aspirations are inferior.

Although they are common to the śrāvakas and others, those who lack the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) are inferior; this means they are "weak. Conversely, however, they should be understood as "superior" in the sense of being "intense," which is the opposite of what was just described.
When the wise one, having dwelt in the Brahma-abodes, is born among those subject to desire,
he thereby fulfills the accumulations and matures sentient beings.

And everywhere he is never separated from the sublime states (brāhmī vihāra), yet he is free from their opposites; even when confronted by intense conditions for them, he does not undergo transformation, even if he were to become heedless.
The distinction consists of cause, fruit, and characteristic.
Among these, "having dwelt in the sublime abodes" refers to the cause;
[it is directed] toward sentient beings who possess desire.
"It is born" refers to the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*);
"it fulfills the accumulations" refers to the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*); "it ripens sentient beings" refers to the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*).

To be born everywhere never separated from the sublime abodes (*brāhmya-vihāra*) is the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*); to be free from their opposites is the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-phala*). Not undergoing transformation even under intense conditions for them is the sign (*liṅga*).
"Even when negligent" means even when the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) is not present.

By another four verses, the distinction between virtues and faults is shown: "For a bodhisattva who is possessed of malice, harmfulness, discontent, malice, and sensual desire encounters many kinds of misfortune. (MSA 17.24)
Such is the fault: because when the sublime abodes (brāhmyavihāra) are absent, one is joined with their opposites.
In this regard, ill-will (*vyāpāda*) and the others are, respectively, the opposites of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the others;
ill-will and sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) are the opposites of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
How does one encounter manifold disadvantages? To this he says:

"By means of the afflictions, one destroys oneself, harms sentient beings, and ruins one's ethical discipline; one is accompanied by remorse, deprived of gain, and likewise deprived of protection by the Teacher. (MSA 17.25)
One who possesses a basis for transgression and does not acknowledge it is reborn in the states of non-leisure;
having lost both what was attained and what was not yet attained, he experiences great suffering in his mind.
Therein, by the first three phrases—"he intends for his own harm, for the harm of others, and for the harm of both"—he demonstrates this disadvantage (*ādīnava*).
By the six phrases beginning with "with remorse" (*savilekha*), he demonstrates that one generates fault (*avadya*) pertaining to the present life (*dṛṣṭadhārmika*).
And how does one generate it?
One's own self reproaches one;
others, the deities,
and even the Teacher as well as other wise fellow-practitioners, censure one in accordance with the Dharma.
"An evil report and ill-fame concerning him issue forth in all directions and intermediate points"—by this, he shows [the consequences] in their proper order, from being full of remorse up to infamy.

By the remaining three phrases, he shows the disadvantage (*ādīnava*) in their proper order: that one produces fault (*avadya*) pertaining to the future life, to the present life, and to both; and that one experiences the mental suffering and dejection born thereof.
All these faults do not occur for one who is well-established in loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables].
Unafflicted, they do not abandon cyclic existence for the sake of sentient beings.

Thus, he demonstrates three kinds of qualities in the application of the divine abodes (*brāhmavihāra*): the absence of the aforementioned faults; the non-abandonment of cyclic existence for the sake of sentient beings who are undefiled;
and the fact that such [qualities] do not exist even toward one's own virtuous only son as they exist toward all sentient beings.
This volition of loving-kindness and so forth toward sentient beings belongs to the sons of the Conquerors.
Thus, these [verses] demonstrate the intensity of a bodhisattva’s loving-kindness and so forth.
Regarding the classification of compassion, there are two verses concerning the distinctions of its objects.
Those who are ablaze, fallen under the power of enemies, overcome by suffering, shrouded in darkness,
set upon difficult paths, and bound by great fetters;
He feels compassion for sentient beings who are greedy and overcome by the poison of great food, who have lost their way, who have set out on a wrong path, and who are weak.
In that regard, those "blazing" are those who are inflamed by sensual passion and devoted to sensual pleasures.
Those "under the power of enemies" are those hindered by Māra and not engaged in the wholesome; they are "overcome by suffering" and have become suffering itself in the hells and other realms.
Those "enveloped in darkness" are butchers and others who are exclusively devoted to misconduct.
Because they are deluded regarding the ripening of karma,
those whose nature is not to attain parinirvāṇa have ascended a difficult path, as the track of saṃsāra is never severed for them;
and other heterodox teachers are bound by great fetters.
Those who have set out for liberation are bound by the tight fetters of various wrong views;
they are greedy, being overcome by the poison of great food, and are attached to the bliss of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
For them, that bliss of meditative attainment is indeed afflicted (*kliṣṭa*).
Just as delicious food is overcome by poison, so too are those who have strayed from the path— the conceited ones— because they have wandered from the path to liberation.

Those who have set out on a wrong path, those engaged in the inferior vehicle, those who are not fixed [in their destiny], those who are weak, and those whose accumulations are incomplete— these ten kinds of beings are the objects of a bodhisattva’s compassion.

A verse on compassion regarding the demonstration of the five fruits: For one who relies upon the Dharma—which removes affliction, is the seed of supreme enlightenment, brings happiness, is the means of protection, is the cause of what is desired, and bestows its own nature—enlightenment is not far off for that Son of the Victor. (AMsa 17.31)
Thereafter, by virtue of its being the destroyer of affliction, it shows the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-phala*) through the abandonment of violence, which is its opposite;
by virtue of being the seed of supreme enlightenment, it shows the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*);
and by virtue of bringing happiness to both self and others respectively, it shows the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
The fruit of maturation [is attained] by virtue of being the cause of what is desired;
the outflowing fruit [is attained] by virtue of giving its own nature, because it bestows the fruit of distinguished compassion in the future.
Thus, by relying on these five kinds of compassion, it should be understood that Buddhahood is not far off.
Regarding the state of neither abiding in saṃsāra nor in nirvāṇa, there is this verse:

Having understood that everything within saṃsāra consists of suffering and is indeed devoid of self, the compassionate one of supreme intelligence feels neither agitation nor is he oppressed by defects. (AMsa 17.32)
Having thoroughly understood the entirety of saṃsāra as it truly is, the bodhisattva does not experience distress because of his compassion;
nor is he afflicted by defects because of his supreme intelligence.
Thus, he is established neither in nirvāṇa nor in saṃsāra, respectively.
There is a verse regarding the thorough understanding of cyclic existence:

Observing the world as being of the nature of suffering, the compassionate one feels its suffering and knows it as it truly is; likewise, he knows the means for its abandonment and does not succumb to weariness even in the future. (MSA 17.33)
"He feels pity" means he feels compassion.
And "he knows that as it truly is" means he knows suffering as it really is, and he knows the means for the complete abandonment of that suffering,
by which his suffering is ceased.

By this, it is shown that even though he knows the suffering of saṃsāra as it truly is, as well as the means for its abandonment, the bodhisattva does not fall into despondency due to a particular excellence of compassion (*karuṇā*).
There are two verses concerning the classification of compassion:
"Compassion arises by nature and through analytical reflection (*pratisaṃkhyā*), and from the application of the practice of its prior cultivation."
And it is free from opposing factors due to the attainment of purity; this fourfold [compassion] belongs to those whose nature is compassion.
This [distinction] is, respectively, due to the excellence of the lineage (*gotra*),
due to the examination of virtues and faults,
and due to cultivation in previous births.
It should be understood that it is also [to be known] by way of the attainment of dispassion (*vairāgya*);
that is, by way of the attainment of purity when its opposite, harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*), has been abandoned—this is "by way of the attainment of dispassion.
That is not compassion which is not impartial, or not constant, or which does not arise from resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) or from practice (*pratipatti*).
A Bodhisattva is not one who lacks compassion simply because of dispassion or non-perception; such is the case for him who [acts otherwise].
In that regard, it is "equal" because, toward those who are happy and so forth, one understands that whatever is felt here is [ultimately] suffering;
it is "constant" because it is not exhausted even in the nirvana without remainder;
and it is "from resolute intention" because those who have entered the stages attain the intention of the equality of self and others.
By way of practice, through the act of protecting others from suffering;
by way of detachment, through the abandonment of violence which is its opposite;
and by way of non-apprehension, through the attainment of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena.
There are five verses on the reflection of the tree of compassion:

Compassion, patience, reflection, aspiration, birth, and the ripening of sentient beings—this great tree of compassion has its roots and so forth, and possesses flowers, leaves, and fruit. (AMsa 17.36)
Thus, this tree of compassion should be understood as consisting of the stages of root, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit; of this tree,
compassion is the root and patience is the trunk.
Contemplation of the welfare of sentient beings is the branch;
aspiration for auspicious births is the leaves;
and an auspicious birth is the flower.
The ripening of sentient beings is the fruit. If compassion, which is the root, did not exist, there would be no endurance of difficult practices;
and a wise person who cannot endure suffering would never contemplate the welfare of sentient beings.
One whose intellect is devoid of reflection would not make a vow for virtuous births;
and following after such virtuous births, one would certainly not bring sentient beings to maturity. (MSA 17.38)

By these two verses, he establishes that compassion and the other [virtues] function as the root and so forth, due to their similarity to the production of a tree from its preceding and succeeding stages:

"Compassion is watered by loving-kindness; through the happiness felt in the suffering of others, there is abundant nourishment. The extensive growth of the branches is to be understood as arising from thorough mental attention. (AMsa 17.39)
Through the relinquishing and taking up of leaves, through the non-interruption of the continuum of vows,
and through the accomplishment of the two kinds of conditions, the flower and the fruit from this are not barren.

By these two verses, he demonstrates the similarity between the tree of compassion and the watering of its roots and so forth. For compassion is the root-tree; its watering is loving-kindness (*maitrī*), because by means of that, it is nourished.
For one whose mind is imbued with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one suffers through the suffering of others;

consequently, for the bodhisattva engaged in his own welfare, the suffering born from the arising of compassion gives rise to happiness therein, which means there is an extensive nourishment—that is, a nourishment of patience (*kṣānti*).
That [patience] is indeed called a "heap" (*skandha*).
The trunk is vast;
through appropriate mental attention (*yonisomanaskāra*), there is manifold growth of branches within the Mahāyāna.
For it is said that "reflection" (*cintā*) is the branch.
Because the continuum of the vow is not interrupted through the sequence of the cessation of the former and the arising of the latter,
the similarity of the vows to the shedding and taking up of leaves should be understood.
Because the internal conditions are established and one's own continuum reaches maturity, birth should be understood as fruitful, like a flower.

The ripening of sentient beings, which is the fruit resulting from the maturation of the mental continuum of others through the accomplishment of external conditions, should be understood [in this way].
There is a verse regarding the benefits of compassion:
Who would not practice compassion toward sentient beings, who possess the quality of great mercy?
Even in suffering, there is incomparable happiness for them, which arises from compassion.
Here, the quality of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is demonstrated by the second half [of the verse].
The remainder has already been explained.
There are verses concerning the non-attachment of compassion.
The minds of the compassionate do not abide in peace even when they are possessed by suffering out of pity;
how much less could there be attachment to worldly happiness or to their own lives?
For all people in the world have affection for worldly happiness and their own lives;
yet even among them, the minds of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—who are devoid of such affection—rest in Nirvāṇa, which is the cessation of all suffering.
[This is not so] for the Bodhisattvas.

However, because he is permeated by compassion, his mind does not rest even in nirvāṇa; how much less could there be attachment to those two? There are three verses concerning the distinction between compassion and affection.
That affection which is blameless does not exist, nor does that which is worldly;
for the wise, the affection of compassion is blameless and transcends the world.
For the affection consisting of craving toward one's mother, father, and so forth, is faulty;
that which consists of worldly compassion, though faultless, is still worldly.
But for Bodhisattvas, the affection consisting of compassion is both faultless and transcendent of the world.
Furthermore, how is it blameless? It says:
How could that means which serves to uplift the world—resting as it does upon the great flood of suffering and ignorance and within the great darkness—not be blameless? (AMsa 17.44)
The phrases "in the great flood of suffering" and "in the great darkness of ignorance" should be applied [to the preceding].
The remainder has its meaning already explained.
To the question "How is he transcendent of the world? he says:
That affection does not exist in the world among Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas, let alone among others; how then could it not be supramundane?
They have awakened to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
the rest has its meaning already explained.
There is a verse regarding the signs of both fear and delight:
In the absence of suffering, that suffering which arises for Bodhisattvas through compassion terrifies them at first; yet once touched by it, they rejoice in it intensely.
Regarding the phrase "in the absence of suffering," the absence of suffering is the cause.
The suffering that arises in Bodhisattvas through compassion for sentient beings initially causes them trepidation on the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*),
