because they have not yet touched suffering as it truly is by means of the equality of self and others.
The meaning is that once it has been touched upon, on the stage of pure resolute intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*), one indeed rejoices in it.
Regarding the overcoming of happiness by the suffering of compassion, there is this verse:
"What could be more wondrous than this: that suffering overcomes all happiness?"
That which is produced by compassion is mundane, yet even one who is liberated through it has fulfilled his purpose.

There is nothing more wonderful than this: that very suffering born of compassion becomes such a happiness for Bodhisattvas that it surpasses all worldly happiness; by means of this happiness, even Arhats who have accomplished their purpose are surpassed, let alone others.
Regarding the benefits of giving performed out of compassion, there is this verse:
The gift accompanied by compassion produces for the wise that bliss of giving which no enjoyment within the three realms can touch, even in its smallest fraction. (MSA 17.48)

And whatever happiness belonging to the three realms is produced by enjoyments, that happiness does not touch even a fraction of that [bodhisattva’s] happiness; this is the meaning of the second half of the verse. The remainder is self-evident.
There is a verse regarding the acceptance of suffering out of compassion:
Since he does not abandon the cycle of existence, which consists of suffering, out of compassion for the sake of sentient beings—
for what suffering that is for the sake of others' benefit has not been encountered by those possessed of compassion?
For all suffering is included within the suffering of cyclic existence;
by accepting that [suffering], all suffering becomes accepted.
Regarding the increase of its fruit therein, there is this verse:
For one who possesses compassion, compassion, generosity, and enjoyments always continue to increase;
and from this, there arises happiness produced by affection and assistance, as well as that which is brought about by power.
For Bodhisattvas, three things increase throughout all their births: compassion through its application;
compassion through the cultivation thereof;
and generosity through the power of compassion.
And enjoyments arise from the power of giving; and from that triad, a threefold fruit of happiness results:
that born of affection arises from compassion.
That which is produced from the favoring of sentient beings arises from giving;
that which is produced by the power of the act of favoring them arises from enjoyments.
Regarding the encouragement toward giving, there is this verse:
"I grow and I cause [others] to grow; I bring to maturity, I bring happiness;
I attract and I lead"—thus it speaks, as it were, to those who are clothed in compassion regarding generosity.
The phrase "those who have desisted from giving" is to be connected [to the following].
Compassion, as if through its own nature’s increase, encourages Bodhisattvas who have desisted from giving on account of six factors.
By means of enjoyments, through their increase;
by means of giving, through the ripening of sentient beings;
and because it produces happiness for the giver.
Because it draws forth other accumulations for great enlightenment and leads one close to great enlightenment,
there is a verse concerning the absence of happiness through the happiness of others.
One who suffers when others suffer cannot become happy by not bestowing happiness upon them out of compassion;
therefore, the compassionate one makes himself happy by bestowing happiness upon others.
Out of compassion, the bodhisattva is pained by the sufferings of others; how could he be happy without bestowing happiness upon sentient beings?
Therefore, it should be understood that by bestowing happiness upon others, the bodhisattva brings happiness to himself alone.
There are six verses concerning the instruction on giving out of compassion.
The compassionate teacher, always desiring no happiness for himself, as it were instructs his own gift:
"Make others happy with enjoyments, or else let me too share in that inseparable happiness."
For there is no happiness for the compassionate one without the happiness of others;
because his happiness is inseparable from theirs, the Bodhisattva does not desire the happiness that is the fruit of his giving without them.
He gives a gift along with its fruit, thinking: "May that [fruit] belong to sentient beings through my happiness being their happiness."
If you have any duty toward me, let the fruit [of my merit] belong to them alone as much as they desire.
While giving a gift, both the gift and the fruit of that gift are given by me to sentient beings;
since their very happiness is my happiness, therefore, the imperative *phalati* means: "as long as there is fruit to be borne, let it bear fruit for them alone."
The Bodhisattva instructs on giving out of compassion:
"For a donor who has no aversion toward wealth, riches approach him even more abundantly and auspiciously.
For I do not consider that to be true happiness, since I am one who seeks the further shore through giving. (MSA 17.55)
For a donor who is detached from enjoyments, even greater and more excellent enjoyments come to him;
this is simply the nature of things, because of the loftiness of his mind.
For that is not considered happiness by me which consists in the enjoyment of pleasures as they present themselves;
because I am intent on the perfection of giving, desiring its continuous succession, and not for the sake of pleasure itself—
that you constantly behold me out of compassion as I renounce all my possessions.
Surely you should know by that [fact] that he has no desire for the fruit of my [teaching]. // AMsa_17.56 //

"I, who constantly relinquish the entirety of the fruit of my giving out of compassion—surely from this very fact it should be understood that I have no desire for the fruit of my giving. Thus does the Bodhisattva instruct regarding giving:
"If I were not devoted to giving, I would not relinquish its fruit once it had been obtained;
for it is thus:"
One who delights in giving does not fail to give even for a single moment.
Thus the meaning of the verse is understood:
"Since you do not bear fruit for that which has not been done, you are not equal to me in my expectation of a return."
You bear fruit for whoever treats you;
therefore, out of expectation for a return, you are not my equal,
for such am I.
Expecting no recompense, may this [merit] of yours grant you the fruit you desire in the future.
The meaning of this is already understood.
Regarding the gift of compassion, there are two verses:
"Blameless, pure in its basis, beneficial, and indeed protective."
The compassionate giving of the sons of the Conquerors is free from seeking and free from attachment.
In that regard, it is "blameless" because one gives without depriving others of their supreme [needs];
it is a "pure basis" because one gives appropriate goods,
by way of avoiding poison, weapons, intoxicants, and so forth.
It is beneficial because it brings about welfare by gathering others through generosity and enjoining them to virtue;
it is protected because one gives to another after ensuring that one's own retinue suffers no deprivation;
it is unsought because one gives of one's own accord upon perceiving a need or distress even when not asked, and because one does not seek out a recipient solely for the sake of merit.
It is "unstained" because it is free from desire for recompense or karmic maturation.
There is another classification:
it is complete, vast, excellent, constant, joyful, disinterested, and pure.
The giving of the victors' sons, which is inclined toward enlightenment and inclined toward the wholesome, is like plowing.
In that regard, it is "complete" because of the giving of all internal and external things;
"extensive" because of the giving of abundant things;
and "excellent" because of the giving of sublime things.
Because of constant and frequent giving;
because of giving with joy, having reflected with discernment, and being delighted;
and because it is non-material, just as it is stainless.
It is pure like the pure state;
it is inclined toward awakening because of its dedication to great awakening;
and it is inclined toward the wholesome just as that which brings about benefit.
Regarding the excellence of enjoyment, there is this verse:
An enjoyer does not obtain such satisfaction from enjoyment as the compassionate one attains through renunciation, his mind nourished by the three kinds of happiness. (MSA 17.61)
In this regard, there are three kinds of happiness: the joy of giving, the joy of benefiting others, and the joy of accumulating the equipment for enlightenment.
The remainder has been explained.
There is a verse concerning compassion that brings about the accomplishment of the perfections:
Compassion for the wretched, compassion for the fierce, compassion for the agitated, compassion for the heedless,
compassion for those dependent on sense objects, and compassion for those who are wrongly attached.
In that regard, the "miserly" are those who are stingy; the "fierce" are those of immoral conduct who torment others;
and the "agitated" are those who are prone to anger.
The heedless are those who are indolent;
those dependent on sense objects are those whose minds are distracted by sensual pleasures;
and those with false attachments are the heterodox teachers and others who possess poor wisdom.
The compassion directed toward those who abide in states that are the opposites of the perfections is "compassion for the wretched" and so forth.
And because it refutes those opposites, it leads to the accomplishment of the perfections;
therefore, it is called "the compassion that accomplishes the perfections."
There is a verse regarding the demonstration of the conditions for compassion:
The compassion of Bodhisattvas arises from pleasure, from suffering, and from that which follows them;
the compassion of Bodhisattvas arises from a cause, from a friend, and from its own nature. (MSA 17.63)
Therein, the first half [of the verse] demonstrates the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) of compassion:
because one feels compassion by taking the three types of sensation as objects through the three forms of suffering (*duḥkhatā*).
For the sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant is a consequence of pleasure and pain, since it leads to their recurrence.
By the second half [of the verse], he demonstrates, in their respective order, the causal, dominant, and immediate conditions of compassion through its causes, friends, and intrinsic nature.
Regarding the state of great compassion, there is this verse:
"The compassion of Bodhisattvas should be known as equal because of their intention."
Because of practice, because of detachment, because of non-apprehension, and because of purity.

In that regard, it is "equal" because, among those in the three states of feeling, one understands that whatever is felt here is suffering; furthermore, it is equal through intention, by means of the mind’s compassionate concern,
and through practice, by means of protecting them.
It is also [characterized] by detachment, because of the abandonment of violence which is its opposite;
by non-apprehension, because of the non-apprehension of self, others, and compassion;
and by purity, because of the attainment of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena on the eighth stage.
The cultivation of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables] is supreme by virtue of one's own mind, by way of the Dharma, and through resolute conviction;
it is also supreme by way of intention, mastery, non-conceptuality, and unity.
Thus, the meaning should be understood according to the previous explanation.

Having conceived great faith in the Blessed One, honoring him with abundant material offerings and steadfast veneration, constantly serving virtuous and beneficial friends, and feeling compassion for the world, he attains all success. (AMsa 17.66)
By this, he briefly demonstrates the sequence and the quality of the aforementioned worship, service, and immeasurables.

One should be understood as "one who worships with great material gifts, constancy, and extreme honor" because of performing worship that is characterized by great material gifts (*mahopadhi*), constancy (*dhruva*), and extreme honor (*satkriyā*).
Furthermore, "honor" (*satkriyā*) should be understood as correct practice (*samyakpratipatti*).
In this way, one becomes a worshiper through honor and practice.
A friend possessing many qualities should be understood as beneficial by virtue of their compassion, even if they lack other qualities.
"He attains all success" means he achieves the accomplishment of the welfare of both himself and others.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, on Worship, Service, and the Immeasurables, in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
The eighteenth chapter [now begins].

There are sixteen verses on the analysis of moral shame (*lajjā*). In the steadfast one, moral shame is free from its opposites, accompanied by non-conceptual knowledge, directed toward inferior yet blameless objects, and brings sentient beings to maturity. (AMsa 18.1)

By this, he demonstrates the fourfold characteristic of a bodhisattva’s shame through the terms "intrinsic nature," "companion," "object," and "action. Its inferior and blameless object refers to that of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
That which is devoid of it is irreproachable within the Mahāyāna;
because of that, the bodhisattva feels shame.
How does he bring sentient beings to maturity?
In that very context, shame arises from the excessive production of shame due to the increase of the factors opposed to the perfection of shame (*lajjā-pāramitā*) and the decline of its antidotes;
it arises from the laziness of practicing the six perfections,
and likewise for the wise, from the application of factors conducive to the afflictions.

This is the shame of non-application, because it arises from not applying oneself to the cultivation of the perfections (*pāramitā*) and from applying oneself to factors conducive to the afflictions (*kleśa*), such as failing to guard the doors of the sense faculties;
it is of an unconcentrated nature, and is weak or middling, belonging to an inferior stage.
Those with inferior intentions are equal [to those with inferior intentions], for they are indeed inferior; otherwise, they are superior.
This is the degree of shame that is "mild.
The meaning of this verse is to be understood according to the previous explanation.
Hereafter, by means of four and three verses respectively, he demonstrates the distinction between the faults in the opposite of shame and the virtues in shame.
The wise one who lacks a sense of shame endures the afflictions through improper mental application;
harboring resentment, indifference, and pride, he harms sentient beings and his own ethical discipline.
In this context, it is demonstrated that one intends for one's own harm, for the harm of others, and for the harm of both;
"unmethodically" means by way of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*).
How does one harm sentient beings through equanimity? By being negligent regarding all their welfare;
due to remorse, one becomes dejected and suffers a loss of honor.
Therefore, one is disregarded by the assembly of men and by the scriptures because of faithlessness.
He is censured by his fellow followers of the Dharma, the sons of the Conqueror, and incurs ill repute among the world;
by the phrase "in this present life," it is shown that he produces an offense pertaining to the present life (*dṛṣṭadhārmika-avadya*).
Respectively, this is because one is censured by oneself, by others, by deities, and by teachers; because one is reproached according to the nature of reality (dharmatā) by wise fellow-practitioners;
and because an evil reputation spreads in all directions.
Otherwise, one is born again deprived of the favorable moment.

By this, it is demonstrated that one incurs blame pertaining to both the present life and future lives through the loss of wholesome qualities already attained and the failure to attain those not yet attained, respectively. This is because one undergoes the loss of wholesome dharmas already acquired and the loss of those not yet acquired.
He dwells in suffering; therefore, he also attains a state of mental unease.
By this, it is demonstrated that one experiences shame as a mental factor, which is suffering and dejection (*daurmanasya*).
"All these faults exist in those who possess shame, but not in the sons of the Conqueror"— starting from this point, the virtue of shame is to be understood.
Since these faults do not exist,
the wise one is always reborn among gods and humans.
This is its fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
Furthermore, by means of that sense of shame, the wise one quickly fulfills the accumulations for awakening;
this is its dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
And the Son of the Conqueror does not grow weary from maturing sentient beings.
This is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*):
he is born constantly both free from and not free from the adverse factors and their remedies.
Thus, these are the fruits of dissociation and outflow,
namely, being free from the adverse factors and not being separated from the remedies; the son of the Conqueror who possesses a sense of shame attains this benefit.
Thus it has been demonstrated that one attains the absence of the aforementioned faults and the possession of virtues:
"For the fool is stained by faults due to the lack of shame (hrī), even if well-concealed by fine garments;
but the Son of the Victor, though without garments, is clothed in shame and is thus free from the stain of faults. (MSA 18.11)
By this, clothing is a qualification of shame;
for even one covered by other garments is stained by faults if devoid of shame,
whereas even a naked person is stainless if possessed of shame.
Like space, the Son of the Victor endowed with moral shame (hrī) is unstained by worldly phenomena (*dharma*);
"phenomena" here refers to the worldly conditions (*lokadharma*).
Adorned with moral shame, he shines when in the company of the Sons of the Victor.
By this verse, he shows that shame is equal to the ornament of space;
for bodhisattvas, shame possesses a motherly affection toward those to be trained,
because they feel shame at neglecting sentient beings who ought to be protected.
And shame is also the protection for those wandering in saṃsāra against all faults.
Because it serves as the foundation for the elephant corps,

the cavalry, and so forth; by means of these analogies of clothing and the like, [the monastery] represents the antidote to the afflictions while residing there, the antidote to worldly dharmas while wandering abroad,
conformity with dwelling together with fellow practitioners of the Dharma, and conformity with the ripening of sentient beings.
And it demonstrates that shame is conducive to an unafflicted saṃsāra:
non-acceptance toward all [unwholesome things], engagement in acceptance toward all [wholesome things],
and engagement in all [virtuous activities]— these are the signs of one possessed of shame as ordained by shame.
By this, he demonstrates the fourfold mark produced by a sense of shame (*hrī*) in one who possesses shame:
namely, non-acceptance and non-engagement with all faults.
The cultivation of shame (*hrī*) is primary for the endurance and engagement in all virtues; it arises from one’s own mind, from the Dharma, from resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*),
and also from intention (*āśaya*), from mastery (*vibhutva*), from non-conceptuality (*akalpanā*), and from unity (*aikya*).
The explanation of this is as before.
Regarding the analysis of steadfastness (*dhṛti*), there are seven verses:
"The steadfastness of Bodhisattvas is [defined] by its characteristics and its divisions."
And by virtue of its firmness, it excels all others distinct from it.
Vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom are considered to be essence, steadfastness, and fortitude,
because the bodhisattva proceeds fearlessly from these three.
By this, the definition of fortitude (*dhṛti*) along with its synonyms and its acquisition (*samādana*) have been stated;
likewise, the definition of vigor (*vīrya*) and so forth,
and its synonyms such as "courage" (*satva*) and so forth.
The remainder is the proof.
To the question "From which three is one free from fear as one proceeds?", he says:
"Fear arises from despondency, from wavering, and from delusion."
Therefore, among one's own three [virtues], they should be understood as being designated by the term "fortitude" (dhṛti) with respect to duties to be performed.
For in the tasks of the śrāvakas, fear arises either from a depressed mind due to a lack of enthusiasm for them,
or from a wavering mind due to mental instability,
or from delusion due to ignorance of the means for them.

And their respective antidotes are vigor and the other [faculties]. Therefore, the designation "fortitude" (dhṛti) should be understood as applying to one's own threefold vigor and so forth— namely, that which is "inherent" (*nija*), meaning that which is performed without deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyāna-karaṇīya*),
by natural disposition (*prakṛtyā*), and through aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) as well as through indifference (*nirapekṣatva*).
And toward the misconduct of sentient beings, as well as upon hearing of their profundity and magnanimity.
Regarding the difficulty of disciplining those to be trained, the inconceivability of the Victor’s body, various difficult feats, and the non-abandonment of cyclic existence; (18.20)
And in that very state which is free from affliction, steadfastness arises for the wise one;
it is unequalled compared to others, since he is therefore considered the foremost among those possessed of steadfastness.
By these three verses, he demonstrates the divisions of steadfastness (*dhṛti*): respectively, [the steadfastness] of the lineage (*gotra*),
the production of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), and so forth.
From the perspective of one's own welfare, from the perspective of the welfare of sentient beings, and from the perspective of power.
[It is characterized] by the maturation of sentient beings and by supreme enlightenment.
In this regard, "regardlessness" should be understood as the disregard for one's own body and life on the part of one who is devoted to his own welfare.
Furthermore, there is a distinction based on the practice of austerities,
based on intentional rebirth,
and also based on the absence of affliction therein.
The hero does not tremble at hearing of evil friends, suffering, or the profound [truth], just as Mount Sumeru is unshaken by locusts, the wind from their wings, or the oceans.
By this, he demonstrates the firmness of the bodhisattva’s fortitude. The three similes are to be understood as corresponding respectively to the three types of immovability.
There are two verses concerning the analysis of indefatigability.
The indefatigability of Bodhisattvas is peerless regarding three things:
insatiability in hearing, great vigor, and [endurance] toward suffering; it is based upon moral shame and fortitude.
Intense aspiration for great enlightenment and tirelessness are considered the [defining characteristics] of the wise;
they are unaccomplished, accomplished, and well-accomplished across the stages.
By means of these two, indefatigability is explained in terms of its basis, its intrinsic nature, and its classifications,
with respect to three objects.
In being insatiable regarding what has been heard,
in initiating vigor for a long period of time,
and in [enduring] the suffering of saṃsāra.
Relying upon shame (*hrī*) and steadfastness (*dhṛti*), one feels shame at the arising of weariness through those two, and does not produce it; thus,
having intense aspiration for great enlightenment is its essential nature.
For when one turns back, the zeal becomes exhausted;
it is unaccomplished on the stage of practice through aspiration,
but accomplished on the seven stages.
"It is perfectly accomplished by another"—this is the explanation.
Regarding the knowledge of the treatises (*śāstrajñatā*), there are two verses:
"It is distinguished by its subject matter (*vastu*), its scope (*adhikāra*), and its activity (*karman*)."
By way of its characteristics, its inexhaustibility, and the attainment of its fruit.
For the wise, mastery of the treatises consists in the gates of meditative concentration and the dhāraṇīs;
once acquired, they serve for the ripening of sentient beings and for the preservation of the true Dharma.
In that regard, the subject matter (*vastu*) of knowledge of the treatises consists of the five fields of learning:

the inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*), the science of logic (*hetu-vidyā*), the science of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*), the science of medicine (*cikitsā-vidyā*), and the science of arts and crafts (*śilpa-karma-sthāna-vidyā*).
Its purpose (*adhikāra*) is the accomplishment of the welfare of oneself and others.
In the first subject matter, the activity consists of one’s own practice and the explanation of that to others;
in the second, the thorough knowledge of its faults and the refutation of opposing disputants;
and in the third, the expression of well-articulated terminology oneself and the conviction of others.
In the fourth [case], there is the alleviation of others' diseases;
in the fifth, there is the sharing of those [remedies] with others.
These five things are what are heard as the characteristics of being learned in the treatises.
They have been retained; they have been mastered through speech;
they have been examined by the mind.
They are thoroughly penetrated by vision; having heard them in due order, they are grasped accordingly.
Through private recitation;
through reflecting on the meaning with a serene mind by understanding its faults and virtues as appropriate;
and through the discernment of what is well-expounded and what is poorly expounded.

Its inexhaustibility consists in its not being exhausted even in the nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*). The full attainment of the fruit is the omniscience regarding all phenomena in all their aspects (*sarvadharma-sarvākārajñatā*).

Furthermore, this expertise in the treatises (*śāstrajñatā*) of the bodhisattvas is comprised of the gateways of meditative concentrations (*samādhimukha*) and the gateways of mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇīmukha*).
And it serves for the ripening of sentient beings,
because through the gateways of meditative concentration one carries out their welfare;
and it serves for the mastery of the true Dharma, because through the dhāraṇīs one retains it.

There are four verses concerning knowledge of the world: "Knowledge of the world belonging to the wise is indeed incomparable in terms of body, speech, and the knowledge of the truths; it is thus distinguished from all others. (AMsa 18.27)
How [does one act] with the body? It says:
"Always having a smiling face. How [does one act] with speech? It says:
The wise are those who speak first.
To the question "For what purpose is that?", he says:
"In order to make sentient beings into suitable vessels."
In what sense? For the sake of being a vessel for the practice of the true Dharma.
How is it by means of the knowledge of the truths? He says:
"Since the repeated arising of worlds is desired from the two truths, and their cessation from those two, therefore one who knows them is called a knower of the world. (AMsa 18.29)

The world’s repeated arising— that is, saṃsāra— is due to two truths, considering both that which arises and that by which it arises. Its cessation is due to two truths, considering both that which is the cessation and that by which it is brought about.
Therefore, one who knows that is called "one who knows the world," because they are endowed with the wisdom that perceives the arising and passing away of the world.
For the sake of their pacification and attainment, the wise person applies themselves to the truths.
For it is because of his knowledge of reality that the wise one is indeed called "one who knows the world."
By this, the function of knowing the world (*lokajñatā*) is indicated.
In that context, "for tranquility" refers to the truths of suffering and its origin; "for attainment" refers to the truths of cessation and the path.

In the analysis of the reliances, there are three verses: The Dharma of the teaching is that of the Sage; its meaning is intentional; it is authoritative and of definitive meaning; and its attainment is beyond verbal expression. (AMsa 18.31)
This is the characteristic of the reliances (*pratisaraṇa*).
In this context, the authoritative meaning is that which has been established and analyzed by one who has become an authority, whether by the Teacher himself or by one authorized by him.
Non-discursive attainment is supramundane knowledge of realization.
Because that [reality] is inexpressible.
The remainder has its meaning already explained.
[This applies to] the one who rejects it, as previously described, and the one who has falsely determined it.
And here, the attainment of that which is accompanied by longing is taught as being prohibited.
In the first reliance, the rejection of a person who repudiates the Dharma of the Sage is taught;
in the second, [the rejection] of the literal phrasing rather than its intended meaning;
and in the third, [the rejection] of a meaning that has been wrongly conceived and led astray by perversion.
By the fourth [verse], there is the [attainment] of knowledge accompanied by verbal expression,
which is to be personally realized,
through resolute conviction and investigation, and by hearing correctly from others.
Moreover, even from non-conceptual knowledge, there is indeed no destruction for the wise.
Now, the benefits of the reliances:
by the first reliance, through conviction in the Dharma of the Sage, they do not perish;
by the second, through personally investigating the intended meaning and the definitive meaning.
By the third [verse], because of hearing the method of the opposite meaning from others;
by the fourth, because of supramundane knowledge.
Regarding the analysis of the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), there are four verses.
The four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of the bodhisattvas are peerless;
they are considered such because of their knowledge regarding synonyms, characteristics, speech, and cognition. (AMsa 18.34)

The first [type of knowledge] concerns synonyms: it is the knowledge of as many synonyms as there are for each individual object. The second concerns characteristics: it is the knowledge of the name belonging to a particular object. The third concerns sentences: it is the knowledge of the various languages used in each respective region.
The fourth is that which is self-manifested in knowledge;
this is the characteristic of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
It concerns that which is taught, by whom it is taught, and the manner in which one engaged in teaching teaches.
The teaching of both the Dharma and its meaning is carried out through speech and through knowledge alone.

The fourfold analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) arises from the summary and detailed exposition of the Dharma, from the complete attainment of both [the meaning and the letter], and from the thorough knowledge and removal of objections. (AMsa 18.36)
This is the reason for the fourfold nature.
For one engaged in teaching, there is the purpose regarding that which is taught, that by which it is taught, and the knowledge therein; but as for whom is the teaching?
By what means is there the teaching of the Dharma and its meaning? It is by means of speech and knowledge.
In that regard, there is the teaching of the Dharma and its meaning.
Teaching by means of speech occurs through the brief statement and detailed explanation of the Dharma, because it brings those two to their full realization in every respect.
Teaching by means of knowledge occurs through the resolution of objections.
Therefore, based on the knowledge of both that which is taught and that by which it is taught, the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are established.
Having attained internal equanimity, that subsequent realization for the sake of destroying all doubts is defined as *pratisaṃvid* (analytical knowledge).
By this, both the etymological definition (*nirvacana*) and the function of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are shown.

The etymological definition is as follows: having personally realized the equality of all phenomena—that is, suchness—by means of supramundane knowledge, one subsequently possesses an analytical understanding of synonyms and so forth by means of the knowledge obtained subsequent to that; this is "analytical knowledge" (*pratisaṃvid*).
The activity [of this teaching] is for the sake of destroying all doubts of others.
There are four verses concerning the classification of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
The equipment (*saṃbhāra*) of the Bodhisattvas consists of merit and gnosis, and it is peerless.
One [type of person] is for the sake of prosperity within saṃsāra; the other is for the sake of an unafflicted existence in saṃsāra.
It demonstrates both the equipment and its purpose.
The equipment is twofold:
therein, the equipment of merit leads to exaltation within saṃsāra.
The equipment of wisdom is for the sake of wandering through cyclic existence without being afflicted.
Generosity and ethical discipline are the accumulation of merit; wisdom is the accumulation of knowledge.
The other three [perfections] belong to both, while all five are the accumulation of knowledge.
By this, there is a summary of both accumulations through the perfections;
for it is by the power of patience, vigor, and meditation that both are accomplished.
Therefore, there are three accumulations of the two [merit and wisdom].

Furthermore, because they are dedicated toward wisdom, all five perfections should be understood as the accumulation of knowledge (*jñāna-saṃbhāra*). For, by means of continuous cultivation, one repeatedly increases that which is virtuous.
That which is nourishment is the equipment for the wise, which accomplishes all goals.
This is the etymological explanation and the function of "saṃbhāra":
*sam* means by way of continuity;
*bhā* means having attained cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
*Ra* means repeated nourishment;
*sarvārthasādhaka* (the accomplisher of all aims) refers to its function, because it accomplishes the welfare of both oneself and others.
The accumulation for the wise is gathered for the sake of entry, for the signless, for effortlessness, for consecration, and for the ultimate goal.
This is the classification of saṃsāra.
Therein, on the stage of conduct through aspiration (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*), there is the accumulation for the sake of entering the stages;
and on the six stages, there is the accumulation for the sake of the signless (*animitta*) which is comprised within the seventh stage.
Because of the manifestation of signs in that [sixth stage],
there is [the cultivation] for the sake of effortlessness in the seventh stage;
and for the sake of the equipment and the consecration pertaining to those two other stages included in the tenth stage.
In that [state], there is the equipment for reaching the culmination comprised within the Buddha-stage.
Regarding the analysis of the applications of mindfulness, there are three verses:
the cultivation of the applications of mindfulness occurs through fourteen aspects.
Because it is peerless among the wise, it excels all others.
In what fourteen ways? It is distinguished by way of reliance, by way of counteragent, and likewise by way of entry, as well as by way of object, mental attention, and attainment. (AMsa 18.43)
Another [type of perfection] arises from thorough knowledge through conformity and following;
it is further distinguished by its measure and its supremacy, due to the attainment of cultivation.
Thus, by these fourteen aspects, the cultivation of the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) by bodhisattvas is distinguished.

How [is it distinguished] by way of basis? Because it relies upon the wisdom consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation within the Mahāyāna. How [is it distinguished] by way of antidote? Because it serves as the antidote even to the notions of impurity, suffering, impermanence, and non-self—which are themselves the antidotes to the four perversions—by means of entering into the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya) regarding the body and so forth.
How is it by way of entry?

It is because one enters the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path through the four applications of mindfulness in their respective order, and because one causes others to enter them as well.
As it has been said: (Msa 141)
In the *Madhyāntavibhāga*:

How is it [practiced] by way of the object? By taking as objects the bodies and so forth of all sentient beings. How is it by way of mental attention? By the non-apprehension of the body and so forth.

How is it "by way of attainment"? It is so that there is neither dissociation from nor association with the body and the other [bases]. How is it "by way of conformity"? It is through conformity with the perfections (pāramitās), because they serve as the antidotes to those factors which are their opposites. How is it "by way of following along"? It is by following along with worldly beings, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas, practicing the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness associated with them for the purpose of instructing them.
How is it fully understood? By the full understanding of the body as being like an illusion, because it appears as a form that is likewise unreal.
Of sensation:
by the full understanding of it as being like a dream, because it is likewise a false experience.

Through the wisdom that realizes the intrinsic luminosity of the mind, it is like space; through the thorough knowledge of the adventitious nature of phenomena, they are like the adventitious defilements of dust, smoke, clouds, and mist in space. How is there non-defilement from the perspective of origination? It is because one intentionally takes birth in existence—such as becoming a universal monarch (*cakravartin*)—and, despite the excellence of body, sensations, and so forth, remains undefiled by them.

How is it "by way of measure"? Because even a mild cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness is superior to others [such as those of the śrāvakas] due to the natural sharpness of their faculties. How is it "by way of supremacy"? Because for those who have reached perfection, there is a cultivation that is effortless, mixed, and uninterrupted.

How is it [immeasurable] by way of cultivation? Because through that cultivation, it is not exhausted even in the nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*). How is it by way of attainment? Because it is attained in the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and in Buddhahood.
In the analysis of the right abandonments, there are five verses:
The right abandonment of the wise is unequaled by all embodied beings;
it is cultivated as the antidote to the defects of the applications of mindfulness.

The general definition of the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) is that the cultivation of the right abandonments serves as the antidote to those factors which are the opposites of whatever cultivations of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) have been taught.
Furthermore, in terms of their specific divisions:
[they function] regarding the enjoyment of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), the abandonment of the hindrances (*nivaraṇa*), and...
And in the relinquishing of mental attention, as well as in the entry into the stages.
In the dwelling in the signless, in the attainment of the prophecy,
in the ripening of sentient beings, and in the empowerment of the wise.
For the sake of purifying the field and for the very attainment of the ultimate goal,
the cultivation of the remedies for the opposing factors is practiced by Bodhisattvas.
This is the classification of the cultivation of the right efforts:
[namely] regarding the unafflicted enjoyment of the prosperities of cyclic existence,
and regarding the abandonment of the five hindrances.
In the relinquishing of the mental attention of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; in the entry into the [bodhisattva] stages;
and in the dwelling in the signless on the seventh stage.
In the attainment of prophecy on the ninth stage, in the ripening of sentient beings on the ninth stage,
and in the empowerment on the tenth stage.
For the sake of purifying the field, throughout all three [stages],
and upon reaching the culmination on the Buddha-stage—
the cultivation of the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) should be understood as the antidote to those factors that are adverse.
This is its classification:
based upon desire, the cultivation of yoga accompanied by signs is designated as the antidote in all the right abandonments.
By this, one generates desire,
exerts oneself, arouses energy,
and uplifts the mind.
"He applies himself rightly"— this is the explanation of the meaning of these terms.
For, relying upon desire (*chanda*), one exerts oneself by cultivating the yoga known as calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
And that cultivation is cultivated together with the signs of tranquility, exertion, and equanimity;
therefore, it is accompanied by signs.
But how is it cultivated?
One initiates vigor as an antidote to the secondary afflictions of laxity and excitement— the opposites of serenity and exertion—
and thus uplifts the mind and applies it with effort;
furthermore, once serenity has been attained and equanimity is reached, one applies oneself to that state.
This cultivation of yoga is said to be the antidote in all the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) according to the aforementioned classifications.
Regarding the analysis of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), there are five verses:
"The bases of psychic power are four, characterized as supreme for the wise."
They arise for the accomplishment of all goals, both for oneself and for others.
The accomplishment of all aims, both mundane and supramundane, is to be understood;
the rest has its meaning already explained.
[This is known] through reliance, through differentiation, through means, and through actualization.
The establishment of the bases of psychic power is intended in every respect for those possessed of wisdom.
This is the brief statement; the detailed explanation follows:
"Relying upon the perfection of meditation, a fourfold distinction, as well as the means and the sixfold accomplishment, are prescribed."
The perfection of meditation has fourfold reliance and fourfold differentiation, based on the distinctions of concentration through desire, vigor, mind, and investigation.
Its means are likewise fourfold.
Its accomplishment is sixfold.
What are the four kinds of means? The first is that of exertion, the second is that which consists of favoring others, the third is that of binding, and the fourth is that of the antidote.
Among the eight formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*), zeal (*chanda*) and exertion (*vyāyāma*)— together with faith (*śraddhā*)—
constitute the means for undertaking [the practice], because one who possesses faith and seeks the goal exerts effort.
Pliancy has the nature of assistance; mindfulness and clear comprehension are the means of binding [the mind].
This is because by the first [mindfulness], there is no forgetting of the object of focus, and by the second [clear comprehension], there is the discernment of distraction.
Volition and equanimity are the remedial means,
because they serve as the antidotes to the secondary afflictions of lethargy and restlessness, as well as to the primary afflictions.
What are the six kinds of accomplishment?
The accomplishment of vision, instruction, the play of stability,
mastery over vows, and the attainment of the Dharma.
In this context, "vision" refers to the fivefold eye: the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the noble wisdom-eye, the Dharma-eye, and the Buddha-eye.
"Instruction" refers to the six supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) in their respective order;
for by means of these, having approached [beings], and having understood their language, their thoughts, and their coming and going, one instructs them for the sake of liberation.
The "play of stability" (*sthitivikrīḍita*) refers to the manifold play of meditative absorption (*samādhivikrīḍita*) of the bodhisattvas through various emanations and so forth.
"Vow" (*praṇidhi*) refers to that knowledge of vows by which bodhisattvas, empowered by their vows, sport through the excellence of their aspirations—
the number of whose bodies, radiance, or voices is not easily calculated, as described at length in the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*.
Mastery is as described in that same [text], where the ten masteries are specified.
The attainment of qualities is the attainment of the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, and the unique buddha-qualities.
Thus, this sixfold accomplishment consists of vision and the others.

Regarding the analysis of the faculties, there is this verse: "Awakening, conduct, learning, tranquility, and insight—these should be known as the domain of faith and the other faculties, according to their respective roles in accomplishing the goal. (MSA 18.55)
The meaning is that for the faculty of faith, awakening is the "foot," which is to say the objective support;
for the faculty of vigor, it is the conduct of a bodhisattva;
and for the faculty of mindfulness, it is the learning comprised within the Mahāyāna.
The basis of the faculty of concentration is tranquility (śamatha),
and the basis of the faculty of wisdom is insight (vipaśyanā).
It is precisely with reference to these objects that faith and the other [faculties] are called "faculties" (indriya) in the sense of predominance (ādhipatya).
Regarding the classification of the powers, there is this verse:
"Faith and the other [faculties], when they have entered the stages and are no longer defiled,
are designated as 'powers' because their opposing factors have become weak."
The meaning of this verse has already been explained.
There are seven verses concerning the analysis of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
The formal establishment of the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) is prescribed for one who has entered the [first] stage,
because of the realization of the equality of all phenomena and all sentient beings.
By this, it has been taught in which state and through the realization of what the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) are established.

It is because, in the state of having entered the stages (bhūmi), there is a realization of the equality of all phenomena and all sentient beings; thus, respectively, there is the selflessness of phenomena and the equality of self and others.
Hereafter, he demonstrates the analogy of the seven jewels, such as the wheel, for the factors of enlightenment.
Mindfulness operates everywhere for the sake of conquering unconquered objects of knowledge;
it is for the conquest of unconquered objects of knowledge,
just as the wheel-treasure of a universal monarch [operates] for the conquest of unconquered territories.
And his investigation is for the sake of destroying all conceptual constructions and signs.
Just as the precious elephant is for the defeat of adversaries,
so does vigor proceed toward swift and complete awakening,
because it gives rise to the superknowledges quickly.
Just as the precious horse [is capable] of swiftly traveling across the great earth bounded by the ocean,
so too is he surely filled with joy through the increase of the light of the Dharma.
For the Bodhisattva who has initiated vigor, the lights of the Dharma increase;
from that, joy arises, which always gladdens every undertaking,
just as a precious jewel gladdens a universal monarch with its extraordinary radiance.

Through liberation from all obscurations, one attains happiness by means of pliancy, because all forms of functional rigidity have been eliminated; just as a universal monarch experiences happiness through the jewel of a woman.
And the fulfillment of intended aims arises from meditative concentration.
Just as from the householder-treasure of a universal monarch,
he dwells everywhere according to his desire through equanimity;
always supreme, he dwells with both the subsequently attained non-conceptual wisdom and with conceptualization.

Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is said to be non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*); by means of it, the Bodhisattva dwells everywhere according to his wish. This is because he approaches others through the dwelling subsequently attained (*tatpṛṣṭhalabdha-vihāra*), and because he establishes his residence there through the non-conceptual dwelling by remaining free from purposeful activity (*nirvyāpāratā*).
Just as the counselor-jewel of a wheel-turning monarch brings forward the fourfold army when it is to be led forth and withdraws it when it is to be withdrawn,
and goes there to establish his residence wherever the fourfold army proceeds without fatigue.
A Bodhisattva endowed with such qualities proceeds like a universal monarch (cakravartin),
constantly surrounded by the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) which are comparable to the seven jewels.
Thus he concludes the comparison of the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅgas) to the seven jewels:
"The factor of reliance, the factor of intrinsic nature, and the third, the factor of departure;
the fourth is the factor of benefit, and the [remaining] threefold factor is that of non-affliction. (AMsa 18.63)
By this, it has been explained which limb of enlightenment is a limb in what manner:
mindfulness is the limb of support, because all [the others] proceed by depending upon it;
the investigation of phenomena is the limb of essential nature, because awakening has that as its essential nature.
Vigor is the factor of departure, because by means of it one persists until the ultimate goal is attained; joy is the factor of benefit, because it consists of mental happiness;
and serenity, concentration, and equanimity are the factors of non-affliction.
"By which, that which is relied upon, and that which is non-affliction"— thus,
the three factors of non-affliction are to be understood.
Regarding the analysis of the factors of the path, there are two verses.
And following that, there arises a conformity to awakening;
there is the establishment according to awakening, and entry into that established state.
And there is the purification of the three types of action, the cultivation of the antidote, [the purification] of the obscuration to the knowable, of the path, and of the distinguished qualities.
Right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is the continued engagement with the realization of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtāvabodha*) following the time of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
Right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*) is the stabilization and discernment of that very realization.
Furthermore, regarding the stabilization of that [realization], there is entry into the Sūtras and so forth composed by the Blessed One, because through them one realizes that meaning.
The purification of the three types of action consists of right speech, right action, and right livelihood, because these encompass the sequence of both speech and body.

The cultivation of the antidotes—namely, right effort and the others—should be understood respectively as the cultivation [of the remedies] for the obscuration of the knowable, the obscuration of the path, and the obscuration of the distinguished qualities. Through right effort, for a long time...
Indeed, without becoming weary over time, one cultivates the antidote to the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Through right mindfulness, by means of the signs of tranquility (*śamatha*), exertion (*pragraha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), and because of the absence of laxity and excitement, one cultivates the antidote to the obscurations for the sake of bringing the path into manifestation.
Through right concentration, one cultivates the antidote to the obscuration for the sake of bringing forth the distinguished qualities; thus the eight factors of the path are established.
There are three verses concerning the distinction between calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*):
"From the mind’s abiding in the mind, and also from the discernment of phenomena..."
Relying upon right stability, there arise both calm abiding and insight.
Based on right concentration, because of the mind’s abiding within the mind and the discernment of phenomena, calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) are to be understood respectively;
however, they do not exist without right concentration— this is the definition of calm abiding and insight.
It is considered to be universal, partial, and the proximate cause for what is not partial.
That [pair of] calm abiding and insight is universal because one cultivates them wherever one desires a particular quality,
as it is said in the Sūtra:
If a monk should desire, "O, may I [be possessed] of sensual pleasures," and so on in detail up to that point, then that monk must cultivate these two very dharmas:
namely, serenity (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), and so forth.
Serenity and insight are one-sided when he cultivates serenity alone.
Or [the cultivation of] insight;
when one cultivates both simultaneously,
that is the basis considered to be the access to calm abiding and insight for Bodhisattvas on the stage of conduct through aspiration.
In penetration, in departure, in the signless, and in the unconditioned.
In both the purified and the completely pure states, calm abiding and insight—
this yoga, present on all stages, accomplishes everything for the steadfast one.
By the passage beginning with "Thus is the Upanishad," the divisions and the function of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) are indicated.
Yoga should be understood as the means (*upāya*). In this context, penetration (*prativedha*) refers to the entry into the first stage (*bhūmi*).
The departure extends as far as the sixth stage,
because through those stages there is the determination of practice with signs;
the seventh stage is signless.
The other three stages are unconditioned because they proceed without volitional effort;
for "conditioning" (saṃskāra) refers to that which is conditioned (saṃsṛta), and since that does not exist here, they are unconditioned.
And it is by relying on those very three stages that the Buddha-field is to be purified.
And Buddhahood is to be attained;
these two, respectively, are purification (*pariśuddhi*) and complete purity (*viśuddhi*). There are two verses concerning the analysis of skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*).
One attains skill in fulfilling the qualities of a Buddha, in bringing sentient beings to maturity,
in the swift attainment [of the goal], in the purity of action, and in the non-interruption of the path.
The skillful means of the Bodhisattvas on all the stages is peerless;
relying upon this skillfulness, they accomplish all aims. (MSA 18.70)
By this, the classification and the function of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) have been shown.
In that regard, non-conceptual gnosis (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is the skillful means for the fulfillment of the qualities of a Buddha;
the four bases of sympathy (*saṃgrahavastu*) are [the skillful means] for the maturation of sentient beings.
For the sake of swift awakening, one confesses all evil, [vowing] "may there be knowledge for the sake of complete awakening"— this constitutes confession, rejoicing, entreaty, and dedication.
Regarding the purity of action, there are the gateways of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇī*),
because through them all purposeful activities are accomplished.
Regarding the non-interruption of the path and the non-abiding nirvana:
this fivefold skillful means constitutes the peerless expertise of Bodhisattvas across all stages, which is unequalled by others; this is its differentiation.
Its function is the accomplishment of the welfare of both oneself and others.
There are three verses on the classification of dhāraṇīs:
"By way of maturation, through the practice of hearing, and by means of meditative concentration, there is also dhāraṇī;
it is either limited or great, and that which is great is further of three kinds. (AMsa 18.71)
For the wise who have not yet entered or have already entered [the stages], it is weak or middling;
for those on the impure stages, it is indeed great, while for those on the pure stages, it is vast.
Relying upon the state of dhāraṇī, bodhisattvas repeatedly proclaim the true Dharma and constantly uphold it.
Here too, the classification and the function of the dhāraṇī are shown.
In that regard, the dhāraṇī is of three kinds:
[that which arises] through the maturation of previous karma;
Through the practice of hearing,
by means of extensive learning regarding the phenomena of the present life— which is characterized by a specific capacity for grasping and retaining—
and by relying upon meditative concentration.
Furthermore, that [compassion] should be understood as limited when it arises from the ripening of karma or from the practice of hearing the teachings;
it is great when it arises from meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Moreover, that great compassion is of three kinds:

it is weak for those who have not entered the stages (*bhūmi*); it is middling for those who have entered the stages but remain on the levels of the unwholesome; and it is great for those on the seven stages.
However, that which belongs to the perfectly pure stage is superior; this is the distinction of the *dhāraṇī* across the remaining stages.
Its function is the illumination and the preservation of the True Dharma.
Regarding the classification of the vow (*praṇidhāna*), there are three verses.
Volition conjoined with aspiration and impelled by knowledge—
this is indeed the vow of the wise, which is peerless across all stages.
It should be understood as being both the cause and the immediate fruit arising from the mind;
for the sake of accomplishing one's welfare in the future, success arises from "mind-only."
Wondrous, great, and pure, on each successive stage up to enlightenment, it accomplishes the welfare of both oneself and others for Bodhisattvas.

In this regard, the vow (*praṇidhāna*) is elucidated by way of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), its cause (*nidāna*), its stage (*bhūmi*), its classifications (*prabheda*), and its function (*karman*).
Its intrinsic nature is volition (*cetanā*) associated with aspiration (*chanda*).
Knowledge is the primary cause;
"in all stages" refers to the stage itself,
and that vow serves as its causal basis.
Because the fruit arises immediately from the mind alone;

or rather, for the sake of accomplishing a desired object in the future, it should be understood that the attainment of the fulfillment of one's purpose proceeds from the mind alone, which yields immediate fruit—
by means of which powerful bodhisattvas sport with their aspirations.
"It is not easy to calculate the number of his bodies," and so forth; "variegated" refers to the stage of practice through aspiration (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), thinking, "May I be thus";
and for one who has entered the great stages (*mahābhūmi*), there are the ten great vows (*daśa mahāpraṇidhānāni*).
It is pure because of its increasing excellence of purity through the successive stages up to enlightenment; this is [the explanation] according to its differentiation.
Its activity is the accomplishment of the welfare of oneself and others.
Regarding the classification of the three concentrations, there are three verses.
The two kinds of selflessness should be known, as well as the basis for the grasping at a self;
its perpetual pacification is the objective domain of the three concentrations.
The range of the three concentrations should be known as being of three kinds:
the selflessness of persons is the range of the concentration on emptiness;
the five aggregates of clinging, which are the basis for grasping at both of those [persons and phenomena] as a self, are the range of the concentration on wishlessness.
The absolute pacification of that basis is the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*).
That very concentration should be known as threefold by way of the state of the grasped and the grasper;
it refers to those concentrations which are the graspers of the threefold objects of grasping.

Regarding those concentrations on emptiness and so forth, it should be understood that there are three concentrations by way of the relationship between the grasped and the grasper. Furthermore, these are, respectively:
non-conceptual, turned away [from objects], and always associated with delight.
The samādhi of emptiness is non-conceptual because it does not conceptualize a self in persons or phenomena;
the wishless [samādhi] is turned away from that basis which is the grasping at a self.
The signless [samādhi] is associated with joy at all times during the pacification of that basis;
the purpose of the samādhis such as emptiness is proclaimed to be threefold: for full comprehension, for abandonment, and for realization.
Emptiness is for the sake of thoroughly understanding the selflessness of persons;
the wishless is for the sake of abandoning the basis of that grasping at a self;
and the signless concentration is for the sake of realizing its pacification.
Regarding the analysis of the summaries of the Dharma, there are two verses:
The four summaries of the Dharma have been taught to the Bodhisattvas as the secret foundation of meditative concentration, out of a desire for the welfare of sentient beings. (AMsa 18.80)
In that regard, "conditioned phenomena are impermanent" and "all conditioned phenomena are suffering" are taught as the basis for the wishless concentration (*apraṇihita-samādhi*);
"all phenomena are without self" is taught as the basis for emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
"Peaceful is nirvāṇa"—this refers to the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*).
Furthermore, what is the meaning of "impermanent" up to the meaning of "peaceful"? He says:
"The meaning of non-existence, the meaning of non-conceptualization, and indeed the meaning of mere imagination."
And for the wise, that fourfold [practice] has the purpose of the pacification of conceptual construction.
For Bodhisattvas, the meaning of impermanence is the meaning of non-existence;
that which is eternally non-existent is impermanent for them, namely the imagined characteristic (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*).
The meaning of suffering is the meaning of unreal conceptualization (*abhūta-vikalpa*), namely the dependent characteristic (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*).
The meaning of "selflessness" (anātma-artha) is the sense of being merely imagined.

By the word "only" (eva), there is a restriction: a self does not exist as something imagined, but rather there is only the mere imagination; thus, it is stated that the meaning of selflessness is the non-existence of the imagined characteristic.
The perfected characteristic (pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa), which is nirvāṇa, is the meaning of the cessation of conceptual construction (vikalpa).
The meaning of impermanence should also be understood as the meaning of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) with respect to the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, for the purpose of establishing that, there are ten verses in the analysis of momentariness:
"Because of impossibility, because of the cause, because of arising, because of contradiction, and because of not remaining by itself..."
Because of non-existence, because of the exclusivity of the characteristic, because of conformity, and because of cessation.

And because transformation is perceived, because it is both the cause and the fruit of that [transformation], because it is appropriated, because it is sovereign, and because it conforms to pure beings. // AMsa_18.83 //
In this context, this thesis—that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary—should be understood from the statement made later.
Furthermore, how is that established?
Because the occurrence of conditioned phenomena is impossible without momentariness.
For activity (*pravṛtti*) consists in a continuous series (*prabandha*);
and that is not tenable without arising and ceasing at every moment.
Now, if it is maintained that activity occurs as a series by way of the cessation of the preceding and the arising of the succeeding after having remained for a period of time—
Immediately thereafter, there would be no further occurrence because of the absence of continuity; moreover, it is not logical for that which has arisen to exist at another time without continuity.
What is the reason? Because [all things] arise from a cause.
For everything conditioned arises from a cause; this is the meaning of "it exists."
Therefore, if something, having come into being, exists again at a later time, it must necessarily have a cause;
for without a cause, it would not exist, just as it did not exist at the beginning.
Nor can it arise from that very same cause, because that cause has already been exhausted.
And no other cause is perceived;
therefore, it should be understood that at every moment something else necessarily arises with a preceding cause as its condition.
Thus, for that which has arisen without such a continuity, existence at another time is not tenable.

Furthermore, if it is maintained that what has already arisen does not arise again— such that there would be no need for a cause— but rather that what has arisen ceases later after some time, and not immediately upon arising,
then by what is it subsequently ceased?
That it [exists] by means of the very cause of its arising is illogical.
What is the reason? Because arising and cessation are mutually contradictory.
For indeed, no common cause is found for two contradictory things,
such as shadow and sunlight, or cold and heat;
this applies only to cessation at a later time.
And because of contradiction. By what contradiction? By scripture as well.
As it was said by the Blessed One:
"O monk, those conditioned phenomena are like an illusion; they are subject to ruin, temporary, and fleeting.
And [this is realized] by yogins through mental attention (*manaskāra*).
For they, attending to the arising and passing away of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), perceive their cessation at every moment.
Otherwise, they too would lack revulsion, dispassion, and liberation, just like others who perceive cessation only at times such as death.
Moreover, if a produced conditioned phenomenon were to persist for a period of time, it would either persist by itself or be capable of persisting by its own power.
Or by some cause of duration;
first of all, its own abiding is untenable.
What is the reason?
Furthermore, because it does not abide by itself,
for what reason would it be unable to abide again at the end?
It is also not logical that there is a cause for its abiding, since such a cause does not exist.
For nothing at all is perceived [as such a cause].
However, it might be argued that even without a cause of duration, a thing persists because of the absence of a cause of destruction;
but when a cause of destruction is encountered, it is subsequently destroyed, just as blackness is by fire.
That is incorrect because such a cause does not exist;
for there is no cause of destruction whatsoever even subsequently.
It is well known that even fire destroys blackness.
However, its capacity for producing a dissimilar [result] is well-established;

for, due to its connection with that [fire], the continuity of the dark color is perceived as becoming dissimilar, rather than ceasing entirely. Likewise, when water is being boiled, through its connection with fire, it is perceived that because each subsequent production is less and less [in quantity], it becomes extremely weak and finally ceases to arise.
Because the characteristic is exclusive.
For the Blessed One has stated that the characteristic of the conditioned is exclusive, namely, the impermanence of the conditioned;
therefore, if it were not destroyed immediately upon arising, [it would contradict that].
It is argued that its impermanence would not exist for some time, and thus the definition of impermanence is shown to be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Furthermore, it might be argued that if there were a new production at every moment, there would be no recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) that "this is that very same thing.
But such recognition does indeed occur because of the persistence of similarity, like the case of a magician’s peacock-feather fan.
"The cognition of that [object] arises from similarity, not from the actual existence of that object"—
how is this known?
From its cessation.
For if it remained exactly as it was, there could be no cessation at the end, because it would be indistinguishable from its initial characteristic.
Therefore, it is determined that "it is not that very same thing," because transformation is perceived at the end;
for transformation indeed means becoming otherwise.
If that transformation of internal and external entities had not begun from the very outset, no change would be perceived at the end.
Therefore, alteration has indeed begun from the beginning, gradually increasing until it becomes manifest at the end, just as milk does in its state as curd;
however, as long as that alteration is subtle, it is not discerned.
Thus, it is established that "this is that very same thing" is known due to the persistence of similarity;
and consequently, because there is change at every moment,
momentariness is proven.
And from what is it established?
From its being the cause and the fruit;
that is, because it has momentary causes.
The meaning is: "and because they have momentary results.
For it is well-established that the mind is momentary, and other conditioned factors—such as the eye and visible forms—are its causes;
therefore, it is established that they too are momentary.
But that which is momentary cannot arise from that which is non-momentary, just as that which is impermanent cannot arise from that which is permanent.
Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are indeed the fruit of the mind;
how is this understood?
Because they are appropriated, because of their sovereignty, and because they follow pure beings:
for by the mind all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), such as the eye and so forth, together with their bases, are appropriated along with their coagulated matter, since they follow and support it.
Therefore, these are the fruit of the mind, and the mind possesses sovereignty over the conditioned phenomena.
As it was said by the Blessed One:

"By the mind this world is led, by the mind it is dragged along; it remains under the sway of every mind that arises. Likewise, it has been stated: "Name-and-form have consciousness as their condition."
Therefore, it is the fruit of the mind;
and because they follow the pure mind,
for the formations of yogins indeed conform to their pure mind.
As it has been said:
"A meditating monk who possesses supernormal powers and has attained mastery over the mind, if he were to resolve that this block of wood be gold, it would indeed become so for him.
Therefore, conditioned phenomena are the fruit of the mind.
And it is also due to conformity with sentient beings;
for thus, among sentient beings who commit evil deeds, external objects become inferior, whereas among those who perform meritorious deeds, they become sublime.
Therefore, because they follow that mind, it is established that conditioned phenomena have the mind as their fruit;
and from that, their momentariness follows.
For it is not logical that a non-momentary thing should be the fruit of a momentary thing, since [the fruit] must conform to its cause.
Thus, first of all, the momentariness of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) has been established without distinction by means of two verses.
Furthermore, five verses should be understood for the purpose of establishing it specifically regarding internal phenomena:
"By the initial [moment], by the gradual increase, by accumulation, and by the state of having a basis..."
Likewise, through transformation and maturation, as well as by way of being inferior or superior.
Arising occurs through luminosity and non-luminosity, through movement to another location, through the state of having seeds or being seedless, and through reflection.

In the fourteenfold arising, [the storehouse consciousness] is the cause without distinction; because accumulation would be purposeless, because [it would be] illogical, and because the state of being a support is impossible. (AMsa 18.86)
Because that which is established cannot arise [again], and because there is no change due to the non-destruction of the original state;
likewise, this applies to the inferior and the superior, as well as to the luminous and the non-luminous.
Because there is no going, because staying is impossible, because a final state is inconceivable,
and because the mind continues in succession, all conditioned phenomena are momentary.
"From the first, through the degrees of intensity, up to 'all conditioned things are momentary.
How is their momentariness established by these [reasons]?
For the arising of internal conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is of fourteen kinds."
The first is origination, which is the initial manifestation of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*).
That which occurs by way of gradual progression is that which follows the characteristics of the first birth.
That which occurs by way of accumulation is that which results from the accumulation [of growth] through food, sleep, celibacy, and meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
In terms of its state as a basis (*āśrayabhāva*): that which [occurs] through the bases such as the eye for the visual consciousness and so forth;
that which occurs through transformation by passion and so forth due to the alteration of complexion and other qualities;
and that which occurs through maturation through the stages of embryo, infant, child, youth, middle age, and old age.
That which consists in inferiority and superiority refers, respectively, to those being born in the miserable destinies;
and that which consists in luminosity refers to those born among the gods of the Heaven of Magical Creations, the Heaven of Those Who Enjoy Emanations, and in the realms of form and formlessness.
Because it depends solely upon the mind;
because of its luminosity, which belongs to those born elsewhere;
and because of its movement to another location, which is the arising in one place upon the cessation of arising in another place.
In terms of having seeds, it is that which excludes the final aggregates of an Arhat;
in terms of being seedless, it is those very same final [aggregates] of that Arhat;
and in terms of being a reflection.

The arising of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) as reflections through the power of meditative concentration (samādhi) for those who practice the eight liberations (vimokṣa) constitutes this fourteenfold arising. Within this, the momentariness of internal conditioned phenomena is to be understood by means of reasons such as the distinction of causes and so forth.
First, regarding initial arising, it is due to the distinction of causes.

For if there were no distinction in its status as a cause, then no progressive distinction would be perceived in the subsequent activity of the formations, due to the lack of distinction in their causes.
But since such a distinction exists, it follows that this [initial state] is different from those that follow;
thus, momentariness is established.
Because there is a distinction in measurement (*māna*) when there is production in degrees of intensity (*taratama*). "Measurement" means "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*).
For indeed, without difference [in the entity] at every moment, there could be no distinction in dimension (*parimāṇa*).
Because accumulation would be purposeless in the arising of an increase;
for accumulation is indeed support,
and that would be purposeless if there were no momentariness, since [the thing] would remain exactly as it was.
And because accumulation [occurs] only through conjunction;
for accumulation would not be logical without a more robust production at every moment,
since if it were produced as the very basis, it would be impossible for it to be supported by that basis.
For it is not logical that while the substratum remains, that which depends upon it should not remain;
for if it were otherwise, the status of being a substratum would be impossible, just as one who has mounted [a vehicle] cannot remain stationary while the vehicle moves.
This is because [the substratum] cannot exist if change or maturation occurs.
Because there is no modification due to its being both beginningless and indestructible.

For a modification by passion and so forth is not possible for that which remains exactly as it is; nor is there ripening in other states, because if there is no destruction at the beginning, there is an absence of modification at the end.
Likewise, momentariness should be understood to apply to the arising of the inferior and the superior, just as it does to the arising of transformation and maturation.

For the latent impression of karma (*karmavāsanā*) cannot gain its functional activity while conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) remain exactly as they were; for [if they did], birth would have to occur either in an evil destiny or a happy destiny simultaneously.
Rather, the attainment of such activity is logical only through a gradual process, due to a specific transformation of the continuum (*saṃtatipariṇāmaviśeṣa*).
Momentariness is likewise logical even in the case of arising as luminous or non-luminous.
First, in the case of the luminous, it is because that which is so established cannot possibly exist [otherwise], given its dependence on the mind for its activity.
In the case of the non-luminous as well, there is no transformation at the end without destruction at the beginning.
Because there is no motion in the arising [of conditioned phenomena] through movement to another location;
for it is not logical that there exists any action called "motion" characterized by the transition of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to another location.
For such [an action], whether already arisen or not yet arisen, would have to cause the conditioned phenomenon to go to another location.
If [the action] has already arisen, then at the time of going, it has not gone anywhere; thus, for that which is already stationary, going is not possible.
If, on the other hand, it has not yet arisen, then since going does not exist, it is not logical to say "it has gone.
Furthermore, if that action performs its function while the conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskāra*) remains in that very same location, it is not logical.
Because that which is stationary does not reach another location;
nor is it logical for that which is already in another location [to move],
since reaching another location cannot occur without action.
Furthermore, no action distinct from the conditioned formation (*saṃskāra*) is perceived, whether it resides in that same location or in another location.
