Therefore, there is no "going" for conditioned formations other than their arising in a continuous series in another place.
And because of the absence of such [going], momentariness is established.
Motion, characterized by the continuous arising [of a thing] in successive locations, should be understood through various causes:
there is that which occurs by the power of the mind, as in states such as walking;
and there is that which occurs by the impetus of prior karma, as in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
There is [movement] by the force of impact, as in the case of a discharged arrow;
there is [movement] by the force of connection, as in the case of those mounted on a vehicle or a boat crossing a river;
and there is [movement] by the force of propulsion, as in the case of grass and other things driven by the wind.
There is [movement] by virtue of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), such as the horizontal movement of wind, the upward flaming of fire, and the downward flowing of water.
There is [movement] by virtue of power (*anubhāva*), such as through the power of mantras and medicinal herbs,
or for certain [objects], through the power of magnets acting upon iron.
Through the power of supernatural faculties (ṛddhi), for those possessing such powers,
momentariness (kṣaṇikatva) should be understood in the arising [of things] by way of being with seed or without seed,
because of the impossibility of duration and because of the impossibility of a final [moment].
For it is not logical that something remaining in that same state should again possess the nature of a seed at another time without having functioned as a cause at every moment;
nor is it logical for it to be seedless in the final moment.
Furthermore, it is impossible to maintain that it possesses the nature of a seed previously and becomes seedless only in the final moment.
Because in the absence of that [object], the state of being the final [moment] is impossible;
for in such a case, the very status of being the final moment cannot occur.
Furthermore, in the production of a reflection, its momentariness should be understood as following from the nature of the mind.
Because it arises by the power of the mind at every moment,
it has been conclusively established that all internal conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are momentary (*kṣaṇika*).
Now, he establishes the momentariness of external phenomena with three verses.
The momentariness of the sixfold objects of the elements is established because of their drying up and increasing,
because of their inherent mobility, and because of their waxing and waning.
Because it arises from that [earth], because it is a fourfold transformation of earth,
and because its color, odor, taste, and touch are identical, it is likewise [of the same nature].
Because its existence depends on fuel, because it is perceived as having degrees of intensity,
because it follows the mind, and because of [the Buddha's] questioning, external objects are therefore also momentary.
What, then, is that external [object]?
It consists of the four great elements and the sixfold object.
Color, odor, taste, touch, sound, and the form belonging to the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana)—
therefore, the momentariness of the primary elements and of the sixfold object is established.
How is it established?
Regarding water, [its existence is known] from its drying up and increasing:
in wells, ponds, and the like, the gradual increase of water and its drying up are both perceived.
And both of these would not be possible without a transformation occurring at every moment, because there would be no cause for a subsequent distinction;
furthermore, this is because wind is mobile by its very nature and undergoes increase and decrease.
For it has already been established that what is stationary cannot possess mobility, as that would contradict its inherent nature.
And there is no increase or decrease, because it remains exactly as it is;
for [the earth] arises from that [water], and because of the fourfold transformation.
By the word "that," both water and wind are included.
For at the time of evolution, the earth is produced from water together with wind;
therefore, because it is the fruit of that [water], it too should be understood as momentary.
Furthermore, a fourfold transformation of the earth is observed.
That which is produced by karma arises from the specific variety of the karma of sentient beings;
that which is produced by assistance arises through Prahlāda and others;
and that which is produced by the elements arises through fire and so forth.
That which is produced by time arises from transformation over a period of time;
and that [transformation] is not tenable without the arising of something else at every moment, because there is no cause for destruction.
Since color, odor, taste, and tangibility have the same causes as earth and the other elements, their momentariness should be understood in exactly the same way.
Furthermore, fire is momentary because its existence depends upon fuel;
for once fire has arisen, the fuel that arose simultaneously with it does not remain in that same state,
nor is fire capable of persisting once its fuel has been consumed.

Lest there be a persistence even at the end of that which lacks fuel, the mention of color and the other [sensory qualities] is placed first and fire last, in accordance with the requirements of the verse.

Furthermore, even that sound of bells and the like which is perceived over a period of time should be understood as momentary (*kṣaṇika*), because it is perceived as varying in intensity; for if it were not momentary, there would be no perception of it becoming gradually weaker and weaker at every moment.
It may be so;
for even the form belonging to the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) is established as momentary because it follows the mind, just as was stated previously.
Therefore, momentariness is established even for external [form].
Furthermore, it is indeed asked: how is the momentariness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) established? First of all, this proponent of non-momentariness must be questioned:
"For what reason do you accept impermanence (*anityatva*) but do not accept the momentariness of conditioned phenomena?"
If he should say, "Because otherness is not perceived at every moment," he should be addressed with this:
"Why is non-momentariness not accepted even in the case of things like lamps, whose momentariness is well-established, since that [otherness] is not perceived during their steady state?
If he should say, "Because it is not perceived later as it was before," [the response follows].
He should be addressed as follows:
"Why is it not accepted that the same applies to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as well?
If he should say, "Because lamps and other such things are of a different nature from other conditioned phenomena," [then...]
He should be addressed as follows:
"For there are two kinds of dissimilarity—dissimilarity of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vailakṣaṇya*) and dissimilarity of mode of existence (*vṛtti-vailakṣaṇya*).
If, first of all, it is dissimilarity of intrinsic nature that is intended, then for that very reason the status of being an example is appropriate."

For that which is of the very same nature cannot serve as its own example, just as a lamp cannot be an example for a lamp, or a cow for a cow. Alternatively, if you argue that it is an example precisely because of the difference in their modes of occurrence (*vṛtti*), since the case of lamps illuminating other lamps is well-established,
then he must be questioned again regarding the persistence of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*).
"Do you wish that one who has mounted a vehicle should go while the vehicle remains stationary?
If he should say, "Certainly not," then he should be addressed as follows:
It is not tenable to say that while the eye and other [faculties] remain, the consciousness supported by them proceeds as a continuum;
for if one were to argue, "But is it not observed that when a lamp rests upon a wick, it moves as a continuum while the wick remains stationary?
he should be addressed as follows:
"It has not been seen [to persist] through its continuity because a transformation arises at every moment.
If one were to say this, one might ask: "If conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are indeed momentary, why is their momentariness not established as clearly as that of a lamp?
To such a person, this should be said: "Because it is a matter of cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*)."

For their momentariness is not perceived due to the occurrence of a continuous stream of similar succession; because, despite the fact that they are distinct from one another, the misconception arises that "this is that very same thing. Otherwise, the misconception of permanence regarding the impermanent would not occur; and in the absence of that, there would be no affliction (*saṃkleśa*). If there were no affliction, how could there be purification (*vyavadāna*)? It is through such inquiry that the momentariness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is established.
This is well known.
There are twelve verses in the "Analysis of Selflessness" for the purpose of establishing the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*):
"The person (*pudgala*) is to be described as existing as a designation (*prajñapti*), but not as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*)."
Because of non-apprehension, because of perversion, because of affliction, and because of the cause of affliction.
Therefore, it cannot be described as either identical to or different from [the aggregates], because of those two faults;
furthermore, because it would follow that the aggregates are the self, and it would follow that the self is a substantial entity.
If it were a substantial entity yet inexpressible, a purpose for its expression would have to be stated;
however, it is not logical for something to be inexpressible in terms of identity or difference without such a purpose.
Neither from the perspective of characteristics, nor from worldly observation, nor even from the treatises,
is it tenable that fuel and fire are inexpressible [as identical or different], for they are perceived as a duality.
And since consciousness arises when there is a duality, that [duality] is not the condition;
therefore, from being purposeless, it is not tenable for anything from the "seer" up to the "liberator" to exist.
If there were a master, one would not engage in that which is impermanent and undesirable;
thus, the definition of karma as something to be accomplished is sublated in three ways by perfect enlightenment.
And that effort for seeing and so forth is not self-arisen even from the three [causes];
furthermore, seeing and so forth would be effortless if they were caused by such an effort.
Because there is no agent, because of impermanence, and because of non-activity at once,
it is not logical that effort in seeing and so forth is self-existent.
For that which remains as such, or for that which has perished, causality is not tenable because of its prior non-existence, its impermanence, and the absence of a third alternative.
All phenomena are without self; in the ultimate sense, they are emptiness.
Furthermore, it is precisely because of this that the fault in perceiving a self has been taught.
Regarding defilement and purification, as well as their distinct states and divisions,
the distinctions in activity and continuity are indeed demonstrated by means of the person (pudgala).

The view of a self is not something to be produced; its practice is beginningless. There would be effortless liberation for all, or else there is no liberation at all, because the person (pudgala) does not exist.
Should it be said that the person exists, or should it be said that it does not exist? He replied:
The person should be said to exist as a conceptual designation, but not as a substantial reality;
for it should be said that it exists as a designation, but it should be said that it does not exist as a substantial reality.
Thus, when one adopts the doctrine of manifold aspects (anekāṃśavāda), there is no room for fault in either existence or non-existence.
Furthermore, how is it to be understood that [the person] does not exist as a substantial entity (dravyataḥ)?
Because of non-apprehension (anupalambha).

For it is not perceived as a substantial entity (*dravya*) like form (*rūpa*) and so forth; for "perception" (*upalabdhi*) indeed means comprehension by the intellect (*buddhi*). Nor is it the case that the proponents of the person (*pudgalavādin*) do not comprehend the person through the intellect.
And it has been said by the Blessed One:
If one perceives a self even in this very life, how is it that it is not apprehended?
When it is perceived in this manner, it is not apprehended as a substantial entity.
What is the reason?
Because it is due to perversion; for the Blessed One has stated that "self" in what is not-self is a perversion.
Therefore, this grasping at a person is itself a perversion.
How is this understood?
Because it is due to affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
For this affliction—namely, "I" and "mine"—is characterized by the defilement of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);
and yet, a cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*) cannot itself be the affliction.
And how is it to be understood that this is not affliction?
Because its cause is afflicted;
for its causes are indeed afflicted.
Attachment and the other afflictions arise.

Furthermore, regarding that entity designated as "form" and so forth, upon which the designation "person" (pudgala) is applied—should that person be described as being identical to it, or rather as being different from it? He replied:
Therefore, it should be described in terms of both identity and difference.
What is the reason? Because of two faults.
Which two faults?
Furthermore, because it would follow that the aggregates are the self, and because it would follow that the person is a substantial entity;
for if there were identity, it would follow that the aggregates are the self and the person is substantially real,
whereas if there were difference, the person would be substantially real.

For in this way, because the person (pudgala) exists as a conceptual designation (prajñapti), its being "inexpressible" is logical; by this, the status of the [nine] indeterminate points (avyākṛtavastu) is established.
However, those who, transgressing the Teacher’s instruction, maintain that the person exists substantially (dravyataḥ), should be addressed as follows:
If it were a substantial entity (*dravyasat*) yet inexpressible, one must state the purpose [for its being so].
For what reason?
It is not logical for something to be inexpressible in terms of identity or difference without a purpose.
Now, if they should desire the ineffability of the person (pudgala) on the basis of a mere analogy— just as it is said that fire is neither different nor non-different from its fuel—
then they should be addressed as follows:

Neither from logical definition, nor from worldly observation, nor even from scripture is it tenable that fuel and fire are inexpressible [as either identical or different], for they are perceived as a duality;
namely, as oneness and as otherness. For "fire" is the element of heat (*tejo-dhātu*), while "fuel" consists of the remaining primary elements (*bhūta*).
And since their characteristics are distinct, fire is indeed other than fuel.
Furthermore, in the world, fuel is seen even without fire, and fire is seen even without fuel; thus, their difference is established.
Moreover, in the treatise, the Blessed One nowhere stated that fire and fuel are inexpressible [as being either identical or different]; therefore, this [position] is untenable.
Furthermore, how is it known that fire exists without fuel?
It is known from perception; for instance, when fanned by the wind, it travels even a great distance while burning.
Moreover, if it were argued that the wind itself is the fuel there, it is precisely for this reason that the distinctness of fire and fuel is established.
From us; for it was stated [in the previous context] that "because of perception by means of a pair.
For in that case, a pair is perceived: namely, flame and wind as fuel.

There indeed exists a person (*pudgala*) who is this seer, up to the knower, the agent, the enjoyer, the cognizer, and the liberator. Yet, it is not tenable that he is a seer, nor even that he is a liberator.
For he [the Self] would have to be either the causal condition or the master of the consciousnesses designated as "seeing" and so forth.
In that regard, first of all:
since consciousness arises in dependence upon a duality, he is not its causal condition.
What is the reason?
Because it is purposeless;
for no efficacy whatsoever is observed therein.
And if he were a master, he would not bring about what is impermanent and undesirable;
for being the master over the arising of consciousness, he would not produce an impermanent consciousness that is undesirable,
nor one that is undesirable.
Therefore, since it is impossible in either way,
it is not tenable that this [person] is the seer, up to and including the liberator. Furthermore, if the person (pudgala) exists substantially (dravyataḥ), [it is untenable].
If that characteristic of action, which is to be established, exists substantially, then its action is also perceived,
just as the eyes and so forth have the characteristic of seeing and so on, and consist of translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*).

But it is not so for the person (pudgala); therefore, that [person] does not exist substantially. And if that were accepted as existing substantially, [there would be a contradiction] regarding the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Perfect awakening is obstructed in three ways:
by the profound perfect awakening,
and by the uncommon perfect awakening.
It is supramundane perfect awakening;
for in the perfect awakening of a person, nothing profound has been perfectly awakened that is not shared with the non-Buddhist outsiders.
It is not unworldly,
for this grasping is accessible to all the world and is clung to by the non-Buddhists.

Furthermore, a person who has been accustomed to long-term saṃsāra— being a seer up to a cognizer— must be either exerting effort or effortless in the acts of seeing and so forth. Moreover, if he were exerting effort, that effort would have to be either self-originated or accidental.
And the conviction regarding that [reliability] in the act of seeing and so forth, as well as the effort toward it, is not self-evident even from those three;
for there are precisely those three faults which will be explained hereafter.
And the phrase "not being dependent on effort" carries over [from the previous context].
Alternatively, it is established for that which exists without effort.
Regarding the statement that seeing and so forth are effortless: if there is no activity on the part of the person in seeing and so forth, how can he be a seer?
It has been stated that [the agent] is known [to be non-existent] because of three defects; from which three defects?
Because of being a non-agent, because of impermanence, and because of not acting simultaneously:
it is not logical for effort in seeing and so forth to be self-arisen.

If effort (*prayatna*) in regard to seeing and so forth were accidental—that is, if seeing and so forth occurred by chance—then the person (*pudgala*) would not be their agent. How, then, could he be a "seer" or, up to, a "knower"? Furthermore, if it were accidental, because of its independence [from causes], effort would never fail to exist, and thus it would not be impermanent.
Furthermore, if effort were eternal, there would be the fault that seeing and the other [sensory functions] would occur simultaneously and eternally;
therefore, it is not logical for effort to be self-existent with respect to seeing and the rest.
Likewise, because it does not exist prior to its occurrence, it is impermanent whether it remains or perishes.
Furthermore, because a third alternative does not exist, its status as a condition is not tenable.
Now, if the effort of the person were to constitute "effort," it would be untenable for that which remains thus [static] to possess the nature of effort.
Because it did not exist previously;
for if that effort were already present, the person would never be non-existent.
Why, then, would there be no prior effort when [the person] has not yet arisen?
It is not tenable for that which has already perished to be a causal condition, because it would entail the consequence that the person (pudgala) is impermanent.
Furthermore, there is no third position such that something could be neither abiding nor perished;
therefore, even an effort that serves as its condition is not tenable.
Thus, relying first upon reasoning, the person (*pudgala*) is not found as a substantial entity;

all phenomena (*dharma*) are without self (*anātman*), for in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) they are emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Furthermore, the fault in apprehending a self has been taught for this very reason.
For in the *Dharmoddānas*, the Blessed One taught that all phenomena are selfless; yet in the *Paramārthaśūnyatā*, he taught:
"Karma exists and its maturation exists, but an agent is not found who casts off these aggregates and reconnects with other aggregates."

It is taught [in the *Pañcavastuka*] that "except for the conventional designation of dharmas. In the *Pañcaka*, it is taught that there are five disadvantages in the apprehension of a self (*ātman*):
there arises the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), the view of a living being (*jīvadṛṣṭi*), and one becomes indistinguishable from the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
He has entered upon a wrong path;
his mind does not enter into emptiness, does not find confidence in it, does not become established in it, and does not resolve upon it;
the noble dharmas do not become purified for him.

Thus, it is also not tenable from the standpoint of scripture; for the Blessed One has taught the person (pudgala) here and there— such as the one who fully understands, the bearer of the burden, and the classification of persons such as the follower by faith— and if it did not exist substantially, why would he have taught it?
Regarding affliction and purification, which are distinguished by their states and their interruptions,
the distinction between modes of activity and mental continua is indeed demonstrated by means of the person (pudgala).
For, regarding the distinctions of states in affliction and purification, as well as the distinctions of severance,
it would be impossible to teach the differentiation of their occurrence and the differentiation of the continuum without the designation of a person (*pudgala*).
In the *Parijñā-sūtra*, the phenomena to be fully known are affliction, and full knowledge is purification.
In the Bhārahāra-sūtra,
the burden and the taking up of the burden are defilement;
the laying down of the burden is purification.

Without the designation of the person who has fully understood and who carries the burden, it would be impossible to teach the difference in their activity and the difference in their mental continuum.
Furthermore, the factors conducive to enlightenment exist in many states due to the distinctions of the paths of preparation, seeing, cultivation, and final consummation;
without the designation of persons such as those who follow through faith and so forth, it would be impossible to teach the difference in their activity and the difference in their mental continuum.
Therefore, this principle should be understood here: that the person (pudgala) was taught despite the absence of existence as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*).
Otherwise, the teaching of the person would result in being purposeless;
for it is not reasonable that this [teaching] was intended for the sake of producing the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), because—
The view of a self is not to be produced, because it has already arisen from the very beginning;
nor is it for the sake of practicing that [view], because the practice of the view of a self is beginningless.
Furthermore, if liberation were taught as being through the vision of a self, [it would be a false teaching].
If this were so, there would be effortless liberation for everyone; for indeed, the view of a self does not exist for all those who have not yet seen the truths.
Alternatively, it follows that there is no liberation at all.

For no one, having previously grasped the self as non-self, would grasp it as a self at the time of the realization of the truths; just as one does not grasp suffering as suffering after having failed to grasp it as such before. If liberation were like the former state, there would be no liberation even afterwards. Furthermore, if a self exists, there will inevitably be the notions of "I" and "mine," craving for a self, and other causes based upon it.
Since it would follow that one must be possessed by the afflictions (*kleśa*), there could likewise be no liberation; or else, one must admit that the person (*pudgala*) does not exist,
for if such a person were to exist, these faults would necessarily ensue.
Thus, always endowed with these qualities, bodhisattvas do not neglect their own welfare and they accomplish the welfare of others.
The function of the qualities beginning with shame (*hrī*) and steadfastness (*dhṛti*) has been briefly indicated.
The eighteenth chapter, the Section on the Factors Conducive to Enlightenment, in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, is completed. [Now begins] the nineteenth section.

There are three verses on the classification of wonders: The renunciation of one’s own body and even of prosperity for the sake of others; and patience toward the weak by one who is indifferent to body and life. (MSA 19.1)
Indeed, the undertaking of vigor, the absence of relishing even in the bliss of the meditative absorptions,
and non-conceptuality regarding wisdom— these constitute the state of wonder attained by the wise.
Birth in the family of the Tathāgatas, the attainment of the prophecy,
the reception of empowerment, and the realization of awakening are considered the marvels.
Here, through two verses, the wonder of practice is described with reference to the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).

For, through generosity (*dāna*), the renunciation of one’s own body is a wonder; and for the sake of the restraint of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), there is the renunciation of noble prosperity.
The remainder has its meaning already explained.

By the third verse, the marvel of the fruit is explained with reference to the four fruits of a bodhisattva: three are the fruits of those in training (śaikṣa) on the first, eighth, and tenth stages, while the fourth is the fruit of no-more-training (aśaikṣa) on the stage of a Buddha. Regarding the analysis of what is not a marvel, there is this verse:
Having cultivated dispassion, compassion, and even the supreme meditative concentration,
as well as equanimity— it is not surprising that one is disciplined in these qualities.
"In them" refers to the perfections (*pāramitā*).
Having attained freedom from passion (*vairāgya*), there is nothing marvelous in the practice of giving.

Having recourse to compassion, and having attained the supreme cultivation of ethical discipline and patience on the eighth stage, the application of vigor and the other perfections that is free from effort and non-conceptual is not a marvel.

Having attained the state of mind in which self and others are equal, the application toward all the perfections is not a marvel, because there is no weariness in seeking the welfare of others as if it were one's own.

There are three verses concerning equanimity of mind: The affection that beings have for themselves, for their wives, children, friends, and kinsmen is not as great as the affection that the wise have for all sentient beings. (AMsa 19.5)

Impartiality toward those in need, the constant non-violation of ethical discipline, patience in all circumstances for the sake of sentient beings, and even great exertion of vigor for the sake of all goals; AMsa 19.6.
Dhyāna that is always wholesome and wisdom that is non-conceptual should be understood as the equanimity of mind of Bodhisattvas toward those very [perfections].
One verse concerns equanimity toward sentient beings;
two concern the perfections.
For the affection that sentient beings feel for themselves and others is neither characterized by equality nor is it ultimate.
For instance, they may even kill themselves;

however, for Bodhisattvas, there is an absolute equanimity toward all sentient beings regarding the perfections. Furthermore, in generosity, there is an even-mindedness due to the absence of partiality toward those who seek; in ethical discipline, there is the constant non-violation of even the slightest infraction.
Patience consists in non-differentiation toward all sentient beings.
Regarding vigor, it arises from the exertion of vigor for the sake of sentient beings, from applying oneself equally to the welfare of both self and others, and for the sake of all that is wholesome.
The remainder is self-evident.
In the analysis of beneficence, there are sixteen verses:
establishing [others] in the state of being a vessel, planting them in the very precepts, enduring harm, and engaging in activity for the sake of others. *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* 19.8.
Winning others over to this teaching, cutting through doubt,
and acting for the benefit of sentient beings— this is held to be the characteristic of the wise.
By these two verses, the manner in which Bodhisattvas provide assistance through the six perfections is elucidated.
For by means of generosity, they establish sentient beings in the state of being fit vessels for wholesome action;
and by means of meditative concentration, they win them over through their possession of extraordinary power.
The remainder has its meaning already explained.
By the remaining verses, their quality of being benefactors is shown through their similarity to a mother and so forth:
"Those who always sustain sentient beings with an impartial intention..."
They cause [beings] to be born in the noble realm and cause them to increase through wholesome qualities.
They protect beings from misdeeds and cause them to develop learning;
through these five activities, the sons of the Victors are like mothers to sentient beings.
They are like mothers to sentient beings, acting as mothers to beings;
for a mother provides five kinds of assistance to her son:
she bears him in her womb.
It gives birth,
nourishes, sustains, causes to grow, protects from misfortune, and teaches speech;
these five activities of a bodhisattva are to be understood as being analogous to that.
The noble dharmas should be understood as the ground for exertion,
because faith is planted among all sentient beings at all times,
and because they are joined to the training in higher ethics and so forth, as well as to liberation.
Through these five activities— soliciting the Buddhas and abandoning their obscurations— the sons of the Conquerors are like fathers to sentient beings.
For a father provides five kinds of assistance to his sons:
he plants their seeds,
and he teaches them their craft.
He unites them with suitable wives and makes them free from debt so that they are not made to pay their father's debt;
by analogy with this, these five activities of the bodhisattvas are to be understood.
For faith is the seed for sentient beings to obtain the noble body;
the trainees are the craft;
liberation is the wife; and the experience of the joy and bliss of liberation is the enjoyment.
The Buddhas are spiritual friends;
they indeed conceal from sentient beings that which is a ground for obscuration and that which is unworthy of being taught.
They censure failure in the training and praise its perfection.
They bestow instruction and indeed make the Māras known;
through these five activities, the sons of the Conquerors are like kinsmen to sentient beings.
For relatives provide five kinds of assistance to their kin:
they conceal their secrets,
and they censure their misconduct.
They praise good conduct, provide assistance in what ought to be done, and restrain one from situations of calamity.
By analogy with these, the five activities of Bodhisattvas are to be understood:
because they conceal the teaching of the profound Dharma from those for whom it would be harmful; and because they respectively censure failure in training and praise its successful accomplishment.
Because they provide instruction for spiritual realization and because they perceive the activities of Māra,
their own intellects remain untiring regarding both affliction and purification; thus,
they bestow all worldly prosperity as well as that which transcends the world.
Those who are undivided in their pursuit of happiness and welfare— undivided because they never grow weary— and who always desire the happiness and welfare [of others],
such sons of the Victors are like friends to sentient beings by virtue of five activities.
For that indeed is a friend which is not distracted from the welfare and happiness of a friend;
it bestows both happiness and benefit,
remains unbreakable, and always seeks their welfare and happiness.
Likewise, it should be understood that Bodhisattvas are like friends to sentient beings by means of five kinds of actions;
for worldly prosperity is the crest,
because one experiences happiness through it.
Supramundane is that which is beneficial because it is the remedy for the disease of the afflictions;
those who are always exerting themselves in the ripening of sentient beings,
who speak of the correct departure [from suffering], and who are patient toward wrongdoings.
The sons of the Victorious Ones bestow the two kinds of perfection and are skilled in the means thereto; by these five activities, they are like servants to sentient beings.
For a servant conducts himself properly by means of five qualities:
he is endowed with diligence in his duties,
and he is not a deceiver.
He is patient toward verbal abuse,
physical beating, and the like;
he is skillful because of his performance of all tasks.
He is discerning and knows the skillful means;
by analogy with that, these five activities of the bodhisattvas are to be understood.
The two kinds of accomplishment—the mundane and the supramundane—are also to be understood.
Those who are considered to have attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena are the instructors of all vehicles and those who engage others in the accomplishment of yoga.
With pleasant countenances, and indifferent toward both recompense and karmic maturation, the sons of the Victors are like teachers of sentient beings through these five actions. (AMsa 19.21)
By means of five kinds of action, he becomes a benefactor to his disciples:
he is himself well-trained,
and he trains them in everything.
He teaches quickly;
he is pleasant-faced and of a gentle disposition;
and his mind is free from worldly motives.
By analogy with that, these five activities of the bodhisattvas are to be understood:

"Those who, being dedicated to the welfare of sentient beings, fulfill the accumulations; who, once the accumulations are fulfilled, swiftly liberate them and cause the opposing factors to diminish. (MSA 19.22)
The sons of the Victors, who are like preceptors for sentient beings, unite them with various worldly prosperities and with supramundane states through five kinds of actions. (MSA 19.23)
The preceptor assists his co-residents through five kinds of actions:
he causes them to go forth, he grants them full ordination,
and he instructs them in the avoidance of faults.
One gathers [beings] through material gifts and through the Dharma; by analogy with that, these five activities of the bodhisattvas are to be understood.
Regarding the analysis of requital, there are two verses:
"By means of non-attachment to enjoyments, and by not violating moral discipline..."
And through devotion to gratitude and through application to practice.
For embodied beings who abide precisely in the six perfections become, in that way, benefactors in return to the Bodhisattvas.
"So be it," [he said], just as those Bodhisattvas were benefactors;
therein they engage in giving through non-attachment to enjoyments,
and in ethical discipline through its non-violation.
Through the application of gratitude, one is established in patience;
for, out of gratitude toward the bodhisattva who has been a benefactor, one recognizes that "they indeed love patience.

Through the application of practice, one is established in the perfections of vigor and wisdom, based on the consideration of both the means by which one practices and the object in which one practices.
There is a verse concerning the classification of aspiration:
They always desire the increase [of merit] and the decrease [of faults], the maturation of sentient beings, the progression to excellence on the stages, and unsurpassed enlightenment. (AMsa 19.26)
Bodhisattvas always aspire to five things:
the perfection of the transcendent virtues, the abandonment of their opposites,
and the ripening of sentient beings.
The progression through the specific stages and the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. There is a verse concerning the classification of non-vain application:
In the abandonment of fear, in the generation [of the thought of awakening], in the cutting off of doubt,
and in the instruction on practice, the sons of the Conquerors are always unfailing.
It should be understood that the application of bodhisattvas toward the fourfold welfare of sentient beings is never in vain:
[namely] in the application of fearlessness regarding the profound and vast Dharma,
in the generation of the thought of awakening, and in severing the doubts of those who have already generated the thought of awakening.
And regarding the instruction on the practice of the perfections,
there are two verses in the section on the analysis of correct application:
"The giving of one who is free from expectation and has no longing for rebirth..."
Morality and patience in all circumstances, and vigor for the arising of every virtue.
Likewise, without the formless realm, there is meditative concentration joined with skillful means;
this is the correct application of the wise toward the six perfections.
As it is said in the *Ratnakūṭa*:
"The maturation [of fruit] for one who does not expect [anything] from giving," and so forth.
There are two verses concerning the distinction between the factors conducive to decline and those conducive to excellence.
Attachment to enjoyments, having flaws, pride, seeking mere pleasure,
relishing [meditative states], and conceptualization are the causes of decline for the wise.
For those Bodhisattvas who abide in those very antidotes,
the factors conducive to distinction (viśeṣabhāgīya) should be known as being the opposite of these [hindrances].

The adversaries of the six perfections are to be understood as belonging to the class of decline; their opposites are to be understood as belonging to the class of distinction. There are two verses concerning the distinction between the counterfeit and the genuine.
One [type] has six feet:
hypocrisy regarding the invitation (pravāraṇā), showing a pleasant countenance,
behaving likewise out of greed, and likewise having tranquility of speech and body.
Perfection in eloquent speech devoid of practice—
these are taught as leading to the non-reality of Bodhisattvas; conversely, for those who apply themselves [to practice], they are taught as leading to that reality.
The six qualities of a bodhisattva, beginning with *pravāraṇā*, should be understood as the counterfeits of the six perfections (*pāramitā*).
The remainder has its meaning already explained.
There is a verse in the section on Discipline (*vinaya-vibhāga*):
For by means of the consolations beginning with generosity, those wise ones indeed discipline sentient beings throughout all the stages, [overcoming] the sixfold class of adversaries.
The adverse factors (*vipakṣa*) are of six kinds:
stinginess, immorality, anger, laziness, distraction, and faulty wisdom, corresponding respectively to the six perfections (*pāramitā*).
The prophecy for the wise is twofold, according to the distinction of time and person;
furthermore, another [type] is proclaimed regarding enlightenment and the prophecy itself.
Through the attainment of the patient acceptance of the non-arising [of phenomena], through the abandonment of pride and effortful striving,
and through attaining oneness with all the Buddhas and the Sons of the Conquerors.
Furthermore, that [teaching] is intended [to be understood] by way of its field, its name, its time, its designation by eon,
and its persistence through the retinue of the True Dharma.

In that regard, there is a twofold prediction (vyākaraṇa) according to the distinction of persons, because of the prediction made for a person who is established in the lineage, one who has generated the thought [of awakening], one who is present before one's eyes, or one who is face-to-face.
There is also a prediction according to the distinction of time, because of the prediction made for a limited or unlimited period of time.
Furthermore, there is a prediction regarding awakening.

A prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*) is when it is predicted that "a Tathāgata of such-and-such a name will [attain enlightenment] at such-and-such a time. Furthermore, there is another, the Great Prophecy (*mahāvyākaraṇa*), which occurs on the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) through the attainment of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and through the abandonment of the conceit "I shall become a Buddha."
This is because of the abandonment of the enjoyment of all signs,
and because of attaining a state of oneness together with all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
due to no longer perceiving any distinction between their own mental continuum and that of others.
Furthermore, there is a prophecy by way of the field and so forth: "In such a buddha-field, one named thus, after such a length of time, will become a Buddha;
in a kalpa of such a name, and he will have such a retinue.
Regarding the analysis of the certainty of attainment, there is a six-line verse:
For the wise, there is the certainty of the arising of success, indefatigability, constancy in cultivation, non-falling from meditative concentration,
the accomplishment of tasks, effortless spontaneity, and the attainment of receptivity in every respect.
With reference to the six perfections, this sixfold certainty is taught:
certainty regarding prosperity, because of the constant attainment of magnificent success in enjoyments;
and certainty regarding rebirth, because of the constant assumption of rebirths according to one's wish.
The certainty of being untiring consists in never becoming weary due to the sufferings of saṃsāra; the certainty of constant cultivation consists in the perpetual practice of cultivation;

and the certainty regarding non-falling from meditative concentration and the accomplishment of what is to be done consists in never losing meditative concentration and practicing with thorough dedication.

And there is the certainty of falling [into the state of non-retrogression] upon attaining the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) through dwelling constantly in effortless, non-conceptual gnosis (*anābhoga-nirvikalpa-jñāna*). Regarding the analysis of what must necessarily be done, there is a verse of six lines:
Worship, undertaking the training, compassion, cultivation of the beautiful,
heedfulness in the forest, and likewise insatiability regarding what has been heard and its meaning—
these are the necessary duties for the wise on all stages.

With reference to the six perfections, this sixfold necessity of what must be done is established; the meaning of the verse is clear. There are two verses concerning the analysis of what must be done with urgency.
Knowledge of the defects in sensual pleasures, scrutiny regarding transgressions,
the endurance of suffering, and the cultivation of the wholesome.
Non-savoring even in pleasure and the non-conceptualization of signs constitute what must be practiced continuously by the wise throughout all the stages.
For the sake of bringing the six perfections to completion, there are six constant duties.
The two verses [that follow] have their meaning already explained.
In the section on the analysis of the primary subjects, there is a verse of six lines.
The gift of Dharma, purity of ethical discipline, the very patience of non-arising,
the undertaking of vigor in the Mahāyāna, the final state accompanied by compassion,
and wisdom— these are considered the primary [perfections] among the perfections for the wise.
Among the six perfections, these are the six primary types:
therein, purity of ethical discipline is the morality beloved by the noble ones;
the final one is the compassionate abiding, which is the fourth, being endowed with the immeasurable of compassion.
The remainder has already been explained.
There are four verses concerning the analysis of the establishment of designations.
The establishment of the fields of knowledge is according to the distinctions in the forms of the sūtras and so forth.
The wise should understand the systematic arrangement of the teachings across all the stages.
The establishment of the vehicles and the logical methods is fourfold and indeed threefold.
Proper mental attention, right view accompanied by its fruit,
investigation by means of the valid cognitions, and the inconceivable object of knowledge— this is the fourfold reasoning.
The vehicle is held to be threefold by way of difference in intention, teaching, application, equipment, and full attainment. (AMsa 19.46)
The establishment of designations is fourfold,

distinguished by the designations of phenomena (*dharma*), truths (*satya*), reasoning (*yukti*), and vehicles (*yāna*). Among these, the establishment of the five fields of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) should be understood as the establishment of phenomena, according to the various forms such as *sūtra*, *geya*, and so forth.
The other branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), which are indeed included within these, are taught in the Mahāyāna for the sake of the Bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, the establishment of sentient beings proceeds by relying upon seven kinds of suchness (*tathatā*): the suchness of activity (*pravṛtti-tathatā*), the suchness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-tathatā*), the suchness of representation (*vijñapti-tathatā*), the suchness of arrangement (*saṃniveśa-tathatā*), the suchness of wrong practice (*mithyā-pratipatti-tathatā*), and the suchness of right practice (*samyak-pratipatti-tathatā*).
The establishment of the designation of reasoning is fourfold: the reasoning of dependence, the reasoning of cause and effect, the reasoning of logical proof, and the reasoning of natural law.
The reasoning of logical proof and the reasoning of the nature of phenomena;
and the formal establishment of the designations of the vehicles is threefold.
The Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Mahāyāna.
In this context, the principle of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*) refers to appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manaskāra*) within all three vehicles;

for, depending upon that and with that as a condition, supramundane right view (*lokottara-samyagdṛṣṭi*) arises. The principle of causal efficiency (*kāraṇa-yukti*) is that right view is accompanied by its fruit.
The reasoning of establishment by proof is the investigation by means of the valid cognitions, such as direct perception;
the reasoning of the nature of phenomena is the inconceivable state.
For the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is established and is not to be reconsidered; why?
Because right view arises from appropriate mental attention (*yoniśomanaskāra*), and from that, the fruit is the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśaprahāṇa*), and so forth.
The establishment of the three vehicles (yāna) should be understood through five aspects:
by way of intention, teaching, application, equipment, and attainment.

Among these, the Śrāvaka vehicle consists of inferior intention, teaching, application, equipment, and attainment; the Pratyekabuddha vehicle consists of middling [intention and so forth]; and the Mahāyāna consists of superior [intention and so forth].
For the teaching of the Dharma prevails according to the disposition and according to the intention;
as is the teaching, so is the application;
as is the application, so is the equipment.
"And the attainment of enlightenment according to the equipment.
Regarding the analysis of seeking, there is this verse:
"The seeking of the adventitious nature consists in the mutual [distinction] between name and thing."
In this context, there is the investigation into the fact that both kinds of designation consist of nothing more than that [designation].
There are four kinds of investigation regarding phenomena: the investigation of names, the investigation of things,
and the investigation of the designation of intrinsic nature.
And there is the investigation into the designation of specific qualities.
In this regard, the investigation into the adventitious nature of a name with respect to an object should be understood as the investigation into names;
the investigation into the adventitious nature of an object with respect to a name should be understood as the investigation into objects.

When both are connected, the investigation into the mere-ness of the designation of intrinsic nature and specific qualities is to be understood as the "investigation into the designation of intrinsic nature and specific qualities.
There are ten verses in the section on the analysis of the correct response:
"Because of the non-apprehension of everything, there is fourfold knowledge of reality."
For the wise, it arises on all the stages for the sake of accomplishing every goal.

The fourfold thorough knowledge of phenomena as they truly are consists of that which arises from the investigation of names, that which arises from the investigation of things, and that which arises from the investigation of the designation of intrinsic nature.
And it includes the investigation into the designation of specific qualities;
this should be understood as resulting from the non-apprehension of all these, beginning with names.
With the second half-verse, he demonstrates the greatness of the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*) through its function:
"For the basis, the enjoyment, and the seed are indeed the cause of bondage;
yet it is the mind and mental factors, together with their support and their seeds, that are bound herein. (AMsa 19.49)
In this context, the cause as the locus of support is the receptacle world;
the cause as objects of enjoyment consists of the five sense-objects, beginning with visible form;
and the cause as the seed is the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which is the seed of those [objects].
In this regard, the mind and mental factors, together with their bases, are bound by three kinds of causes;
and their seed is the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Furthermore, the bases should be understood as the eye and the other sense organs.
The wise one, by thoroughly discerning every sign— both that which is placed before him and that which exists of its own accord— attains supreme enlightenment.

In this context, the "sign" (*nimitta*) placed before one is that which has been made an object through the application of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, and is thus conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*).
The "abiding" [sign] is that which, by its very nature, has become an object without being conceptually constructed through effort.
The realization of its dissolution (*vibhāvanā*) is the state of no longer having it as an object.
Non-conceptualization is the means for that [realization] and is the antidote to signs;
and both of these occur in sequence:
first for that which has been established [by effort], and subsequently for that which is established spontaneously.

In that regard, by dissolving the sign of a person (pudgala-nimitta) which is accompanied by the four perversions, the yogi attains the enlightenment of a śrāvaka or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
by dissolving the signs of all phenomena (sarvadharma-nimitta), he attains great enlightenment (mahābodhi).
Through this, having thoroughly understood according to reality, there occurs a thorough understanding as it truly is, which leads to liberation.
That has been elucidated:

"The wisdom that has suchness as its object, which is free from the grasping of duality and directly perceives the body of corruption— this is held by the wise to be [the knowledge] at the time of its destruction."
By this, it is elucidated how, through the thorough knowledge of the three natures as they are, one proceeds toward the exhaustion of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*);
that is, by thoroughly knowing the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) through its having suchness (*tathatā*) as its object.
The imagined nature (*parikalpita*) is characterized by the absence of grasping at duality;
the dependent nature (*paratantra*) is characterized by the direct perception of the body of corruption (*dauṣṭhulyakāya*).
It leads to the destruction of that very body of corruption—the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)—for the sake of its destruction, and upon its destruction.
Knowledge that has suchness as its object, cultivated without differentiation of aspects,
is said to be direct perception regarding the reality of existence and non-existence, and to be sovereign over conceptualization.
It is cultivated as being of non-differentiated form because one perceives no difference between the sign (*nimitta*) and suchness (*tathatā*).
By this, the distinction of the Bodhisattva’s signlessness from that of the Śrāvaka is illuminated;
for the latter perceive a difference between the sign and the signless.
They enter the signless by not attending to any signs and by attending to the signless realm (*dhātu*).

However, because Bodhisattvas do not perceive any sign apart from suchness (*tathatā*), they perceive the sign itself as signless; therefore, their knowledge is cultivated through that mental attention.
And when the objective referent exists, direct perception is said to be pervasive with respect to conceptual construction;
because of the attainment of mastery over conceptual construction, all objects are successfully realized exactly according to one's conceptualization.
For the foolish, reality is completely concealed, and unreality appears everywhere.
But for Bodhisattvas, having cast that aside, reality appears from every perspective.

By this it is demonstrated that just as for the foolish, by their own natural disposition, only the non-reality appears as the causal sign and not reality— that is, suchness— so too for Bodhisattvas, by their own natural disposition, only reality appears and not non-reality.
The non-appearance and appearance of the non-existent object and the existent object, respectively, are to be understood.
This transformation of the basis is liberation, because of the attainment of mastery over one's desires.

The non-appearance of the unreal object as a causal sign and the appearance of the real object as suchness should be understood as the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*); for by that [revolution], there is the non-appearance of the former.
That very [revolution] should be understood as liberation.
What is the reason?
Because of acting according to one's will;
for then one becomes independent, having mastery over one’s own mind by nature due to the non-occurrence of signs (*nimitta*).
An object appears everywhere as mutually similar and vast.
Therefore, having fully understood that which creates obstacles, one should abandon it.
This is the knowledge of reality as it is regarding the means for purifying the field:
the great receptacle world, existing in mutual relation and of a similar nature, appears as "this is that very same thing.
Because it appears in this way, it becomes an obstacle to the purification of the Buddha-field.
Therefore, having fully understood that which creates an obstacle, one should indeed abandon it; thus it is proclaimed. Regarding the classification of the immeasurable, there is this verse:
That which is to be matured, that which is to be purified, that which is to be attained, and that which is suitable for maturation.
For the wise, the subject matter of the teaching on rightness is indeed immeasurable.

For there are five kinds of immeasurable objects for bodhisattvas: the object to be matured, which is the realm of sentient beings; the object to be purified, which is specifically the world-realm comprised of the container-world;
and the object to be attained, which is the dharma-realm.

The realm of those to be converted is that which is fit for ripening; the realm of the means of conversion is the subject matter of correct teaching. There are two verses on the analysis of the power of teaching.
The arising of the bodhisattva-mind and the very patience regarding non-arising;
the stainless eye that is yet inferior, and the destruction of the outflows.
The long endurance of the true Dharma, proficiency, the cutting off of doubts, and the enjoyment [of the Dharma]—
these should be known as the fruits for the wise one who is devoted to teaching. (AMsa 19.58)
For a bodhisattva engaged in teaching, eight kinds of fruits of that teaching should be understood:
some among the listeners generate the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*),
while others attain the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Some produce the dustless, stainless Dharma-eye regarding phenomena— comprised within the Lesser Vehicle—
while others attain the destruction of the outflows;
and the True Dharma becomes long-enduring through its successive preservation.
For those who have not yet attained proficiency, there arises proficiency in the meaning;
for those who are doubtful, there is the cutting away of doubt;
and for those who have reached certainty, there is the enjoyment of the true Dharma, which is the faultless essence of joy.

In the analysis of the greatness of the Mahāyāna, there are two verses: "The greatness of the objective support, likewise that of the practice of the two, of knowledge, of the exertion of vigor, and of skill in means. (AMsa 19.59)
The greatness of its attainment and the greatness of the Buddha's activity—
it is indeed because of this possession of greatness that it is designated as the "Great Vehicle" (Mahāyāna).
It is called the Mahāyāna because of its association with seven kinds of greatness: (1) greatness of objective support, due to its association with the immeasurably vast teachings such as the sūtras;
and (2) greatness of practice, due to the practice of two aims: one's own welfare and the welfare of others.

By the greatness of knowledge, because at the time of penetration there is the realization of both—the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*);

by the greatness of the undertaking of vigor, because of continuous and respectful application for three incalculable eons (*kalpāsaṃkhyeya*); and by the greatness of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), because of not abandoning *saṃsāra* while remaining undefiled by it.

By way of the greatness of realization, because of the realization of the powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities of a Buddha; and by way of the greatness of the Buddha-activity, because of the repeated manifestation of perfect enlightenment and great final nirvana:
lineage, inclination toward the Dharma, and likewise the production of the thought [of awakening].
The practice of generosity and the other perfections, as well as the very entry into the correct method.
The ripening of sentient beings, the purification of the field, non-abiding nirvāṇa, and supreme enlightenment—these arise from seeing [the Buddha]. Seeing [the Buddha] again and again.
By these ten kinds of subjects, the entirety of the Mahāyāna is subsumed.
The maturation of sentient beings is to be understood as belonging to one established on the stages from the first up to the seventh stage.
The purification of the buddha-field and non-abiding nirvāṇa belong to the threefold irreversible stage.
Supreme enlightenment exists on the Buddha-stage,
and therein alone are the manifestation of perfect awakening and great final nirvāṇa. The remainder has already been explained.
In the analysis of the bodhisattva, there are ten verses:
one is characterized by resolute belief, another by pure high resolve;
[the others pertain to] the sign, the signless, and the unconditioned.
For these five types of bodhisattvas are to be recognized throughout all the stages.
In that regard, one who courses with signs does so from the second stage up to the sixth;
one who courses without signs does so on the seventh;
and one who courses without volitional effort does so beyond that.
The rest has been explained.

One who is unattached to sense-pleasures, whose threefold action is pure, who is not overcome by anger, who is devoted to virtue, who is immovable in the Dharma, whose vision of reality is profound, and who yearns for enlightenment—such indeed is a bodhisattva. (MSA 19.64)
By this, the characteristic of a bodhisattva is elucidated through the practice of the six perfections and the aspiration for great enlightenment:

"Desiring to benefit others, having a view that does not harm, and enduring injuries from others; steadfast, vigilant, and learned—one who is indeed devoted to the welfare of others is a bodhisattva. (AMsa 19.65)

19.65 Commentary: In this context, "steadfast" means one who has initiated vigor because he does not despond in the face of sufferings; "heedful" means one who is unattached to the pleasures of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). The remainder of the meaning is already explained.
A Bodhisattva is indeed one who recognizes the dangers in his own possessions, is unattached to enjoyments, does not conceal his enmity,
is skilled in signs, free from wrong views, and established within the internal self.
In that regard, one who is unattached to enjoyments renounces the world after abandoning them;
one is skilled in signs due to proficiency in the three signs such as calm abiding (*śamatha*);
and one is inwardly established because of being unshakable from the Mahāyāna.
For the Mahāyāna is the internal [domain] of the bodhisattvas;
the rest has its meaning already explained.
Endowed with compassion and established in the quality of moral shame, one endures suffering and remains unattached to one's own pleasures.
Preeminent in mindfulness, with a well-composed mind, the Bodhisattva is indeed unshakeable in his vehicle.
In that regard, one who possesses meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) has mindfulness as primary, because the mind is concentrated through the power of mindfulness; such a person,
with a well-concentrated self, possesses non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpajñāna*).
The rest has been explained.
The Bodhisattva indeed does not remove suffering, nor does he cause suffering; he does not endure suffering, nor is he afraid of suffering.
He is liberated from suffering, yet he does not conceptualize it as suffering, for he has truly embraced suffering. (AMsa 19.68)
In that regard, "liberated from suffering" means being free from the state of suffering-as-suffering through detachment from the desire realm by means of possessing meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
"Accepting suffering" refers to the acceptance of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
The remainder has its meaning already explained.

Delighting in the Dharma and not delighting in what is non-Dharma, not delighting in the Dharma and delighting in what is non-Dharma by nature, loathing [evil] through the Dharma, devoted to the Dharma, masterful in the Dharma, free from darkness regarding the Dharma, and having the Dharma as his primary concern— such indeed is a Bodhisattva.
In that regard, he is one who loathes unwholesome states because of his loathing for non-forbearance; he is one who has mastery over the Dharma through meditative attainment;
he is one for whom the Dharma is paramount, with great enlightenment as his ultimate goal.
In this context, *dharma* alone is referred to as *dharama* for the sake of following established usage;
the rest has already been explained.
One should be heedful regarding enjoyments, heedful regarding restraints, heedful regarding protection, and heedful regarding wholesome qualities.
A Bodhisattva is indeed heedful regarding happiness, heedful regarding the Dharma, and heedful regarding the vehicle.
In that regard, he is heedful in protection because he guards the minds of both himself and others;
he is heedful regarding the Dharma through his knowledge of phenomena as they truly are.
The rest has already been explained.
A Bodhisattva is indeed one who feels shame regarding contempt, shame regarding minor faults, shame regarding impatience, shame regarding decline,
shame regarding extensive distraction, shame regarding narrow vision, and shame regarding other vehicles.
In that regard, one who is ashamed of contempt does not treat those who seek [help] with disdain; one who is ashamed of slight faults perceives dread even in the most minute transgressions;
and one who is ashamed of slight views has penetrated the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
The remainder has already been explained.
By all these verses, the characteristic of a bodhisattva is illuminated through another formulation: by means of the practice of the six perfections and the vow for great enlightenment;
and here [in this life] as well as in the next, through equanimity, the application of formative forces, and the attainment of masteries.
The Bodhisattva abides in the act of benefiting others through the teaching of tranquility and complete peace, which yields great fruit.
In this very life, one acts for the benefit of sentient beings through giving;
in the next life, having attained a distinguished rebirth through ethical discipline;
and through the application of formative forces—that is, through the application of vigor.
"By means of the great fruit"—that is, by means of Buddhahood.
The remainder has its meaning already explained.
By this, it is illuminated how a bodhisattva proceeds in the service of benefiting sentient beings through the six perfections and the aspiration for great enlightenment.
In the analysis of the general names of a Bodhisattva, there are eight verses:
A Bodhisattva, a Mahāsattva, the Wise One, and one of supreme splendor; The Son of the Victor, the Support of the Victor, the Conqueror, and the Sprout of the Victor. (AMsa 19.73)
He is valiant, most wonderful, a caravan leader of great renown;
he is compassionate, possessed of great merit, a lord, and likewise righteous.
These sixteen are the names of all bodhisattvas in their general sense.

By means of the awakening to the reality of the teachings (*sūtatvabodha*), the awakening to the great purpose (*sumahārthabodha*), the awakening to all purposes (*sarvārthabodha*), as well as the constant awakening (*nityabodha*),
and the awakening to skillful means (*upāyabodha*)— through these specific causes, one is called a *bodhisattva*.
One is called a "bodhisattva" by virtue of fivefold distinctions in awakening:
through the awakening to the selflessness of persons;
through the awakening to all objects in all their aspects; and through inexhaustible realization even while manifesting parinirvāṇa.

Because of this awakening to the means of discipline according to their respective types— due to the awakening to the self, the awakening to the subtle view, the awakening to the various representations,
and the awakening to all unreal conceptualization— for that reason he is called a "Bodhisattva."

Furthermore, here he demonstrates a fourfold distinction in awakening: through the awakening to mind (*citta*), mentation (*manas*), and discernment (*vijñāna*), and through the realization that these are unreal mental constructions (*abhūtaparikalpa*). In this context, "mind" refers to the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
The mind has that as its object and is associated with the view of self and so forth;
consciousness consists of the six groups of consciousness, [distinguished] by non-awakening and awakening, subsequent awakening and awakening, awakening to non-existence and awakening to origination.
And because of the awakening to non-awakening and the subsequent realization, for that reason he is called a bodhisattva.
Here, moreover, he demonstrates five kinds of distinctions in awakening:
through the awakening to ignorance and through the awakening to knowledge.
And because of the awakening to the three natures, beginning with the imagined;

therein, through the awakening to reality (*avabodhatvena*), one should understand the awakening to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) as the awakening to enlightenment (*bodhi-pratibodha*).
This is due to the awakening to the non-existent, the awakening to the ultimate truth, the awakening to everything, and the awakening to all objects.
Because of his awakening to that which is to be awakened, the basis of awakening, and awakening itself—for this reason he is called a Bodhisattva.
(MSA 175) Here, he demonstrates five kinds of distinction in awakening:
because of the awakening to the characteristic of the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*).
Because of the awakening that is fully perfected;
because of the awakening to all objects of knowledge in all their aspects;
and because of the awakening to enlightenment through the awakening to the purity of the three spheres.
Because of the awakening to perfection, the awakening to the stages, the awakening to the womb, the awakening to the gradual manifestation,
and the awakening that thoroughly eliminates doubt— for these reasons, one is called a bodhisattva.
In that context, "awakening to perfection" is Buddhahood;
"awakening to the place" is that by which he dwells in the Tuṣita heaven;
"awakening to the womb" is that by which he descends into his mother's womb.
In the *Kramadarśana*, there is the awakening by which he displays the departure from the womb, the enjoyment of desires, the renunciation, the practice of austerities, and the perfect enlightenment;
the awakening that thoroughly eliminates doubt, by which he turns the wheel of Dharma for sentient beings in order to cut through all their doubts;
and [the one who is] both a possessor and a non-possessor, established in wisdom, the awakener, the follower of the awakening, and the teacher.
The wise one possesses a non-discursive intellect, has destroyed pride yet appears proud, and possesses both immature and mature understanding.
Here, the bodhisattva is elucidated by means of eleven kinds of awakening, beginning with that which pertains to the past and so forth.
Among these, he is respectively one who has attained [awakening], one who has not attained it, and one whose intellect is established [in the path] by means of the past, future, and present;
and he is an awakener through his own self-awakening.
"One who understands from another" indicates internal and external awakening by this [phrase].
"One who instructs" refers to the coarse and subtle [levels of] cognition, being free from discursive speech.
"The proud one" and "the one whose pride is destroyed" refer to the inferior and the sublime [levels].
And "having both immature and mature intelligence" indicates understanding that is distant and near.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, on Qualities, in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
[The twentieth and twenty-first chapters follow.]
Regarding the classification of the marks, there are two verses:
Compassion, speaking kindly, steadfastness, open-handedness, and the unraveling of profound intentional meanings— these are the marks of the wise.
The fivefold mark should be understood in terms of: embracing [the teaching], attaining resolute faith, being free from weariness, the twofold inclusion, and both intention and application.
Therein, by the first verse he shows the five marks of a bodhisattva;
by the second, their activity and a summary of their inclusion.

In this context, compassion is for the sake of embracing sentient beings through the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*); pleasant speech is for the sake of causing sentient beings to attain faith in the Buddha's teaching;

fortitude is for the sake of being untiring despite difficult practices and the like; open-handedness and the unraveling of profound intentional meanings are for the sake of gathering [beings] by means of the two, namely material gifts and the Dharma, respectively.
Among these five marks, compassion is to be understood as pertaining to one's underlying intention (*āśaya*),
while the remaining ones pertain to one's application (*prayoga*).
There are three verses concerning the distinction between the factions of householders and renunciants.
For Bodhisattvas, constantly becoming universal monarchs (cakravartin),
indeed accomplish the welfare of sentient beings as householders throughout all their births.
The going forth obtained through formal adoption is supreme as it accords with the nature of reality;
and for the wise, this going forth serves as a demonstration throughout all the stages.
The side of the one who has gone forth is indeed endowed with immeasurable qualities;
for that reason, the ascetic is superior to the lay bodhisattva.

By this verse, it is illuminated in what kind of householder state a bodhisattva remains while acting for the benefit of sentient beings; by the second [verse], it is shown in what kind of renunciant state [he does so].
In that regard, renunciation should be understood as being threefold.
It is obtained through formal undertaking,
obtained through the nature of phenomena,
and it is demonstrative by means of emanations.
By the third [verse], the distinction between the side of householders and the side of those who have gone forth is elucidated.
Regarding the analysis of resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), there is a verse of six lines:
"The desire for a desired fruit in the next world, and likewise in this very life, for virtuous conduct..."
And the aspiration for nirvāṇa among the wise is held to be their intention toward sentient beings;
it is considered impure, pure, and utterly pure throughout all the stages.
By this, the fivefold resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) has been briefly elucidated:
the resolute intention for happiness;

the resolute intention for welfare, which is the desire for desirable fruits in the future life; the resolute intention for the engagement in wholesome deeds in this very life; the resolute intention for nirvāṇa; and it should be understood that there is no other [resolute intention] apart from these two [latter] intentions.

The three superior intentions, beginning with the impure, should be understood as belonging respectively to those who have not yet entered the stages, those who have entered the stages, and those who have attained the stage of non-retrogression.

Regarding the analysis of embracing [beings], there is this verse: The embracing by the wise on all stages occurs through aspiration, through equanimity, through sovereignty, and through the drawing in of the multitude. (AMsa 20–21.7)

The fourfold appropriation of sentient beings by bodhisattvas should be understood as follows: first, appropriation through aspiration, because all sentient beings are embraced by means of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*); second, appropriation through equanimity, because at the time of clear realization one attains the equality of self and others;
and third, appropriation through sovereignty, which belongs to those for whom he has become the master.
And there is the drawing in and gathering of a retinue through the acceptance of a group of disciples.
Regarding the classification of rebirth, there is this verse:
"By the sovereignty of karma, and another by that of the vow."
The arising of both meditative concentration and mastery is held by the wise to belong to the intelligent ones.

The rebirth of bodhisattvas is fourfold: that which occurs through the sovereignty of karma, whereby those established on the stage of practice through aspiration (adhimukticaryābhūmi) are born in their intended place by the power of karma; and that which occurs through the power of a vow (praṇidhāna), whereby those who have entered the stages (bhūmi) take birth in inferior states such as among animals for the sake of maturing all sentient beings.
Through the sovereignty of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there is rebirth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) after having turned back from the dhyānas;
through the sovereignty of mastery (*vibhutva*), there is the manifestation of rebirths such as in the Tuṣita heaven by means of emanations (*nirmāṇa*).
There are thirty verses in the section on the distinction between the dwellings and the stages (*vihāra-bhūmi-vibhāga*).
The dwelling and the stage itself are defined by their characteristics, by the person, by the signs of the accomplishment of the aggregate of training, by etymology, and by attainment.
There are five verses concerning the classification of the characteristics:
"Emptiness, the supreme self, the persistence of karma even when it has perished, dwelling in meditative absorptions with ease, and thereafter birth in the realm of desire. (AMsa 20–21.10)
And then there is the dedication of the factors conducive to enlightenment toward cyclic existence,
and the ripening of sentient beings without mental affliction.
Furthermore, there is the intentional protection of defilement regarding rebirth;
this is the path that adheres to the single way, the path that is exclusively signless.
Even in the signless state there is effortlessness, as well as the purification of the field;
thereafter, the perfection of the ripening of sentient beings arises.
The purity of the concentrations, the dhāraṇīs, and awakening itself—
through this very establishment, the characteristics of the stages (bhūmis) are to be understood.
There are eleven dwellings, which are the eleven stages (*bhūmi*).
Their characteristics are as follows:
in the first stage, the characteristic is the realization of supreme emptiness, due to the realization of the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*).
The determination regarding the non-destruction of the second [type of] actions arises from the knowledge of the variety of the paths of wholesome and unwholesome karma and their results.
In the third, having dwelt in the bodhisattva meditations characterized by superior bliss, one is reborn in the desire realm without falling away from those very meditations.
In the fourth, even for one who frequently dwells in the factors conducive to awakening, there is the dedication of those factors conducive to awakening toward cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).

On the fifth [ground], by dwelling extensively in the four noble truths, one brings sentient beings to maturity through the composition of various treatises and arts, without mental affliction caused by pride.
