On the sixth [ground], by dwelling extensively in the non-arising of dependent origination, one protects against affliction while intentionally taking birth in existence.

On the seventh stage, through the state of being mixed and thoroughly blended, there is the path exclusively devoted to the signless (*animitta*), which adheres to the path of single progression (*ekāyanapatha*) that was previously unadhered to.

On the eighth stage, even within the signless, there is effortlessness (*anābhoga*), because one dwells in the signless without volitional construction (*nirabhisaṃskāra*); furthermore, there is the purification of the Buddha-field.
On the ninth stage, through mastery over the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), there is the perfection of maturing sentient beings, due to the capacity to mature them in all their aspects.
On the tenth [stage], there is the purification of the gateways of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the gateways of mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇī*).

On the eleventh, the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*), there is the purification of awakening (*bodhi*), characterized by the abandonment of all obscurations to the knowable (*sarvajñeyāvaraṇa*). Furthermore, concerning the classification of persons established on the stages, there are two verses:
Possessing pure vision and perfectly purified morality, concentrated and with pride dispelled regarding the Dharma;
he has attained awakening in a single moment through the transformation of the distinctions between the continuum, affliction, and purification.
Equanimous, a purifier of the field, skilled in the ripening of sentient beings, and possessed of great supernatural power;
with his body perfected and capable of manifestation, such a Bodhisattva is indeed consecrated.
Ten bodhisattvas are established across the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

On the first stage, they possess pure vision, because they have attained the knowledge that serves as the antidote to the views of persons and phenomena. On the second stage, they possess perfectly pure ethical discipline, because there is an absence of even the slightest occurrence of transgressions or lapses.
On the third [stage], one becomes concentrated due to the attainment of the meditative absorption of unshakable dhyāna.
On the fourth, one has eliminated pride regarding phenomena (*dharmavibhūtamāna*), because pride concerning the diversity of phenomena such as the Sūtras and so forth has been eliminated.

On the fifth, one is free from discrimination regarding the continuum of beings (*saṃtānabheda*), because through the ten equalities of the purity of mental intention, one enters into the equality of all continua.

On the sixth stage, there is mastery over the distinction between affliction and purification because, by dwelling extensively in dependent origination and suchness, one does not perceive the affliction or purification of suchness through the black and white sides,

based on its intrinsic purity. On the seventh stage, one attains awakening in a single moment because, through the power of dwelling in the signless, one cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment at every moment.

On the eighth [ground], he is equanimous and a purifier of the field because he dwells in the effortless signless state and through his mixed and closely mixed applications, together with the bodhisattvas who have entered the irreversible stage.
On the ninth, as before, he is skilled in maturing sentient beings.
On the tenth bodhisattva ground, the bodhisattva is established as one of great supernatural power due to the attainment of the great superknowledges.
He is established as having a complete body because he is capable of manifesting his physical basis through the radiation of immeasurable gates of samādhi and dhāraṇī;
and he is consecrated in Buddhahood because he receives consecration there from all the Buddhas.
There are five verses concerning the establishment of the training.
Having realized the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) here, one trains further in higher ethics, higher mind, and higher wisdom; yet wisdom has two spheres of activity.

The reality of phenomena (dharmatattva), as well as the very mental activity arising from the ignorance or knowledge thereof, is the objective domain of wisdom; therefore, its establishment occurs on two stages.
The fruit of the trainings and of cultivation is further fourfold:
the first fruit is the dwelling that is signless and yet with effort.
That very absence of volitional effort is held to be the second fruit,
as well as the purification of the field and the ripening of sentient beings.
And the accomplishment of the meditative concentrations and the dhāraṇīs is the supreme fruit;
for these four kinds of fruits are based upon the four stages.
Having realized the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) on the first stage, one trains in higher ethics (*adhiśīla*) on the second;
in higher mind (*adhicitta*) on the third;
and in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*) on the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages.
For wisdom subsumed under the factors conducive to enlightenment exists on the fourth stage;
furthermore, that [wisdom] has a twofold objective domain on two stages.
The "twofold" refers, moreover, to the reality of phenomena (dharmatattva) and the truths of suffering and so forth.

And the process consisting of the knowledge of that [dependent origination] and so forth is the forward-order dependent origination (*anuloma pratītyasamutpāda*). For the process beginning with ignorance of that is the series starting with ignorance (*avidyā*),
while the process beginning with knowledge of that is the series starting with clear knowledge (*vidyā*).
Therefore, the establishment of higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*) occurs in both of these stages.
Beyond this, it should be understood that the fourfold fruit of training (*śikṣāphala*) rests upon four stages respectively.

Among those, the second fruit should be understood as that very same dwelling in the signless (*animitta-vihāra*), which is without volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*), as well as the purification of the field (*kṣetra-śuddhi*).
The remainder has already been explained.
There are two verses concerning the establishment of the aggregates (*skandha*):
"In this world, having realized the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), there is the purification of the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*)."
Thereafter follows the purification of the aggregates of concentration and wisdom.
In the other [stages], there is the purification of the knowledge of liberation and the liberation itself from four kinds of obscurations and also from the obscuration of resistance.
"In the others" refers to the purification of both liberation and the knowledge of liberation throughout the seven stages up to the stage of a Buddha.
Furthermore, that liberation should be understood as being [attained] on the Buddha-stage through the removal of the fourfold obscuration to the fruits and the obscuration of resistance,
by which the knowledge of others is obstructed regarding the objects of knowledge.
The knowledge of the Buddhas is unimpeded everywhere because of that liberation; the rest has its meaning already explained. There are three verses concerning the establishment of perfection.
All the stages (bhūmi) should be understood as both unaccomplished and accomplished;
furthermore, even those that are accomplished are considered to be both unaccomplished and accomplished.
Accomplishment is to be understood through mental attention according to the established order,
through the knowledge that it is a conceptual construction, and through the non-conceptualization of that very [construction].
Cultivation is also accomplishment, which is inconceivable on all stages because it is to be personally realized and because it is the domain of the Buddhas.
In this context, the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*) is unperfected, while the remaining stages are perfected; thus, all these stages are [categorized as] perfected.
Furthermore, among those that are perfected, the first seven are unperfected, while the remainder are perfected because they proceed without effortful conditioning (*nirabhisaṃskāravāhitva*).

Furthermore, regarding the perfection of the stages beginning with the Joyous (pramuditā) that was previously mentioned, that perfection is to be understood through the mental attention (*manasikāra*) directed toward the stages as they have been established.
And it should be known as non-conceptualization (*avikalpanā*) because of the knowledge that the establishment of those stages is merely conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātra*).
This occurs when one knows that the establishment of those stages is merely conceptual construction.

Furthermore, that is merely a conceptual construction and does not itself conceptualize; thus, through the attainment of non-conceptual knowledge regarding the grasped and the grasper, the perfection of the stages (*bhūmi*) is said to occur.
Moreover, both the cultivation and the perfection of the stages are inconceivable throughout all the stages.
For they are to be personally realized by Bodhisattvas and are the domain of the Buddhas, not of others.
Regarding the classification of the signs of one established on the stages, there are two verses:
"Indeed, resolute belief accompanied by light is held to be the sign in all cases;
as well as lack of despondency, absence of dejection, and the state of not being dependent on others. (MSA 20–21.27)
Penetration everywhere, equanimity toward all,
freedom from being led astray or partiality, knowledge of skillful means, and birth within the mandala.
Ten kinds of signs of a bodhisattva who has entered these stages (bhūmi) are to be understood across all the stages.
The first sign is that there is illumination regarding the stage he has entered, while there is resolute conviction (adhimukti) regarding the stage he has not yet entered.
The second is the absence of dejection with respect to dharmas that are supremely vast and profound.
It consists of non-dejection in the performance of difficult practices;
independence from others regarding one's own stage;
penetration of all stages through skill in their accomplishment; and the state of mind that regards all sentient beings as equal to oneself.
It is "inflexible" by virtue of the words "praise" and "blame";

it is "without attachment" toward the attainment of [positions such as] a universal monarch (cakravartin) and so forth; and it is "skill in means" because it is the knowledge of the means for attaining Buddhahood through non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).
And rebirth at all times within the circles of the Buddha’s assemblies—these are further signs of a bodhisattva.
Regarding the analysis of the signs of attaining the perfections on the stages, there are two verses:

He has no lack of aspiration, nor is he greedy or small-hearted; he is not prone to anger, nor is he lazy; his disposition is not devoid of loving-kindness and compassion, nor is he possessed of evil intellect ruined by conceptual constructions and discursive thoughts.

One whose mind is not distracted by pleasures, nor struck down by sufferings, does not turn back when relying on a true friend—one who is devoted to sacred learning and intent on honoring the Teacher.

Having performed a vast accumulation of all merit and dedicated it toward supreme enlightenment in common with others, he who knows the supreme means day by day is born in his own proper sphere, always performing what is auspicious, sporting with the qualities of the superknowledges; standing above all, he should be known as a treasury of virtues belonging to the nature of a Buddha.
It demonstrates the sixteenfold mark of a bodhisattva who has attained the ten perfections.
The sixteenfold mark consists of:
being never devoid of the desire to practice the perfections; [and so forth].
Each [perfection] is characterized by being free from its respective opposite;
by non-distraction through mental attention toward other vehicles;
and by non-attachment to the pleasures of prosperity.
It is not turned back from application by the sufferings of misfortune or difficult practices;
it relies upon spiritual friends;
it is devoted to learning and devoted to honoring the Teacher.
Right dedication is through the perfection of skillful means;
birth in a favorable realm is through the perfection of aspiration, because of being born in a place not devoid of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
and constant performance of the wholesome is through the perfection of power, because of the non-intermixture of factors adverse to it.
And there is the play with the qualities of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) through the perfection of gnosis (*jñānapāramitā*).

In this context, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the antidote to malice (*vyāpāda*), characterized by the intention to bestow happiness. Compassion (*karuṇā*) is the antidote to harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*), characterized by the intention to remove suffering.
The conceptualization of intrinsic nature is *kalpa*;
the conceptualization of specific qualities is to be understood as *vikalpa*. Regarding that very [topic], there is a verse in the section on the analysis of benefits:
In both calm abiding and insight, the benefit for the wise is considered to consist of two groups of five, in every respect and on all stages.
In that very attainment of the perfections, the benefit for Bodhisattvas across all stages should be understood as being of five kinds:
at every moment, it dissolves the basis of all functional rigidity (*dausthulya*).
He attains the departure from the perception of diversity and finds delight in the garden of the Dharma;
he perceives the illumination of the Dharma as immeasurable and of an undifferentiated form in every respect; and non-conceptual signs conducive to purification manifest before him.
And for the sake of the complete fulfillment and perfection of the *dharmakāya*, one undertakes the gathering of causes that are progressively higher and higher.
Among these, the first and second should be understood as belonging to the side of *śamatha*,
while the third and fourth belong to the side of *vipaśyanā*.
The remainder applies to both sides.
There are nine verses in the analysis of the etymology of the stages (*bhūmi*).
For those who see that enlightenment is near and that the welfare of sentient beings is being accomplished—
Intense joy arises; therefore, it is called *muditā* (sympathetic joy).
Nothing further needs to be explained here;
this stage is called "The Stainless" because it is free from the impurity of the application of immoral conduct.

It is called "The Stainless" (*Vimalā*) because it transcends immorality, indolence, mental attention to other vehicles, and the very state of indolence. Furthermore, it is called "The Radiant" (*Prabhākarī*) because of the statement, "Therefore, since we are equal in our realization, we must apply ourselves to the realization of purification in all its aspects," and because it produces the great illumination of the Dharma.
For in that stage, by the power of meditative concentration, because of the seeking and retaining of immeasurable dharmas, one produces a great illumination of the Dharma for others.
Since the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas) are like flames—
being burners— it is called the "Radiant" (arciṣmatī) stage because of its connection with them, due to the burning away of duality.
That wisdom, consisting of the factors conducive to enlightenment, is predominantly present as the burning away of duality.
Furthermore, "duality" here should be understood as the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obscuration of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
It also consists of the maturing of sentient beings and the protection of one’s own mind.
The wise conquer suffering; therefore, it is called "difficult to conquer."

Therein, although he is devoted to the maturation of sentient beings, he is not defiled by their hostility; and both of these are difficult to conquer because of their difficulty. Because of the presence here of both cyclic existence and nirvana, [he remains undaunted].
For it has been said that the stage of "Facing" (Abhimukhī) arises from its reliance upon the perfection of wisdom.

For, by relying on the perfection of wisdom, because it does not abide in either nirvāṇa or saṃsāra, this stage is considered "Far-Gone" (*dūraṅgamā*) as it faces both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa due to its proximity to the path of the single way (*ekāyanapatha*).
The path of the single way was previously explained; because of its proximity to that, it has gone far, owing to having reached the culmination of application.
And it is called "Immovable" (acalā) because of the non-fluctuation of the two types of perception.
Because one does not waver from two types of perception— namely, the perception of signs and the perception of effortless non-signification—
and because of the excellence of the intellect that possesses the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), this stage is considered "Excellent Intelligence" (*Sādhumatī*).

Because the wisdom of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) is excellent, it is the primary [stage]. It is called the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*) because it pervades the space of the Dharma in two ways, like a cloud.

Because of the pervasion of the two, [this stage] is called the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*); for, like a cloud, it pervades the entrance to meditative absorption (*samādhimukha*) and the entrance to mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇīmukha*), which are situated within the basis of the heard Dharma as if filling the expanse of space.
Because they always dwell with delight in the accomplishment of various kinds of virtue, the stages of the bodhisattvas are considered to be their "dwelling places" (*vihāra*).
Because they always dwell with delight everywhere for the sake of accomplishing various forms of virtue, the stages (*bhūmi*) of the bodhisattvas are called "abodes" (*vihāra*).
Furthermore, because they proceed ever higher through these immeasurable [stages],
and for the sake of the welfare of beings who are immeasurable and fearless, these very stages are indeed desired as "grounds" (*bhūmi*).

Because they involve ascending further and further through these immeasurable states for the sake of the infinite beings who are without fear, those very dwellings are again called "stages" (*bhūmi*).
"Immeasurable" refers to the fact that each one among the ten stages is itself immeasurable.
"Because they involve ascending further" means because they involve proceeding to the higher stages.
"For the sake of beings, for the immeasurable, and for fearlessness" means for the sake of eliminating the fear of immeasurable beings.
There is a verse regarding the abiding in attainment:
"Because of the acquisition of the stages, because of resolute conviction, and because of proceeding in the practices."
And it is fourfold by way of the penetration of the stages and their accomplishment.
The attainment of the stages is fourfold:
the attainment through resolute belief, which occurs on the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukticaryā-bhūmi*) by virtue of the aforementioned resolute belief;
and the attainment through conduct, which occurs on that very same stage by engaging in the ten religious practices (*dharmacarita*).
And there is the attainment of perfection through the penetration of the ultimate truth upon entering the stages (*bhūmi*),
and through entering the irreversible stage (*avinivartanīya-bhūmi*).
Regarding the classification of conduct (*caryā-vibhāga*), there is a verse of six lines:
For the sake of attracting those embodied beings who are devoted to the Mahāyāna and those who are [devoted] to the Hīnayāna, and for their discipline,
the four practices of the wise have been taught according to the Sūtras.
Therein, the practice of the perfections (pāramitācaryā) was taught for the sake of those who have faith in the Mahāyāna;
the practice of the bodhisattva (bodhisatvacaryā) for those who have faith in the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
and the practice of the supernormal powers (abhijñācaryā) for both those with faith in the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna, for the purpose of attracting them through miraculous power.
The practice for maturing sentient beings is for the sake of maturing these two [the bodhisattva and the sentient being] themselves; for here, "maturing" is taught as "disciplining.
Regarding the classification of the qualities of a Buddha, there are many verses.
In the analysis of the immeasurables, there is one verse beginning with that hymn of praise to the Buddha:

O you who have compassion for sentient beings, whose intention is their union [with happiness] and separation [from suffering], whose intention is their non-separation [from happiness], and whose intention is their welfare and bliss—homage be to you! (AMsa 20–21.43)
Compassion toward sentient beings has been demonstrated;
furthermore, the intention for their happiness is shown through loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which is the intention for their union with happiness,
and through compassion (*karuṇā*), which is the intention for their separation from suffering.
And through sympathetic joy (*muditā*), there is the intention not to be separated from happiness;
through equanimity (*upekṣā*), there is the intention for welfare. Furthermore, that [equanimity] should be understood as characterized by the intention for the absence of afflictions (*niḥkleśatā*).
Regarding the classification of the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), there is this verse:
O Sage, liberated from all obscurations, you who have overcome the entire world; your knowledge pervades all that is to be known. O you of liberated mind, homage be to you! (AMsa 20–21.44)
Here, he demonstrates the excellence of the Blessed One’s liberations through his freedom from all afflictive and cognitive obscurations;

the excellence of his bases of mastery through his sovereignty over his own mind by virtue of mastering the entire world, which consists in the empowerment of manifesting and transforming objects at will;
and the excellence of his totalities through the unimpeded nature of his knowledge regarding all that is knowable.
For this very reason, because he is liberated from the factors adverse to qualities such as the liberations, his mind is liberated (*muktacitta*).
There is a verse in the *Araṇāvibhāga*:
"O destroyer of all afflictions of all sentient beings without exception!"
O destroyer of afflictions, yet compassionate toward those afflicted—homage be to you!

In this context, he demonstrates the Blessed One’s complete absence of hindrances through his subduing of the afflictions of all sentient beings; furthermore, even toward those in whom afflictions have arisen, he manifests compassion for afflicted persons by prescribing the remedies for those very afflictions.
For other practitioners who dwell in the state of non-contention (*araṇā*) merely remove the conditions for the arising of some particular affliction in sentient beings that takes them as its object;
they do not, however, extract it from the continuum of the afflictions.

There is a verse concerning the excellence of the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*): Homage be to you, who are effortless, unattached, unimpeded, and always in meditative equipoise; you who provide answers to all questions at all times! (AMsa 20–21.46)
Here, he demonstrates the excellence of the Blessed One’s knowledge resulting from his vow through five aspects:
by way of its manifestation without effort,
and by way of its manifestation without attachment.
Because there is no obstruction regarding all that is to be known,
because he is always in a state of meditative equipoise,
and because he cuts through all the doubts of sentient beings.
For others indeed bring forth the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*),
yet it is not unattached because it depends upon entering meditative attainments (*samāpatti*),
nor is it unimpeded because it is a knowledge limited to specific regions.
Furthermore, they are not always in a state of meditative concentration,
nor do they sever all doubts. There is a verse regarding the analysis of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*):
O Excellent Teacher, whose wisdom is ever unimpeded regarding the basis and that which is based upon it, as well as the teaching and the knowledge that instructs— homage be to you!

In this regard, in brief, the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of the Blessed One are taught by virtue of his possessing an intellect that is eternally unimpeded with respect to both that which is taught and that by which it is taught.
Therein, two things are taught: the phenomenon (*dharma*) as the basis, and the meaning (*artha*) as that which is based upon it.
It is taught by means of two: by speech and by knowledge.
Through the quality of being a good teacher, their activity is demonstrated.
There is a verse in the analysis of the supernormal powers (abhijñā):

Having approached with words that accord with their conduct, knowing their coming and going, and providing instruction for the sake of beings regarding the state of being devoid of essence— homage be to you!

Here, the Blessed One’s state of providing correct instruction is demonstrated by means of the six higher knowledges (*abhijñā*): by approaching the presence of those to be trained through the higher knowledge of supernatural power (*ṛddhyabhijñā*);

by knowing their speech through the higher knowledge of the divine ear (*divyaśrotrābhijñā*); and by knowing the course of their mental conduct through the higher knowledge of the penetration of others' minds (*cetaḥparyāyābhijñā*), as well as how they have come here from the past limit and how they are to be led out from cyclic existence.
Therein, he gives instruction by means of the remaining superknowledges (*abhijñā*) in their proper order.
Regarding the distinction between the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and the secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*), there is this verse:
"Upon seeing you, all embodied beings attain the state of true manhood."
Homage be to you, who brings about serene faith by the mere sight of you.

Here, the function of the primary marks and secondary characteristics is demonstrated as being the producer of serene confidence through the mere sight [of them], by virtue of the conviction that the Blessed One is a Great Person (*mahāpuruṣa*).
Regarding the analysis of purity, there is this verse:
"In taking up, abiding, and relinquishing; in emanation and transformation..."
Homage be to you, who have attained mastery over meditative concentration and gnosis.
Here, by means of the fourfold mastery of the Blessed One, the four kinds of purification in all their aspects are fully elucidated:
purification of the basis through mastery over the taking up, remaining, and casting off of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*);
and purification of the objective field through mastery over emanation and transformation.
Purity of mind through mastery over all forms of meditative concentration;
purity of wisdom through mastery over all forms of knowledge.
There is a verse concerning the classification of the powers:
Homage to you, the crusher of Māra, who dispels the delusions of sentient beings regarding the means, the refuge, purity, the Mahāyāna, and the final departure.
In this regard, the activity of the Blessed One’s ten powers is demonstrated by way of shattering Māra’s method of deceiving sentient beings regarding four matters; namely:
deceiving them concerning the means for going to good or bad rebirths and so forth;
and deceiving them concerning taking refuge in gods and others when there is no true refuge.
Regarding the denial of purity based on mere mundane purity,
and the denial of the departure via the Mahāyāna:
it should be understood that the Blessed One is the destroyer of Māra in the first sense by virtue of his power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible.
By the power of knowledge regarding the ripening of karma, in the second;
by the power of knowledge regarding the meditations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments, in the third;
and by the power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties and so forth, in the fourth.
Because he avoids inferior faculties and the like, and because he applies [beings] to the superior,
there is a verse concerning the analysis of the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*): "O Teacher of knowledge, abandonment, the path of departure, and the obstacles!"
Homage be to you, who are invincible against the followers of other paths in matters concerning the welfare of both yourself and others.

In this context, the fourfold fearlessness of the Blessed One is manifested respectively as follows: with respect to his own welfare, by virtue of being the one who effects knowledge and abandonment; and with respect to the welfare of others, by virtue of being the teacher who points out the path of deliverance and its obstacles; and because he cannot be assailed by any other non-Buddhist teachers.
Regarding the analysis of the foundations of mindfulness as protection, there is this verse:
O you who speak with confidence in assemblies, free from the two-fold affliction, without need for protection, unerring, and the attractor of the assembly—homage be to you! (AMsa 20-21.53)
By this, the Blessed One’s three ways of non-protection and the three foundations of mindfulness are elucidated;
their function is that of leading a community.
For, by means of these, he respectively becomes one who speaks without hesitation in assemblies due to his lack of need for protection.
He is free from the two-fold affliction because of the absence of attachment and aversion;
and he is characterized by constant and abundant abiding mindfulness due to his state of non-forgetfulness.
Regarding the analysis of the total eradication of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), there is this verse:
In movement and in rest, everywhere there is no action that is not that of an omniscient one; O Omniscient One, you who always perceive the true meaning—homage be to you!

By this, it is demonstrated that because there is no non-omniscient activity whatsoever at any time or in any state—whether in motion or at rest—the Blessed One has utterly eradicated all latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) of the afflictions.

For one who is not omniscient, even if their afflictions have been exhausted, because the latent predispositions have not been eradicated, they might at some time encounter a mad elephant or a mad chariot; such is the behavior of one who is not omniscient.
It acts as stated in the Māṇḍavyasūtra;
however, that omniscience regarding the nature of reality does not exist [in such a person].
Regarding the analysis of non-forgetfulness, there is this verse:
In all deeds for the benefit of sentient beings, you do not let the proper time pass by;
your activity is never in vain and you are ever non-forgetful—homage be to you! (AMsa 20–21.55)

By this, it is shown that because the Blessed One does not let the proper time pass—the time when whatever benefit is to be performed for whichever sentient being is required—his duty is always fruitful; thus, his nature of non-forgetfulness is demonstrated both by way of its intrinsic nature and its activity. There is a verse in the analysis of great compassion:
Six times throughout every day and night, you survey the entire world;
endowed with great compassion and intent on the welfare [of others], homage be to you!
Here, the Great Compassion of the Blessed One is elucidated both by way of its function and its intrinsic nature.
For by means of Great Compassion, the Blessed One surveys the world six times during the day and night, [considering] "Who is declining? Who is prospering? and so forth.
And through its application, the Blessed One possesses a constant intention for the welfare of all sentient beings.

Regarding the analysis of the unique qualities (āveṇikaguṇa), there is this verse: In conduct, in realization, in knowledge, and in activity—homage be to You, the supreme among all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas! (AMsa 20–21.57)
In this regard, there are six unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) comprised within conduct, six comprised within realization,
and three comprised within gnosis.
And by means of the three qualities subsumed under karma,
his status as the supreme among all sentient beings is illuminated through his superiority even over those other excellent beings, namely the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
In this regard, there is no lapse in the Tathāgata.
There is no outcry;
there is no loss of mindfulness;
there is no unconcentrated mind.
There is no perception of diversity;
there is no equanimity lacking discernment—these are the six unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) included within his conduct, which belong to the Buddha alone and not to others.
There is no decline in zeal, nor is there any decline in vigor, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, or liberation—these are the six [qualities] included within his realization.
"The Tathāgata’s unattached and unimpeded knowledge regarding the past;
the Tathāgata’s unattached and unimpeded knowledge regarding the future and the present.
These three are subsumed under knowledge.
All the bodily actions of the Tathāgata are preceded by knowledge and follow after knowledge;
likewise for all vocal actions and all mental actions— these three are comprised within action.
A verse on the analysis of the knowledge of all aspects:
O you who have attained great enlightenment in all its forms through the three bodies, who cuts away the doubts of all sentient beings everywhere—homage be to you! (AMsa 20–21.58)

By this, the Blessed One’s omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) is fully elucidated, because he has attained awakening in all its aspects through the three bodies (*kāya*), and because he possesses knowledge of all aspects regarding all that is to be known.
The three bodies are the essential (*svābhāvika*), the enjoyment (*sāṃbhogika*), and the emanation (*nairmāṇika*).
Furthermore, the knowledge of all aspects regarding all that is to be known is here indicated by the activity of severing all doubts of all sentient beings, including gods, humans, and others.

In the section on the analysis of the fulfillment of the perfections, there is this verse: O you who are unrestrained, faultless, stainless, and non-abiding; O you who are unshakable regarding all phenomena and free from conceptual proliferation—homage be to you!
By this, the Blessed One’s fulfillment of the six perfections is manifested through his liberation from all factors adverse to the six perfections.
In that regard, "absence of grasping" is to be understood as the non-clinging to enjoyments;
"faultlessness" is due to his bodily and other actions being free from stain.
Freedom from turbidity is due to not allowing the mind to become turbid by worldly conditions or suffering.
Lack of fixity is due to not remaining settled upon the attainment of merely a small degree of obscuration.
Immovability is due to the absence of distraction.
It is the state of being free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañcatva*) because of the non-occurrence of all conceptual proliferations of discursive thought.
Regarding the analysis of the characteristics of a Buddha, there are two verses:
"You have perfected the ultimate reality and have emerged from all the stages."
He has attained supremacy over all sentient beings and is the liberator of all sentient beings.
Endowed with inexhaustible and peerless qualities, you are seen in the worlds;
yet even within the maṇḍalas, you are entirely invisible to gods and humans alike.
Here, the characteristic of a Buddha is illuminated by means of six aspects: essence, cause, fruit, activity, endowment, and manifestation.
Among these, purified suchness is the perfected ultimate reality;
and that is the essence of the Buddhas.
The cause is the state of having emerged from all the bodhisattva stages;
the application is the attainment of supremacy over all sentient beings;
and the manifestation is being visible in various world-systems by means of the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

It is said in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, spoken by the Great Bodhisattvas of the Pure Age: "The threefold manifestation of differentiation consists in being visible within the circles of assemblies by means of the enjoyment body (*sāṃbhogika-kāya*), and being invisible in every respect by means of the dharma body (*dharmakāya*)."
The twenty-first chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Foundation of Conduct," is completed;
and thus the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* is finished.
